# Data Center refuses to null a sub-task's `fields.parent` (HTTP 400)

## Provenance

Filed to satisfy [rebar:88d9-fe42-e50f-4067]'s AC11, which pre-authorised this exact outcome:

> UNLESS it reports its explicit `SETUP FAILED` message, which means Data Center refused to null a
> sub-task's `fields.parent`. That is a PLATFORM finding, not this fix failing; record it and file
> it separately rather than weakening the cell.

Observed on harness run **30834117797** (job 91755000385, main @ `25ead49f3e`).

## Evidence — verbatim

> SETUP FAILED (not a rebar defect): Data Center REFUSED to clear the parent of sub-task RBJYRMS-2 —
> BackendHTTPError: HTTP Error 400: JiraError HTTP 400 url:
> http://localhost:2990/jira/rest/api/2/issue/10029

The message came from `test_inbound_clear_parent_round_trips`'s SETUP, not its assertion: the cell could not get Data Center into the precondition state it needed, so it never exercised the code under test. The cell was deliberately built to report this case DISTINCTLY rather than as an ambiguous red, and it did.

## What this does and does not establish

**Does:** DC 8.17.1 rejects a `PUT` that nulls a sub-task's `fields.parent`. A sub-task on DC must have a parent — the field is structurally required — so there is no "detached sub-task" state for the fixture to create.

**Does not:** say anything about whether rebar's inbound parent clear works. That path's evidence is the discriminating trio recorded on 88d9 (measured RED against both wrong states, GREEN against the fix) plus the full 2079-passing suite. The live cell simply cannot reach it on a sub-task.

## Consequence — the inbound clear has no live coverage on DC

This is the honest statement of the gap, and it should not be papered over: the ONLY live cell for the inbound parent clear is blocked by a platform constraint, so on Data Center that path is proven by unit evidence alone. Given that this epic has twice shipped mutation-proven code that was wrong in production (1276, 1288), unit-only coverage of a data-affecting path is a real risk, not a formality.

## Options for restoring live coverage, none yet chosen

 1. Use a NON-sub-task child whose parent is an Epic Link, and clear the epic link instead — a
    different write path (greenhopper sentinel epic `"none"`), so it tests the clear the production
    code would actually take for a non-sub-task.
 2. Assert the refusal itself as the contract: pin that DC rejects the null so a future DC version
    that starts accepting it fails loudly and tells us the coverage gap can be closed.
 3. Accept unit-only coverage for the sub-task clear and record it as a known limit.

Option 1 is the only one that yields real coverage, and it is closest to what a rebar deployment would actually do, since [rebar:1a9f-50c0-e7a5-4fda] casts doubt on the sub-task write path working at all on this version.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] the refusal is confirmed against the target DC version with the raw response body recorded
      (the current evidence is the status code and URL only)
- [x] one of the three options above is chosen, with the rejected ones and the reason recorded
- [x] if option 1 or 2: the cell lands and is GREEN on a live harness run, with the run id recorded
- [x] N/A — option 2 was chosen, not option 3. Condition never held. ~~if option 3: the limitation is documented where a DC operator will see it, not only on a ticket~~
baseline.summary: Data Center refuses to null a sub-task's fields.parent (HTTP 400): the inbound-clear live cell cannot reach its precondition

`rebar transition --help` advertises `[--reason=<text>]` on every transition, but on a plain close the value is parsed, threaded through two call layers, and then discarded. A user closing a ticket with `--reason="..."` reasonably believes the rationale was recorded. It was not.

Evidence:

- `src/rebar/_commands/txn.py:197` — `transition_core(..., close_reason: str = "", ...)`. The name
  appears three times in the file (`:154` is a different symbol, `:197` and `:199` are signatures)
  and is **never read in any body**.
- `src/rebar/_commands/transition.py:130-136` parses `--reason`; `:293-294` shows its only live use
  on a non-force path is `force_reason = (reason or "(no reason given)") if force else ""`, i.e. it
  is meaningful **only** under `--force`. `--force-close=<reason>` carries its own separate value.

## Scope: make the flag honest — do NOT add persistence

An earlier framing of this finding proposed persisting the close reason via the existing comment mechanism. That is rejected. `txn.py:253-259` records the governing decision:

> Bug-close CLASS guard (ticket ed13): a bug closing from a non-idea status now REQUIRES a bounded
> `--class <value>` from the closed vocabulary — REPLACING the old free-text `--reason` (which was
> validated then discarded).

ed13 deliberately replaced free-text close rationale with the bounded `CLOSE_CLASSES` vocabulary, which IS folded onto the `*->closed` STATUS edge and is single-sourced against `common.schema.json#/$defs/close_class`. Re-introducing free text — in any form — reverses a recent, intentional move toward machine-readable close data, and no evidence was found that the decision was wrong. The "why this specific ticket" capability is not missing: `rebar comment <id>` already provides it, it simply is not compulsory, and making it compulsory is what ed13 undid.

Related, already tracked elsewhere — do not duplicate: `bug_close_reason_ok` (`txn.py:154`) is dead with a docstring falsely claiming two consumers; its deletion is covered by ticket `723f-c5b2-d83b-43cb`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `close_reason` is removed from `transition_core`'s signature and every call site that passes it
- [x] `--reason` is documented as applying to the force paths only, in `transition.txt` help, the
      `transition.py` usage string, and any overview/docs line that advertises it more broadly
- [x] Passing `--reason` on a plain (non-force) close either has a documented effect or is refused —
      it must not be silently accepted and dropped
- [x] No change to `--class` / `CLOSE_CLASSES` behaviour, and no new free-text field on any event
- [x] `--force` and `--force-close=<reason>` behaviour is unchanged
baseline.summary: Make transition --reason honest: drop the discarded close_reason, scope the flag to force paths

# A failed identity write DELETES the created Jira issue

## Context / Problem

`dispatch_one.create_one` writes identity markers immediately after `create_issue` succeeds, and on ANY failure in that block it deletes the freshly created issue (`dispatch_one.py:324-328`) and re-raises. Destroying a successfully-created issue to recover from a failure to LABEL it inverts the cost: a created-but-unlabelled issue is recoverable, a deleted one is not.

The trigger is not exotic. Jira rejects a field write with *"Field 'x' cannot be set. It is not on the appropriate screen, or unknown"* in at least three distinct situations, and the message is misleading in roughly half of them: the field genuinely is not on the project's Create/Edit screen; the workflow property `jira.permission.createclone.denied` is set (nothing to do with screens); or the value is MALFORMED on a field that IS on the screen. A self-hosted DC instance with a customised Create screen hits this on the first write.

**A SECOND DEFECT IN THE SAME BLOCK, found while tracing this one and not previously recorded.** The write-ahead records the key BEFORE the identity writes — `record_pending_key(local_id, jira_key)` + `save()` at `dispatch_one.py:307-308`, deliberately inside the try. The rollback then deletes the issue but **never unbinds**, so a KEYED-pending binding survives pointing at a DELETED Jira key. On every subsequent pass `recover_pending`'s keyed branch calls `client.add_label(keyed, …)` on that dead key, raises, is caught into the failure sink, and the entry stays pending — permanently. The ticket never syncs again and each pass re-attempts a doomed write. So the current behaviour does not merely lose an issue; it also strands the local ticket forever. Both symptoms have the same cause and the same fix, so they are handled here rather than split.

## Approach

**Stop deleting. Leave the keyed-pending binding in place and let retro-attach finish the job.**

The recovery path this needs already exists and is already correct: `recover_pending`'s KEYED branch retro-attaches the `rebar-id` label and the `local_id` entity property and then confirms, with **no Jira search** — deterministic, and explicitly documented as such because a crash in the create→label window must not yield a duplicate. A failed identity write leaves exactly the state that branch is built for. The rollback was solving a problem the write-ahead protocol had already solved, and destroying data to do it.

So the change is subtractive: remove the `delete_issue` call, keep the BRIDGE_ALERT (retitled to say the issue was RETAINED for retro-attach, not deleted), keep re-raising `write_err` unmasked so the item is still reported as failed, and leave the binding keyed-pending.

**The one case that is genuinely different: a `BindingPersistError`.** If `record_pending_key` fails to persist, no key was recorded and no label was written, so nothing local points at the issue. The issue is not lost, though — it is an unmarked issue in the project, which the INBOUND pass adopts as a new remote issue on the next run. That is a strictly better outcome than deletion and needs no special handling; it is called out here so the next reader does not add a delete back for that branch.

**Declare the screen requirement rather than solving it.** rebar requires `labels` on the project's Create and Edit screens. The mature precedent is explicit: Sentry's Jira integration states it does NOT support custom required fields — *"The only required fields supported are those that are pre-populated by Sentry"* — with "create the issue in Jira and link it" as the workaround. That is a deliberate scope boundary from the most mature integration in the comparison set.

**Rejected: createmeta-driven pre-flight field discovery.** It would mean implementing DC ≥ 9.0's split `createmeta/{proj}/issuetypes[/{id}]` endpoints with a different response envelope plus version-gating at 9.0 — substantial machinery to predict a failure that the retro-attach path already recovers from once we stop deleting. Explicitly out of scope.

**Rejected: unbinding on rollback.** It would fix the stranded-binding half while keeping the destructive half, and it would re-open the duplicate hazard: an unbound local ticket with a live unlabelled issue in Jira is exactly the state that produces a second issue on the next pass (see [rebar:21fc-51d7-90ca-4a03]).

## Scope

- `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/dispatch_one.py` — remove the rollback delete; retitle the
  BRIDGE_ALERT; leave the binding keyed-pending; improve the error message.
- `docs/user-guide.md` — state the Create/Edit screen requirement for `labels`.
- `tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/` — held-out regression tests (new module).

## Testing

* **the issue survives** — with `add_label` raising, assert `delete_issue` is NEVER called and the
  created key still exists on the client.
* **the binding is left recoverable** — assert the entry is keyed-pending with the created key, then
  run `recover_pending` against a client whose label write now succeeds and assert it CONFIRMS to the
  same key. This is the property that makes not-deleting safe, so it is asserted end-to-end rather
  than by inspecting the entry alone.
* **no duplicate** — a subsequent create pass for the same local ticket creates NOTHING, since the
  binding is now confirmed.
* **the failure is still loud** — `write_err` is re-raised unmasked and the BRIDGE_ALERT is written;
  a retained issue must not read as success.
* **the error message** names the screen requirement AND the two other causes.
* **the persist-failure branch** does not delete either, asserted, since that is the case a future
  reader is most likely to "fix" by restoring the delete.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] a failed identity write NEVER calls `delete_issue`, asserted by a test that fails against the
      current code
- [ ] after a failed identity write the binding is KEYED-pending on the created key, and a subsequent
      `recover_pending` against a recovered client CONFIRMS it to that same key — asserted end-to-end,
      not by inspecting the entry alone
- [ ] a following create pass for that local ticket creates NO second issue
- [ ] the original `write_err` is still re-raised unmasked and a BRIDGE_ALERT is still written, so the
      item is reported failed rather than silently retained
- [ ] the BRIDGE_ALERT text says the issue was RETAINED for retro-attach — it currently claims "Jira
      issue deleted", which would be false after this change
- [ ] the operator-facing error names the Create/Edit screen requirement AND mentions the
      `jira.permission.createclone.denied` workflow property and the malformed-value case, since the
      Jira message is misleading about half the time
- [ ] `docs/user-guide.md` states that `labels` must be on the project's Create and Edit screens
- [ ] the `BindingPersistError` branch also does not delete, asserted
- [ ] createmeta pre-flight is explicitly recorded as OUT of scope with the Sentry precedent
baseline.summary: A failed identity write DELETES the created Jira issue; declare the screen requirement instead

## Context / Problem

The current tests inspect replacement mechanics or final JSON rather than the write window (`test_applier_mapping.py:235-282`, `test_applier_provenance.py:155-185`), permit last-writer record loss (`test_bridge_state_atomic_write_concurrency.py:41-120`), and source-grep impossible-link durability (`test_impossible_links_cicada.py:467-493`). Live sidecars replace full snapshots in `peer_confirmations.py:192-217` and `impossible_links.py:376-401`. The repository already has sibling-file locked read-modify-write prior art in `_store/hlc.py::_hlc_lock` and `_commands/recent_creates.py::_journal_lock`, plus durable same-directory publication in `_store/fsutil.py::atomic_write`.

## Approach

Generalize the established sibling-lock pattern in `rebar._store.fsutil` as a narrow reusable exclusive-path-lock context manager. Migrate HLC and recent-create callers to it so the project has one standard lock implementation. A lock lives at a stable sibling `.lock` path, never on the replaceable JSON inode, and remains an untracked local control artifact for the lifetime of its sidecar workspace; commit-back must not stage it. The context spans re-read, mutation, `fsutil.atomic_write(fsync=True)`, and unlock.

Add `sidecar_transactions.py` only for the reconciler-specific part that existing prior art does not provide: applying a domain mutation or record delta while the shared `fsutil` lock is held. It delegates all locking and atomic publication to the generalized `fsutil` seams. Mapping/provenance mutations load the current valid mapping under that lock, apply their key-level mutation, then publish it.

For peer-confirmation and impossible-link stores, take an independent deep copy of the records loaded at construction as the immutable baseline. At save, calculate upserts and deletions against that copy; while holding the shared lock, reload the latest valid record set and apply the delta. Different keys survive. The concrete same-key rule is last shared-lock holder wins, including a deletion, so the test can assert the later lock acquisition order.

If loading valid JSON, acquiring the lock, or publishing fails, preserve the target bytes, log a path-specific warning, skip persistence for that pass, and continue the reconciliation pass fail-open. This includes malformed/non-object JSON. Readers retain old-or-new complete-document visibility through `fsutil.atomic_write(fsync=True)`. Fresh-reader tests prove the existing commit-back path publishes valid state.

## Scope

- generalized sibling locking and durable publication reuse in `src/rebar/_store/fsutil.py`
- HLC and recent-create adoption of that single lock seam
- reconciler-specific `sidecar_transactions.py` delta application; mapping, peer-confirmation, and impossible-link callers
- focused concurrency, mapping, provenance, malformed-state, and durability tests

## Testing

Characterize HLC and recent-create lock migration against the prior behavior. Use barrier-controlled independent writers, same-key writers, a delete-versus-write pair, and an in-window reader for sidecars. Verify a deep baseline detects both in-place upserts and deletes, verify every lock/load/publish failure warns without overwriting, verify `.lock` files are not commit-back inputs, and prove durability through a fresh reader.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `fsutil` exposes the one sibling-path exclusive-lock primitive used by HLC, recent-create, and reconciler sidecar transactions; each caller holds it over its complete read-modify-write window.
- [x] The stable `.lock` file is never staged or published by commit-back and is intentionally retained for reuse while its sidecar workspace exists.
- [x] Reconciler sidecar publication delegates to `fsutil.atomic_write(fsync=True)` rather than reimplementing temp-file replacement.
- [x] Mapping/provenance updates load the latest valid mapping under the shared lock before applying their key-level mutation.
- [x] Peer-confirmation and impossible-link stores calculate their upserts and deletions from an independent deep copy of the load-time records.
- [x] Concurrent distinct-key updates retain both records; a same-key test proves the later shared-lock holder wins.
- [x] A delete-versus-write test proves a deliberate impossible-link deletion is propagated and a later shared-lock holder determines the same-key outcome.
- [x] An in-window reader sees only complete pre- or post-transaction JSON.
- [x] A malformed target, lock failure, or atomic-write failure logs the sidecar path, preserves its bytes, and allows the reconciliation pass to continue.
- [x] A fresh reader proves committed mapping and impossible-link state survives publication.
baseline.summary: Make reconciliation sidecar persistence conflict-safe and observationally proven

## Context
rebar records NO session identifier on a claim distinct from `assignee` and the event `author`. A claim writes a `STATUS(open->in_progress)` (+ `EDIT(assignee)`); the envelope carries `timestamp`, `uuid`, `event_type`, `author` (git user), and `env_id` — but `env_id` is the tracker init-environment id (written once at `rebar init`, shared by ALL events), NOT a per-session/per-agent id. So an `in_progress` state cannot be attributed to the specific agent **session** that claimed it.

The design for this epic is complete (unknowns resolved, experiments run, OSS surveyed). Full design doc lives with the driving session; the resolved decisions are below.

## What
When a coding-agent session id is present in the environment, automatically record it on the `open->in_progress` transition so an in_progress ticket is attributable to the session that started it — additively, without disturbing `assignee`/`author`, local-only, compaction-safe, tolerated by older clones.

## Design decisions (resolved)
- **Env-var contract (ordered, data-driven list).** Explicit rebar var first, then native
  harness vars by popularity, ambient last: `REBAR_SESSION_ID` -> `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`
  -> `OPENCODE_SESSION_ID` -> `SESSION_ID` -> None. (`CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_ID` captured
  as a secondary `remote_session` field.) **Design correction (story 7656):** Codex is NOT a
  native var in this list — it exposes no supported readable session env var, so it is covered
  by its SessionStart shim exporting `REBAR_SESSION_ID` instead (there is no `CODEX_THREAD_ID`).
  Never fall back to git HEAD (changes per commit). One shared resolver replaces today's two
  divergent ones.
- **Storage.** Record on the claim `STATUS` event's `data["session"]`; fold to reducer
  state key `claimed_session` (mirrors `assignee`). No new event type, no envelope change.
- **Jira.** N/A — a local reducer-state key never enters the reconciler (outbound differ
  is an explicit allow-list).
- **Reliable capture.** `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` is an env var only in the remote runner;
  the local CLI needs a SessionStart hook that exports `REBAR_SESSION_ID`.

## Context (gotchas to respect — from OSS prior art)
- Session ids are NOT stable across `--resume`/`--continue`/fork/subagents; treat the
  record as "the session that emitted this claim event", not a per-ticket lifetime id.
- A leaked/stale env var pollutes unrelated sessions (rebar bug 76e9 class) — prefer
  hook-injected, session-scoped values.
- Keep it local-only + opaque (consent/provenance sensitivity); read the var as a plain
  string, never interpolate/execute it.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] Decomposed into discrete-deliverable child stories parented to THIS epic (via each
      child's `parent_id`, confirmable with `rebar deps 38ec-5f12-fdf5-4340`): S1
      `6014-0863-2e36-41b3`, S2 `68ef-da4f-b64b-4903`, S3 `199b-f56f-5ba1-468b`, S5
      `c557-8f46-0c16-4bf5`, S4 `ec5c-bd06-aa49-42d0`, S6 `7656-0a67-e881-4131`, plus the
      module-size split refactor `458f-5b67-961e-4e80` — all closed.
- [x] Env-var contract implemented as the ordered, extensible resolver above
      (`REBAR_SESSION_ID -> CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID -> OPENCODE_SESSION_ID -> SESSION_ID`, with
      Codex covered by its `REBAR_SESSION_ID` shim rather than a native `CODEX_THREAD_ID` — see
      `src/rebar/_commands/session_id.py`).
- [x] Storage shape implemented (STATUS `data["session"]` -> `claimed_session` state).
- [x] Claim/transition records the id when present; no-op when absent.
- [x] Read surface exposes the claiming session id for a ticket.
- [x] Backward/forward compatible + compaction-safe (regression-tested).
- [x] Local-CLI capture shim ships (Claude Code), plus Codex/Cursor shims.
- [ ] A claim made while a recognized session env var is set durably records that session
- [ ] Absent the env var, behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged (fully backward compatible).
- [ ] The recorded id survives compaction and is preserved-and-ignored by older clones.
- [ ] Works in the LOCAL Claude Code CLI (not only the remote runner), via a capture shim.
- [ ] Session id is attributable across the popular OSS harnesses (Claude Code, OpenCode,
baseline.summary: Track a claim<->session relationship, auto-recorded from environment variables when present

## Discovered from

rebar-debug on bug `masonic-abeyant-stagbeetle` (3a52-2d79-320d-4fed), root cause RC-B. See that ticket's "Phase 1 EXIT" comment for the full evidence trail.

## Problem

Two independent gaps leave the snapshot store with no size-based reclaim at all.

**1. The backstop does not exist.** `docs/adr/0005-snapshot-cache-architecture.md:72-73` and the janitor module's own contract docstring (`src/rebar/_snapshot/janitor.py:13-15`) both state that reclamation is driven by a free-space watermark "backstopped by the incrementally- maintained byte total". `_gc_pass` (`janitor.py:303-345`) reads only `free` (`shutil.disk_usage`) and each entry's `mtime`. It never consults `_cache.byte_total`. The only reader is `startup_sweep` (`janitor.py:251`), and that is reconciliation, not eviction. There is no store-size cap knob in the config surface either (`docs/config.md:474-484`).

**2. The dominant consumer is not byte-accounted.** `cache.acquire` calls `add_bytes(entry_size(dest))` at `src/rebar/_snapshot/cache.py:203`, but `materialize_tickets` (`src/rebar/_snapshot/repo_snapshot.py:616-708`) bypasses `acquire` entirely and never calls `add_bytes`. The `tickets-<sha>` entries are ~620 MiB each and are the largest thing in the store, so even if the backstop above were implemented it would under-count them to **zero**.

(`_is_entry` at `janitor.py:110-122` does recognise `tickets-` entries as evictable, so GC would remove them if a trigger ever fired — the gap is purely in the trigger and the accounting.)

## Impact

On the review-bot host this contributed to `rebar-root-disk-pressure` breaching 85% and reaching 90% with nothing reclaiming: the free-space trigger is unreachable below 93.3% used on that volume (tracked on 3a52), the 7-day cold-trim exceeds the container's lifetime, and the third trigger the ADR promises is absent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `_gc_pass` gains a byte-total-driven eviction trigger with a documented, configurable cap
      (or ADR 0005 and the janitor docstring are corrected to remove the promise — but then the
      store has only one working trigger, so the cap is the expected resolution).
- [x] `materialize_tickets` records its entries in the store's byte total, so the accounting
      reflects the entries that actually dominate it.
- [x] A test observes the untracked bytes RED (a store whose real size far exceeds the reported
      `byte_total`) and GREEN after the fix.
- [x] `docs/config.md`, `docs/repo-snapshot-gates.md` and `docs/env-vars.md` document the new
      cap knob (a docs test pins these — `tests/unit/test_snapshot_docs.py`).
baseline.summary: Snapshot janitor's ADR-promised byte-total backstop is unimplemented, and materialize_tickets never byte-accounts its entries

## Context

Commit 7fa8102477 (2026-08-08, "Bound malformed overlap judge calls") bounded `judge_batch` with `output_token_limit=1024`, `structured_retry_limit=0`, `transport_attempt_limit=1`, `request_timeout_limit_s=60`. The sibling call site `judge_one` in `src/rebar/llm/overlap/judge.py` — the VOLUME site (~18 of 23 LLM calls in one measured plan review, per the module's own comment) — was not given the same bounds.

Measured consequence (local usage logs, 2026-08-06→08-11): 322 terminal `overlap-judge` failures with `finish_reason=length`, each burning 48,000 output tokens = 3 attempts (pydantic-ai `OUTPUT_RETRIES=2` default) x the 16,000 default `max_tokens` cap, ~$132 of pure waste; 20+ occurrences after the 08-08 fix landed, and 7 more reproduced during replay experiments on 2026-08-11. An overlap verdict is ~100 output tokens, so an unbounded retry ladder buys nothing.

## Plan

Mirror `judge_batch`'s bounds onto `judge_one`'s `RunRequest` (same values, same rationale comment): `output_token_limit=1024`, `structured_retry_limit=0`, `transport_attempt_limit=1`, `request_timeout_limit_s=60`. The overlap step is advisory and already abstains on any error, so tighter bounds cannot change a review verdict — a bounded failure degrades to the same abstain as an unbounded one, at ~2% of the cost.

Add a unit test pinning the bounds on the `judge_one` request (mirroring whatever pins judge_batch's; if none pins judge_batch's, add both in one test module touch).

## Resolution (premise refuted — not_a_bug)

The plan-review gate's G6 block was correct and the investigation confirmed it: production overlap traffic flows only through `judge_batch` (already bounded by 7fa8102477); `judge_one` is test-only. The 48k failures observed after 08-08 came from stale checkouts running pre-fix code — every post-update failure is bounded (out=1024, req=1, graceful abstain). No code change is warranted; the original Acceptance Criteria are void with the premise. Evidence in the ticket comment.
baseline.summary: overlap-judge: judge_one lacks the malformed-output bounds judge_batch got — 48k retry storms continue

# Tier-3: CI-scheduled enrichment drain (GitHub Actions)

## Context
Follow-on to the cross-ticket overlap epic (only-crave-art). Because the store is git-backed and already pushed to a remote, a scheduled GitHub Action (`on: schedule:`) can run `rebar enrich --drain` against the pushed store — zero LOCAL setup, the Renovate/Dependabot model. rebar already runs Actions for ticket→Jira sync, so the harness exists.

## Why deferred (product-owner decision)
We want to confirm the system works WITHOUT the CI job before implementing CI as a primary mechanism, because MANY CLIENTS WILL NOT HAVE dedicated CI configured. Tier 1 (opportunistic detached drain) must carry the feature on its own first.

## Known caveats to design around
- GitHub cron has a 5-min floor and 5-30+ min delays under load (best-effort cadence, not an SLA).
- Scheduled workflows auto-disable after ~60 days of repo inactivity.
- Pair `schedule:` with `workflow_dispatch:`; use a GitHub App token / OIDC (the bare GITHUB_TOKEN can't update workflows). The API key must be a CI secret.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A committed `.github/workflows/` drain runs `rebar enrich --drain` on a schedule and pushes results back.
- [ ] Manually triggerable via `workflow_dispatch`.
- [ ] Documented as best-effort (imprecise cadence, inactivity auto-disable) and optional — Tier 1 remains the primary mechanism.
baseline.summary: Tier-3: CI-scheduled enrichment drain (GitHub Actions)

# Gate blindness to world-grounded evidence: force measurement provenance into the record

## Context / Problem

A `/rebar-implement` run of epic `061c-ecd1-8967-4a76` landed five changes through every gate. **The gates performed to their design envelope.** Plan-review blocked infeasible mechanics (a tenacity-transport claim that cannot wrap boto3; an `isinstance` against a botocore-dependent class; a live canary path that would have made billable AWS calls on every CI run). The completion-verifier twice refused a close whose stated criteria had no test. Full-suite pre-flight caught cross-module regressions `tests/unit` missed.

Every one of those catches shares a property: **the ground truth lived in the repo**, where the reviewer's read/grep tools could reach it.

Four escapes got through, and they are one defect wearing different clothes — **a green signal whose measurement could not have observed the failure it claims to rule out**:

1. **Wrong environment.** Bedrock caching and model-availability measurements were taken in account
   `579718921998` / `us-east-2` and recorded as settled fact; the project runs in `896586841071` / `us-east-1`
   (named by the Terraform backend `rebar-tfstate-896586841071`). No gate compares a claim's observation
   context against the project's environment. A human caught it by asking "is that this project's account?"
2. **Instruments that cannot observe the failure — twice, in the same investigation.** This escape is the
   epic's sharpest example precisely because the *first correction was also wrong*.

   **2a.** Live `bedrock:Converse` calls validated a *scoped* IAM grant while running under an identity
   holding `bedrock:*`. Evidence generated under broader privilege than production is structurally unable to
   fail, so its success carries **zero information**.

   **2b.** The prescribed remedy — `aws iam simulate-principal-policy` against the role — then produced a
   confident, recorded, and **wrong** conclusion: that `bedrock:Converse` was the action to grant. The
   simulator answered exactly the question asked ("would this policy permit the action *named*
   `bedrock:Converse`?", legitimately no, since that action genuinely exists) but **not** the question that
   mattered ("which action does the Converse API actually *check*?"). Only a real call FROM the instance
   revealed the truth — `AccessDeniedException ... not authorized to perform: bedrock:InvokeModel` — meaning
   the ORIGINAL plan was right and the "fix" broke it, on a role feeding `eb6e-f43a-e86b-443a`, a cutover
   with no fallback.

   The pair is the lesson: a wildcard identity could not fail, and a simulator could not fail *for the reason
   that mattered*. **Evidence is only as good as its ability to have come out the other way for the reason
   you care about** — and swapping one instrument for a more rigorous-sounding one does not establish that.
3. **Tests that cannot fail** — the code-side form of the same defect: a contrast case whose discriminating
   conjunct was never exercised, and an oracle asserting on an object where production passes a string.
   **Both WERE caught** (mutation testing; the LLM reviewer) precisely because they are repo-checkable. That
   contrast is the evidence for this epic's thesis.
4. **Confidence outrunning method**: "verified by reading" was a hand-picked grep that missed a dependency;
   "18/18 green" was reported while typecheck was red.

## Why 1 and 2 are structural, not a calibration miss

`verified_at_sha` pins the code world completely and the outside world not at all. Plan-review runs **before** the evidence exists, so it cannot audit a measurement not yet taken; the completion-verifier accepts `[operator-attested]` evidence **on trust by design** (ADR-0043). One gate cannot audit it, the other is designed not to. The in-flight T5c rewrite pushes grounding toward current code and IaC state but still cannot observe a live cloud account — nothing in the current design can, and nothing should try.

## Approach

Do **not** make a gate observe the world. Force the measurement's context into the record as text, then let the existing repo-grounded machinery find contradictions in it. Detail lives in the child story; the shape is:

1. Extend the attested-evidence contract with measurement-provenance fields — environment, principal, and
   privilege posture relative to production.
2. Enforce their **presence** deterministically, zero LLM, mirroring
   `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/det_operator_attested.py` (DET-first doctrine).
3. Let an LLM criterion judge the *declaration* against repo facts — once provenance is text, "plan attests
   account X, IaC names account Y" becomes a **repo-checkable contradiction**, which is exactly what the
   gate's strongest criteria already do well.
4. Land the generalized rule as an **advisory** criterion per ADR-0054; corpus replay decides promotion.

## Explicitly rejected

- **Making the completion-verifier re-run world measurements.** Expensive, flaky, recursive — the verifier's
  own credentials carry the same privilege-masking problem, so it would validate using the instrument under
  suspicion.
- **Escape 4 as gate scope.** Reported-green-while-red is *reporting discipline*, already covered by the
  orchestration rule that agents report gate output faithfully rather than narrating success. Filing it as a
  gate gap would be mis-attribution.
- **Wording changes alone.** The contract was followed and still failed; emphasis is not the defect. This is
  the same lesson as epic `9109-2ad9-2477-4cf6` (Serena tool-choice), which is why that epic's structural
  framing is the model here rather than its subject matter.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] an `[operator-attested]` criterion lacking measurement provenance is flagged by a DETERMINISTIC check
      (no LLM) — `det_measurement_provenance.py`, surfaced advisory through `p6_ac_quality`, landed in
      change 1423 with a mutation-tested oracle (breaking the binding rule, placeholder detection or enum
      membership each kills tests)
- [x] the new criterion ships **advisory** (ADR-0054) and rides the `.rebar/` project overlay, leaving the
      shipped default criteria set unchanged for other rebar clients
- [x] an ADR records the amended evidence contract, citing ADR-0043 as the shape it changes
- [x] the completion-verifier is NOT made to re-run world measurements — the rejected alternative stays
      rejected, and a test or grep demonstrates it

## Descoped to `98df-3528-9b1f-405a` (ridiculous-expert-mouse), filed as an `idea`

AC-1 originally also required the wrong-account escape to be **reproduced as a regression fixture** from the real `579718921998` vs `896586841071` case. That clause is NOT delivered and is NOT claimed as done.

Reproducing it means exercising the AGENT criterion's rule (a) semantically, which needs an eval corpus (`.rebar/evals/plan-review-project-measurement-provenance.eval.yaml`) plus a live run — the same behavioural half descoped from story `f161`. Both moved to `98df`, which also carries the rule (b)/(c)/(d) fixtures and the ADR-0054 corpus-replay false-positive rate that would justify promoting the criterion from advisory.

This epic therefore closes on its MECHANISM being delivered and proven — provenance is now forced into the record as text, deterministically enforced, and judged by a tool-enabled criterion — not on that criterion's firing behaviour having been calibrated. The distinction is safe because the criterion ships **advisory**: it cannot block any claim or close, so an uncalibrated advisory criterion is inert-but-useful rather than risky. Promotion is a separate ADR-0054 decision nobody has committed to, which is why `98df` is an `idea`.
baseline.summary: Gate blindness to world-grounded evidence: force measurement provenance into the record

## Context / Problem
A normal post-merge `review-plan` from the project checkout made zero LLM calls and took 512.139s before failing because `git fetch origin` hit the 300s timeout. The checkout is partial/promisor (`blob:none`) and its `origin.fetch` maps every remote head. Attested ref resolution calls `fetch_origin()` without a ref, which executes `git fetch --quiet --no-filter origin`; this can traverse/materialize the enormous tickets history while only a code SHA is needed. The failed attempt left partial packs, including one approximately 153.6 MB.

A normal retry from a temporary clone whose origin fetch refspec was main-only crossed the fetch boundary and completed the same review with signed PASS. This discriminates broad-ref transfer from model latency. It is distinct from `strained-bare-turnstone`, which addressed intermittent transport stalls and durable voting behavior, and from `grassy-cracked-morpho`, which covers completion close history-times-tracker scanning.

## Plan
- Reproduce attested resolution from a partial/promisor checkout whose origin fetch refspec includes both code and the large tickets branch.
- Change snapshot ref materialization to fetch only the requested code ref/object while preserving fail-closed attestation semantics and support for remote refs.
- Preserve blob materialization when the requested snapshot requires it without broadening the remote refspec.
- Add a regression test that records the exact fetch argv/refspec and rejects an unscoped no-filter origin fetch.
- Measure the fetch boundary before and after with a representative main-only target.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] Resolving a specific attested code ref does not fetch unrelated origin heads.
- [x] Blobless/promisor checkouts can still materialize the requested snapshot when required.
- [x] Missing or unreachable requested refs continue to fail closed.
- [x] Tests pin scoped fetch arguments and cover a checkout with an unrelated large branch.
- [x] Before/after fetch duration and transferred-object evidence are recorded.
- [x] No LLM, gate, or tracker behavior is bypassed.
baseline.summary: Attested ref materialization broad-fetches all origin heads

# Outbound parent-set can never be carried by a reconcile pass on Data Center (two gates that do not compose)

## Provenance

Found while building story 5200's missing row-12-OUTBOUND live cell, by an agent instructed to establish the real contract before writing an oracle rather than assume a round-trip was supported. It is a PRODUCT gap, not a test gap.

## Mechanism — each gate is defensible alone; on DC they are DISJOINT

**The APPLY side wants a SUB-TASK child.** `adapters/jira_datacenter/transport.py` `set_parent` (:668-712) reads the issue, checks `fields.issuetype.subtask` (:693-694), and for a sub-task writes `issue.update(fields={"parent": {"key": parent_key}})` (:711-712). For a NON-sub-task child it raises `NotImplementedError` (:695-710) naming the reason: epic membership on DC is the "Epic Link" CUSTOM FIELD written through the Agile API under `greenhopper`, not `fields.parent`. That decline is deliberate and correct — it stops `fields.parent` being written and silently no-op'd.

**The EMIT side wants an EPIC parent.** `outbound_field_diff._resolve_local_parent:136-139` returns `(False, None)` — omitting the parent field ENTIRELY — for any parent whose local `ticket_type` is not `epic`. That is bug 8b25's hierarchy guard, built over `local_ticket_types` (`outbound_differ.py:475-477`) and already unit-covered by `tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/conflict/test_parent_hierarchy_guard.py` — verified UNEDITED: `git diff 7fc96b277 gerrit/main` on that path is EMPTY across the whole epic, and change 1302 adds only a new test file.

**A DC sub-task's parent is a STANDARD issue, which imports as local `ticket_type` `"task"`.** So the one child shape DC accepts (sub-task) can only have a parent shape the emit gate refuses (non-epic). The sets are disjoint: **no reconcile pass can ever emit an outbound parent-set that DC would accept.**

Both gates were written for Cloud's next-gen Epic-parent hierarchy, where they compose fine. Nobody composed them against DC's model.

## Why this is the FIFTH instance of a known class

"Cloud has the translation, DC never got its half" — d067 (outbound status submitted as a field edit, never a transition), 8d68 (inbound UPDATE never minted an identity), 751e (empty assignee never unassigns), 2b16 / 88d9 (inbound link removal and parent clear never emitted). Every one was a SILENT success: no traceback, no alert, the pass reports OK. This is the same shape — a local parent/child relationship simply never reaches Data Center, and nothing reports that it did not.

`dispatch_one.py:571-578` swallows `set_parent`'s exception (warn-and-continue, keyed at :546), so even the DECLINE is invisible; but on DC the decline is not even reached, because the emit gate dropped the field first.

## Scope note — deliberately NOT gating e369

Recorded rather than folded into epic e369, consistent with the operator's ruling on `e39f-5055-f5af-424a` (a DC write-path gap ruled follow-up, not gating). Two supporting reasons:
 * the fix is a HIERARCHY-MODEL change, not a patch — either the emit gate learns DC's sub-task shape or
   DC's `set_parent` learns the Epic Link field. Either is a design pass with a real blast radius.
 * closing e369 does not assert this works. Its operator-attested criterion is bidirectional reconcile
   (an issue created in DC appears locally; a local EDIT appears in DC), both proven live; no criterion
   claims outbound parent sync.

**I am flagging this as a BORDERLINE call.** The operator's earlier ruling on the three J11-surfaced defects took the strictest available option, and unlike e39f this one does NOT fail safe — it is a silent DIVERGENCE, not a safe refusal. If the operator prefers the strict reading, reparenting this under e369 is one command. The tension is recorded here on purpose rather than resolved quietly.

## What story 5200 does and does not now cover

5200's row-12-outbound cell (change 1283) asserts the PRIMITIVE at the transport level — `dc_transport.set_parent(child, B)` then a raw-REST read-back of `fields.parent` — following the same precedent row 14 outbound set for the same reason. It deliberately does NOT assert the pass-level suppression as correct behaviour, because that would freeze this gap into the suite.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] a test asserts, at the pass level, that a local parent/child relationship syncable on Cloud is
      ALSO emitted for DC — i.e. the emit gate and DC's accepted child shape overlap for at least one
      real configuration
- [x] the chosen fix is stated explicitly: either the emit gate learns DC's sub-task shape, or DC's
      `set_parent` writes the Epic Link custom field through the Agile API — with the rejected option and
      the reason recorded. Option B (DC set_parent writes the Epic Link through the Agile API) CHOSEN with three reasons; option A (teach the emit gate DC's sub-task shape) REJECTED with three reasons — both recorded in the CLAIMED comment
- [x] the 8b25 hierarchy guard's Cloud behaviour is UNCHANGED, pinned by its existing tests in
      `tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/conflict/test_parent_hierarchy_guard.py` — verified UNEDITED: `git diff 7fc96b277 gerrit/main` on that path is EMPTY across the whole epic, and change 1302 adds only a new test file
- [x] a parent that genuinely cannot be represented on the deployment surfaces an OPERATOR-VISIBLE signal
      rather than being silently dropped — DONE in change 1305 (merged `364c4e8f5e`): a `bridge_alerts` entry on every set_parent failure arm, three distinct kinds (`outbound-parent-unrepresentable` / `-rejected` / `-failed`), fail-open, warn-and-continue preserved. the swallow at `dispatch_one.py:571-578` is why this class
      stayed invisible for five instances running
- [x] mutation-checked, with verdicts recorded here — 1305: 4 mutations, ALL killed, each by exactly one cell (M1 drop-the-alert, M2 collapse-the-kinds, M3 alert-unconditionally, M4 remove-the-fail-open)
baseline.summary: Outbound parent-set can never be emitted for DC: the epic-parent emit gate and DC's sub-task-child apply gate are disjoint

# Batch-commit write primitive for bulk operations (import/migration scale)

## Context

Discovered from the export/import design brainstorm (`rule-swamp-pupil`, 2026-06-17). rebar's write path commits ONE git commit per event under a per-event lock acquire/release (`src/rebar/_store/event_append.py:82-146`, `src/rebar/_store/lock.py:187-231`); no batch/bulk/transaction primitive exists. A bulk import of N tickets composes N×~3 events → thousands of commits + thousands of lock cycles (~3.3 min of lock overhead alone for ~2,000 events, before commit/push). `rule-swamp-pupil` already mitigates network amplification (`REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off` + single final push), but the per-event commit/lock cost remains. This task is the real fix, deferred until real-world store sizes demand it.

## What / Implementation detail

Add `_store.batch_stage_and_commit(events)`: under ONE write lock, write/rename M event files, one `git add`, ONE commit. Crucially, **each event remains its own file** (unique name) — so cross-clone union-merge and SNAPSHOT compaction (which key off event UUIDs, not commit boundaries) are unaffected, and invariants I5 (single locked writer) and I2 (composed events) hold. Route the importer (and optionally the reconciler applier) through it in chunks (per-ticket or per-N). Atomicity: a single commit of M staged files is atomic at the git level; partial staging before commit is recoverable because import is idempotent (resume by `source_id`).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `_store.batch_stage_and_commit(events)`: one lock, M event files, one commit; each event its own file
- [x] importer routes events through it in chunks; single-event path unchanged
- [x] atomicity + crash-resume (idempotent) tests; union-merge + compaction regression tests
- [ ] benchmark: large-import wall-clock before vs after

Deferred optimization for `rule-swamp-pupil`; build if store sizes demand it.
- [ ] A bulk import of a large synthetic store completes in a fraction of the per-event wall-clock, with the same resulting logical state.
- [x] Cross-clone convergence + compaction unaffected (regression tests).
- [x] The single-event write path is unchanged.
baseline.summary: Batch-commit write primitive for bulk operations (import/migration scale)

## Context / Problem

The bridge has nowhere to record which tracker projects a store syncs, nor which repos each project's tickets belong to. Epic `0e68-41eb-5782-4336` needs that mapping to be a property of the **store** rather than of any one repo, because `.bridge_state/prev_snapshot.json` is shared by every repo using the store: if two repos fetched different project subsets against one shared snapshot, each pass would see the other's projects as vanished from the remote and diff them as deletions.

## Approach

Add `.bridge_state/projects.json` beside the committed bridge state already there (`bindings.json`, `get_rotation.json`, `prev_snapshot.json` — all present on the `tickets` branch), owned by a new `projects_store.py` module rather than by extending `binding_store.py`. The two records have very different write cadences, and keeping them separate means an operator editing the mapping never rewrites the large bindings record.

Record shape:

```json
{"version": 1, "legacy_default": "REB", "projects": {"REB": {"repos": ["rebar"]}}}
```

The `projects` key set **is** the store's sync list, so there is no second list to keep in agreement. `legacy_default` is the project that tickets predating this epic resolve to.

This choice sits well with ADR 0060 ("Keep bridge state committed, but make its formats cheap"): that ADR's constraint is per-pass churn on the tickets branch — it measured 12.79 KB per changed `bindings.json` version and ~4.5 MB/day for `prev_snapshot.json`. The mapping changes only on an operator edit, so it adds no per-pass growth at all.

Surface it as `bridge projects` under the verb group established by story `4752-3afb-e8bd-448a` (`src/rebar/_cli/_bridge_commands.py`), with the library and MCP parity epic `2f79-2b32-28c5-4eb3` requires of every bridge verb. The bridge library surface is `src/rebar/_lib_ops.py` (`bridge_fsck` at `:75`). The MCP layer is split by mutation, not by feature: `register_read_tools` (`src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:36`) hosts tools annotated `_ANN["READ_ONLY"]` — where the existing `bridge_fsck` tool lives at `:259` — while `register_write_tools` (`src/rebar/_mcp_writes.py:33`) hosts mutating tools, and `mcp_server.py:663` registers both. The `projects` verbs therefore split across both modules: `list` is a read tool, `set` and `remove` are write tools. Sub-verbs: `list`, `set <KEY> --repos a,b`, `remove <KEY>`. `set` on a key that is already present **replaces** that key's repos list rather than merging into it, so the command is idempotent and a repo is removed by re-issuing `set` without it.

The bridge group's help is a **pinned byte-exact contract**, not generated text: the group listing lives in `src/rebar/_cli/help/bridge.txt` (which today names only `preview` and `sync` at lines 5-7) and is served verbatim by `_help.subcommand_help` (`src/rebar/_cli/_help.py:52`), while the parser hardcodes the verb set a second time as `metavar="{preview,sync}"` (`src/rebar/_cli/_bridge_commands.py:52-53`). Adding a verb therefore means editing three places, not one; omitting either of the two help sites ships a group whose own help does not mention the command it just gained.

The module exposes two functions so that I/O and rule are separable: `load_mapping(repo_root)` reads and validates the record, and `resolve_project(ticket, mapping) -> str | None` is a pure function over an already-loaded mapping, which keeps the tri-state rule unit-testable without a store on disk.

**Read behaviour when the record is missing or bad** follows the precedent `compat.py` already sets for `.store-compat.json` (`docs/migrations.md:155-165`): an **absent** record is legal and reads as an empty mapping with a `legacy_default` of `None`, while a **malformed** one raises rather than being silently treated as absent — a corrupt record must never degrade into a permissive default. Absent is legal because the record is seeded by an ensure unit that runs at init, `fsck --repair`, and MCP boot; until it does, every ticket resolves to `None` and nothing syncs, which is the fail-safe direction — the bridge writes nothing rather than writing somewhere wrong.

`resolve_project` implements the tri-state rule so the inbound and outbound stories consume one implementation instead of each re-deriving it. The states map to concrete return values:

| ticket `bridge_project` | returns | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| key absent from state | the mapping's `legacy_default` (a `str`) | legacy ticket, predates this epic |
| `""` (explicit empty) | `None` | deliberately not synced |
| `"REB"` | `"REB"` | sync into that project |

`None` is the not-synced sentinel, so every consumer branches on a single defined value: callers treat `None` as "emit no mutation for this ticket" and any non-`None` result as a project key safe to target. A `legacy_default` that is itself empty — a store whose backend had no configured project — also yields `None`, so an unconfigured store degrades to "nothing syncs" rather than to a malformed query.

`--repos` is **required** on `set`; omitting the flag is an argument error and exits non-zero. `--repos ""` is the explicit way to store an empty list, which keeps "no default repo" a deliberate statement rather than an accident of a forgotten flag.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/projects_store.py` (new)
- `src/rebar/_cli/_bridge_commands.py` — the subcommand, and the hardcoded `metavar` verb set at `:52-53`
- `src/rebar/_cli/help/bridge.txt` — the pinned byte-exact group help listing
- `src/rebar/_lib_ops.py`
- `src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py` — the `list` read tool
- `src/rebar/_mcp_writes.py` — the `set` and `remove` write tools
- tests under `tests/`

This story owns the mapping module; the parent epic's file impact is updated to name `projects_store.py` rather than `binding_store.py`, so parent and child agree that the mapping does not extend the bindings record.

`_mcp_writes.py` is the one file this story shares with its sibling that adds the ticket create arguments. The overlap is forced by the codebase's own read/write registrar split rather than chosen, and it is safe because that sibling `depends_on` this story: the two are strictly ordered and can never be edited concurrently. Introducing a third MCP module purely to avoid the shared file would break the established registrar convention for no benefit.

## Testing

Tier per the shared standard's CLI row — a real CLI subprocess with a persisted-state assertion — because the mechanism spans argument parsing, the on-disk JSON record, and exit codes; an in-process unit test would not cross the parsing or exit-code components.

- Happy path: `bridge projects set REB --repos rebar` in a fresh store, then `bridge projects list`
  returns the entry and `.bridge_state/projects.json` on disk contains it.
- Cross-surface contract test: an entry written through the library surface is read back byte-equal
  through the CLI and through MCP — proving one record, not three parallel stores.
- Failure path: `bridge projects remove NOPE` on a store without that key exits non-zero, names the
  key, and leaves the record byte-unchanged.
- Edge: `set REB --repos` with an empty list is accepted and stores `[]` — a project with no default
  repo is legal, not an error.
- Replace-not-merge: `set REB --repos a,b` followed by `set REB --repos a` stores exactly `["a"]`,
  proving the second call replaced rather than merged.
- Pinned help: `rebar bridge` with no verb, and `rebar help bridge`, both render text naming
  `projects`, and the argparse `metavar` matches the pinned listing — asserted against the file so a
  future verb cannot drift the two apart silently.
- Collateral invariant: after any mapping write, `bindings.json` and `prev_snapshot.json` hash
  identically to before.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `bridge projects set|list|remove` exist under the bridge verb group and operate on
      `.bridge_state/projects.json`; checked by a CLI subprocess test asserting the on-disk record
      after each verb.
- [ ] The library and MCP surfaces read and write the same record as the CLI; checked by a test that
      writes through one surface and reads the identical entry through the other two.
- [ ] `resolve_project` returns the `legacy_default` string for an absent field, `None` for an
      explicit empty value, and the key itself for a set value, and returns `None` when the
      `legacy_default` is itself empty; checked by a parameterized unit test asserting the exact
      return value for all four cases.
- [ ] `set` without `--repos` is an argument error exiting non-zero, while `--repos ""` stores `[]`;
      checked by a paired CLI subprocess test.
- [ ] An absent record reads as an empty mapping with a `None` legacy default while a malformed one
      raises; checked by a paired test over a store with no record and one with truncated JSON.
- [ ] `list` is registered as a read tool and `set`/`remove` as write tools; checked by asserting
      `list` carries the READ_ONLY annotation and that `set`/`remove` are registered by
      `register_write_tools`.
- [ ] A mapping write leaves `bindings.json` and `prev_snapshot.json` byte-identical; checked by
      hashing both before and after in the CLI test.
- [ ] `remove` of an unknown key exits non-zero and mutates nothing; checked in the same test.
- [ ] `set` on an already-present key replaces its repos list rather than merging; checked by
      asserting the stored list equals exactly the second call's argument.
- [ ] The pinned group help in `src/rebar/_cli/help/bridge.txt` and the parser `metavar` both name
      `projects`; checked by a test asserting the rendered `rebar bridge` help contains the verb and
      that the pinned file and the `metavar` verb set agree.
baseline.summary: bridge projects: store-level project-to-repos mapping and its CLI, library and MCP surface

baseline.description:
Store the baseline in the projection the comparison already computes: `description` as `normalize_rich_text(raw)`, `status`/`priority` as `.name`. Expected ~-66% on an **18.3 MB** (18,257,550-byte) file. session_log **1cb6-d553-6565-49b4** (measured facts; do not re-derive).

## Why this is safe without a comparator change
`outbound_field_diff.py:187,196` canonicalize BOTH sides at **read** time via `inbound_mapper.map_remote_to_local` (docstring `:183`: "storage stays vendor-shaped, mapped at READ time only"), and both canonicalizers are idempotent on already-normalized values: `normalize_rich_text` (`inbound_fields.py:136-145`) returns `adf_to_text(body)` for dicts and `str(body)` otherwise; `_extract_jira_field_value` (`:92-96`) reads `name`/`displayName` for dicts and passes strings through. So ADF-dict and plain-text baselines canonicalize identically and a mixed store needs no new comparator. This also makes the change **revert-safe** — a normalized-string baseline round-trips unchanged through pre-A3 code.

CORRECTION carried forward: an earlier framing rested on `_extract_jira_field`/`_diff_fields`, which have **zero production callers**. Validate against the live path only.

## Why assignee is EXCLUDED — data loss, not conflict noise
`_assignee_candidates` (`outbound_field_diff.py:56-67`) builds its match set from the scalar **plus every non-None identity form**, and `_suppressed_by_inbound` (`:250-256`) routes assignee through `_assignee_matches`. Collapsing three identity forms to one string shrinks that candidate set and loses inbound-directionality suppression, so local-wins **silently clobbers a concurrent remote assignee edit**. (The strict `assignee_identity` equality at `:390-394` is the lesser, secondary effect.) Keep assignee raw.

## Trap to pin
Store exactly `normalize_rich_text(raw)` — any other text extraction (fit/truncate/strip variants) diverges from what the same ADF decodes to on the read path and fabricates a permanent diff.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A **dict-shaped** baseline fed through the live `compute_update_fields` path yields the **same
      verdict** as its normalized-string equivalent. Tier: **integration** through the real
      production comparison path. **This test does not exist today** —
      `test_binding_baseline.py:36-59` and `test_baseline_arbitration.py:91` use flat strings only, so
      a no-op-on-strings normalizer would leave them green while proving nothing. This is the RED case.
- [ ] The direction-preservation suite, extended with assignee shape cases (email / accountId /
      displayName), passes unchanged — proving assignee arbitration is untouched. Tier: **property/unit**.
- [ ] Baseline entries for `description`/`status`/`priority` are scalars after one pass; `assignee`
      remains a dict. Tier: **integration** asserting stored shapes.
- [ ] A corpus diff over real bindings shows **zero mutation delta** before vs after normalization.
      Tier: **repo-level corpus script**.
- [ ] `bindings.json` size drops by >=50%. Verify: byte comparison before/after one full pass.

## Files
`binding_store.py`, `tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/state/test_binding_baseline.py`, `tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/diffing/test_baseline_arbitration.py`

Scope: S-M. Depends on A2-1.
baseline.summary: A3: text-normalize baseline description/status/priority in set_baseline (assignee deliberately excluded)
