## Context
The completed Gerrit Verified latency RCA optimized the macOS completion path, but Ubuntu jobs still occupy scarce org-wide runners for 11-14 minutes and contribute to queue contention. Follow-up questions identify three candidate levers: replace repeated Pandoc corpus rendering with static expected results plus a smaller boundary test, remove redundant work from the exhaustive 1,440-minute bridge cadence proof, and determine whether expensive Jira DC-oriented default-tier tests can move out of the per-change hot path while retaining fast unit coverage. The genuinely live tests/external/live_jira_dc suite is already excluded from Gerrit Verified by the `not external` selector and runs in its dedicated harness; moving that suite again would save zero. This work must preserve behavioral coverage and must not use extra parallel jobs or unchanged aggregate runner usage.

## Plan
- Build a dated Ubuntu runner-time dossier from final post-remediation run 31752047186, pytest duration logs, workflow routing, and focused local runtime experiments.
- For Pandoc and render_unit, map every current assertion to the code boundary it exercises. Include both full-corpus consumers: test_wiki_render_corpus.py (~884 pass-1 subprocesses plus additional passes) and test_wiki_render_hardening.py (~1,768 subprocesses for byte-equivalence). Compare static golden fixtures, a bounded real-Pandoc contract sample, and full-corpus external execution using defect-seeded experiments to detect any coverage loss. Treat the pinned Pandoc-version-to-output coupling as an explicit external boundary. Any accepted golden fixture must identify its Pandoc version and binary fingerprint, provide a documented regeneration command, and include a fast drift assertion that fails when the installed Pandoc version differs. The full real-Pandoc corpus must remain in the scheduled external-integration workflow as the revalidation destination, including after pin changes.
- For the bridge cadence test, discriminate between the cost of the 1,440 arithmetic checks and invariant workflow YAML I/O; prefer hoisting invariant I/O if it preserves the exhaustive proof.
- Confirm the live Jira DC suite routing, then inventory the Jira DC-oriented harness-free tests that actually execute in the default tier. Identify which, if any, exercise a genuine external boundary rather than our code, and map any proposed lane move to faster existing or new unit contracts before implementation.
- Compare each candidate with current practice in at least three named, popular, actively maintained OSS projects. Consensus means at least two-thirds of the surveyed projects, rounded up, use the practice and no surveyed project documents rejecting it for coverage or reliability; otherwise route the proposal to operator disposition.
- Search tracker history for prior acceptance or rejection of every proposal.
- Measure deterministic savings with paired before/after runs under the same environment. Report per-cell elapsed-time delta, sum the deltas across the three Ubuntu Python cells as runner-minutes freed per Verified run, and report the baseline-normalized Ubuntu occupancy reduction as `sum(cell deltas) / sum(baseline cell durations)`. This occupancy metric is the queue-pressure capacity effect; do not infer queue-wait reduction from one run. If GitHub job records expose queued/start timestamps for a multi-run sample, report the observed wait distribution separately with sample size and confidence, without attributing causality.
- Record a confirmed RCA and measured runner-time/wall-time savings. Create linked implementation tickets only for remediations that preserve coverage; under the operator standing approval, implement those meeting the defined OSS-consensus bar through Gerrit. Back-out for any merged CI behavior change is a Gerrit revert restoring the prior full per-change execution; the scheduled full-corpus lane remains available as the coverage oracle during diagnosis.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] Every Ubuntu operation or test phase over 30 seconds in the final sample is attributed to a specific mechanism and measured with a focused baseline.
- [x] The Pandoc corpus proposal covers both full-corpus consumers and has an assertion-level coverage map plus A/B runtime estimate.
- [x] The render_unit proposal has an assertion-level coverage map and A/B runtime estimate.
- [x] The bridge-cadence proposal has an assertion-level coverage map and A/B runtime estimate.
- [x] [operator-attested] The live Jira DC routing is recorded with workflow citations.
  provenance: environment=production repository workflow definition and GitHub Actions logs; principal=RebarBotNava under operator authorization; privilege_posture=production-equivalent; instrument=static-analysis — committed selectors and dedicated external-workflow routing were inspected without invoking Jira DC.
- [x] The default-tier Jira DC-oriented proposal has an assertion-level coverage map and A/B runtime estimate.
- [x] Each proposal cites tracker history.
- [x] Each proposal cites at least three named popular actively maintained OSS projects and applies the defined consensus rule.
- [x] No accepted remediation removes an assertion, behavioral equivalence class, OS/Python cell, or external boundary.
- [x] Every moved coverage boundary has an explicit destination and schedule.
- [x] Every accepted golden fixture identifies the exact Pandoc version and binary fingerprint that produced it.
- [x] Every accepted golden fixture includes a documented runnable regeneration command.
- [x] Every accepted golden fixture has a fast automated version-drift assertion and a scheduled full real-Pandoc revalidation lane.
- [x] Runner-minute savings are quantified without counting parallel matrix time as critical-path wall time.
- [x] Queue-pressure capacity savings are reported as runner-minutes freed per run and baseline-normalized Ubuntu occupancy reduction; any observed queue-wait distribution is reported separately and not presented as causal.
- [x] Every consensus-backed remediation is implemented on a linked ticket.
- [x] Every implemented remediation passes repository gates and Gerrit LLM-Review +1 plus Verified +1 before merge.
- [x] Every implemented remediation merges before this task closes.
- [x] Non-consensus or coverage-risking proposals are summarized with evidence and left for operator disposition.
- [x] The back-out path for each merged remediation is recorded as a Gerrit revert restoring full per-change execution.
baseline.summary: Reduce Ubuntu CI runner occupancy without losing test coverage

baseline.description:
Forward-looking, LOW. Not a failure on main today.

## What is actually true

tests/unit/test_advanced_cli_parsers.py::test_audit_cli_unknown_subcommand_exits_2_through_the_factory asserts that argparse error output starts with "usage:". On Python 3.14 argparse colorizes help and error output BY DEFAULT, so the captured stderr begins with an ANSI escape:

    "\x1b[1;34musage: \x1b[0m\x1b[1;35mrebar audit\x1b[0m ..."

and startswith("usage:") is False.

## Evidence, both directions

- FAILS on Python 3.14.7: 1 failed.
- PASSES on Python 3.12.13: 1 passed. .github/python-version.txt pins 3.12, and CI runs 3.11/3.12/3.13, so CI is green and main is NOT broken.
- NO_COLOR=1 makes it pass on 3.14, confirming color is the whole cause.

## How this surfaced, and the correction

It was first reported to me as "a pre-existing failure on main". That framing was wrong, and the cause was mine: I briefed a subagent to provision a worktree with a bare , which inherits the host ambient interpreter (3.14.7 here) instead of the pinned one. AGENTS.md warns about exactly this — use → uv venv --python 3.12 .venv   (pinned by .github/python-version.txt)

ERROR: could not provision .venv on Python 3.12.
       That version is what CI tests (.github/python-version.txt); this host's
       ambient python3 is Python 3.14.7.
       Refusing to fall back to it — a venv on an untested interpreter yields
       local failures CI cannot reproduce, and masks the ones that matter.
       Let uv fetch the right one:  uv python install 3.12 / usage: make worktree name=<branch> [dir=<path>]
  Creates a worktree at <path> (default ../<branch>) branched from a freshly-
  fetched origin/main, then provisions .venv + editable install + the pre-commit gate., and treat an ambient-toolchain failure as an environment error rather than repository evidence. Filing the accurate finding rather than the alarming one.

## Why it is still worth fixing

The project will hit this the moment it adds 3.14 to the CI matrix, and it is a brittle-assertion class we have already been bitten by in this epic: asserting on RENDERED text rather than on behaviour.

## Approach

Make the assertion color-independent. Either strip ANSI before asserting, or force plain output for the test (argparse accepts color=False on 3.14; NO_COLOR is the portable env-level lever). Prefer whichever keeps the test asserting the OBSERVABLE contract — exit code 2 and a usage line — without depending on terminal styling. Audit sibling tests in the same file for the same pattern.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC1: the test passes on both Python 3.12 and Python 3.14. Verified by running it under both interpreters.
- [x] AC2: it still fails if the CLI stops emitting a usage line or stops exiting 2. Verified by mutation.
- [x] AC3: sibling assertions in the file that match on rendered argparse text are audited and given the same treatment, or explicitly noted as safe.

## Testing

- python -m pytest tests/unit/test_advanced_cli_parsers.py -q under 3.12 and 3.14 — AC1-AC3.
- make lint && make typecheck.

## Completion evidence (2026-09-03) — Gerrit change 2568 MERGED

- **AC1** — verified on BOTH interpreters. 3.12.13 (what CI pins and runs): 713 passed, 1 skipped. 3.14.7 (a throwaway venv built for this): was 25 failures, now 624 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
- **AC2** — verified by mutation, two ways, against `render_parse_error` in `_cli/_parser.py`, which is the path this test actually exercises. Mutant A (`return 2` -> `return 0`): FAILED, `assert 0 == 2`. Mutant B (suppress the usage write): FAILED, `assert False`. Restored: passes. So the assertion binds on the exit code AND on the usage line, not merely on one of them.
- **AC3** — the audit went well beyond this file. Running the 31 test modules that assert on argparse help/usage text under 3.14 found **25 failures across 9 modules**, all now fixed by the same one-line change. Two of them were PRODUCT regressions rather than brittle assertions: `gen_cli_help.py --check` reported every committed `help/*.txt` stale, and `RebarHelpFormatter._format_usage` wraps on rendered line length, which ANSI escapes inflate — so usage would wrap differently for real users.

Fix: `RebarArgumentParser.__init__` sets `self.color = False`. In 3.14 `ArgumentParser._get_formatter` calls `formatter._set_color(self.color)`, so that attribute is the entire knob; subparsers inherit it via `parser_class`. The attribute does not exist before 3.14, where the assignment is inert. No new mechanism (ratchet reports new=0) — a `NO_COLOR` autouse fixture was rejected for that reason and because it would have masked the two product regressions rather than fixing them.

Trigger worth recording: this needs Python 3.14 AND `_colorize.can_colorize()` true, which requires a TTY or `FORCE_COLOR` in the environment. Plain CI with neither would have stayed green even after moving to 3.14, so the defect would have reached users before it reached the build.

Deliberate follow-up, NOT fixed here: `src/rebar/_cli/__init__.py:147` builds `bridge suggest-mapping`'s parser as a bare `argparse.ArgumentParser`, outside the RebarArgumentParser family, so its help still colorizes on 3.14 — and it also misses every other RebarArgumentParser behaviour. No test covers it; pulling it onto the shared factory is wider than this ticket.
baseline.summary: CLI parser test breaks under Python 3.14 argparse color

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem

Every other story in this epic is validated against fixtures and a stateful fake transport. That is the right tier for each of them, but it cannot exercise the failure modes that only appear against a real tracker: actual JQL evaluation over two projects, real per-project permissions and key allocation, real issue creation, and — the one that matters most — whether a pass scoped to one project can contaminate another. A multi-project bridge that is wrong in that direction writes real issues into the wrong project, which is expensive to detect and worse to undo. This story is the justified live canary the shared test-design standard allows for external-service mapping, run once the functionality is otherwise complete.

## Approach

Rehearse the whole feature live, against an **isolated store copy**, with dry-run gating at every step.

**Isolation comes first.** The rehearsal never runs against the production tickets branch. A copy of the tickets branch is published to an encrypted S3 remote — the capability delivered by epic `cf3c-1444-863e-49d7`, which is why this epic depends on it — and the rehearsal store points its `sync.remote` at that copy. Before any mutating command, the harness asserts the configured remote is the S3 copy and not the production remote, and aborts otherwise. This is a precondition assertion, not a comment: it runs first and fails the test if the store is misconfigured.

**Dry-run gating is the contamination control.** Each scenario runs `bridge preview` first and asserts the previewed mutation set contains **only** targets in the intended project, with an empty intersection against every other configured project. Only then does `bridge sync` run. A preview that names a target outside the intended project fails the scenario before anything is written — which is the same fail-closed posture as the cross-project guard, applied at the harness level.

**Project configuration.** The mapping is loaded with the two live Jira Cloud projects, `REB` and `DIG`, plus dummy projects that exist only in the mapping and never in Jira — these exercise the "configured but empty" and "unknown to the tracker" paths without consuming real projects. Repo configurations deliberately vary: one project mapped to a single repo, one mapped to two repos, and one mapped to none, so the defaulting behaviour is observed across all three shapes rather than only the common one.

**Cleanup is designed in, not bolted on.** Every issue the rehearsal creates carries a run-scoped label. Cleanup is a single JQL sweep over that label across both live projects, and the run is not considered finished until a follow-up query for the label returns zero issues in each project. The label is generated per run so a failed earlier run cannot cause a later one to delete issues it did not create.

## Scope

- `tests/external/live_multi_project/` (new) — the rehearsal harness and its scenarios
- `docs/jira-sync-setup.md` — the operator runbook for performing and cleaning up the rehearsal

## Testing

Tier: a live end-to-end rehearsal against real Jira Cloud, which the shared standard permits for external-service mapping when a fake cannot reach the mechanism — here, genuine cross-project isolation. It is gated to an opt-in external suite so ordinary CI never touches live Jira.

Scenarios, each preview-gated then applied:

- **Inbound from both projects.** An issue created in `REB` and one in `DIG` are both ingested in a
  single pass; each resulting ticket records the project it came from and the repos mapped to that
  project.
- **Outbound to both projects.** Two rebar tickets, one per project, each land as an issue in their
  own project and nowhere else.
- **Not-synced.** A ticket with an explicit empty project produces no issue in either project, and no
  outbound mutation naming it appears in the preview.
- **Legacy resolution.** A ticket with the project field absent syncs to the recorded legacy default
  and to no other project.
- **Repo-config variety, both directions.** Inbound tickets from the single-repo, two-repo and
  zero-repo projects receive exactly those repo lists; outbound tickets created under each config
  reach the correct project regardless of their repos value, confirming repos never influences
  routing.
- **Contamination guard, the negative control.** An update aimed at a project absent from the mapping
  raises `CrossProjectTargetError` in preview and writes nothing — verified by querying both live
  projects afterwards and confirming no issue changed.
- **Promote-only.** Setting a project on an unbound ticket then syncing creates the issue; attempting
  to change a bound ticket's project is refused and the existing binding is unchanged.
- **Capability stamp.** With two projects in the mapping, `.store-compat.json` carries
  `multi-project-bridge`, and a binary lacking that capability refuses to write to the rehearsal
  store.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The rehearsal aborts before any mutation if the configured remote is not the S3 store copy;
      checked by pointing it at a non-S3 remote and asserting it exits non-zero having written
      nothing.
- [ ] Issues created in `REB` and `DIG` are both ingested in one pass with the correct source project
      and repos recorded; checked by querying both live projects and asserting both tickets' fields.
- [ ] Rebar-created tickets targeting each project land in that project only; checked by querying
      both projects and asserting each issue exists in exactly one.
- [ ] A ticket with an explicit empty project creates no issue in either project; checked by a
      post-run query of both projects for the run label finding no issue for it.
- [ ] All three repo configurations produce the expected repos on inbound tickets and correct routing
      on outbound ones; checked per configuration.
- [ ] An update targeting an unmapped project is refused in preview and changes nothing live; checked
      by comparing both projects' issue state before and after.
- [ ] Every scenario's preview contained only targets in its intended project; checked by asserting
      an empty intersection against every other configured project for each preview.
- [ ] All issues created by the run are removed and a JQL query for the run label returns zero
      results in both `REB` and `DIG`; checked as the final step of the run.
baseline.summary: Live multi-project rehearsal against REB and DIG on an isolated S3 store copy

baseline.description:
## Problem
The codebase is jammed against the module-size gate. Measured on origin/main 2026-08-19, these `src/rebar` files sit within 20 lines of the 800-LOC HARD cap, two of them AT it:

| LOC | file | covered elsewhere? |
|---|---|---|
| 800 | `_engine/rebar_reconciler/inbound_differ.py` | no |
| 800 | `signing.py` | YES — `stealthy-appetizing-coelacanth`, excluded from this epic |
| 799 | `_engine/rebar_reconciler/apply_inbound_records.py` | no |
| 799 | `config.py` | claimed by in-flight work, excluded |
| 799 | `_engine/rebar_reconciler/reconcile.py` | YES — RP-03 S5, excluded |
| 798 | `_engine/rebar_reconciler/__main__.py` | handled inline by Gerrit 1916, excluded |
| 795 | `_config_sources.py` | claimed by in-flight work, excluded |
| 793 | `llm/plan_review/det_floor.py` | no |
| 793 | `llm/plan_review/__init__.py` | YES — `sullen-famished-incatern`, excluded |
| 790 | `llm/workflow/executor.py` | no |
| 790 | `llm/plan_review/sidecar.py` | YES — two open tickets, excluded |
| 789 | `llm/prompting/prompts.py` | no |
| 786 | `_commands/init.py` | no |
| 782 | `_engine/rebar_reconciler/applier.py` | YES — RP-03 + others, excluded |

The CI module-size gate is a HARD FAIL with no allowlist, and the limit in `.github/module-size-limit.txt` is LOCKED — a normal contributor change to it fails CI. So any edit to a file at 799 or 800, INCLUDING ADDING A COMMENT, fails the build.

This is not hypothetical. Gerrit change 1916 was failed by exactly this: it added a six-line justification comment to `__main__.py` (798) and landed at 804. That is a queue of latent CI failures sitting in front of anyone who touches these files next.

## Scope
This epic covers ONLY the six files with no other owner: `inbound_differ.py`, `apply_inbound_records.py`, `det_floor.py`, `llm/workflow/executor.py`, `llm/prompting/prompts.py`, `_commands/init.py`. Coverage was verified against the file_impact of all 101 open/in_progress tickets and against the prose of every open RP epic. Files owned by RP epics or by other open tickets are deliberately EXCLUDED so this epic never competes for the same file.

## Non-negotiable constraints on every child
- **Split along LOGICAL CONCERNS and ARCHITECTURAL BOUNDARIES.** Extract a cluster of functions that
  already call each other, following a seam the call graph already has. Do NOT carve mechanically to
  get under a number. The commit message must NAME the concern boundary chosen.
- **Never raise the limit.** `.github/module-size-limit.txt` is locked and is not the fix.
- **No file under 100 LOC** may be created by a split; target 200-500 LOC per resulting file.
- **Leave real headroom.** Landing at 798 recreates this exact problem for the next person — which
  is how 1916 failed. A split that buys 2 lines has not done the job.
- **Behaviour-preserving.** Existing tests for the affected area must pass UNMODIFIED. If a test must
  change, that is evidence the split was not behaviour-preserving — stop and reconsider the seam.
- **Both navigation tools.** Serena `find_referencing_symbols` for the reference set, THEN a plain
  `grep` for every moved symbol's name AS A STRING (monkeypatch.setattr, getattr, importlib).
  Serena returns EMPTY — not an error — for receivers typed `Any`, so the grep is mandatory.

## Provenance
Filed 2026-08-19 under explicit operator authorization to split files at or near the LOC cap that are not covered by existing RP epics, with the instruction that splits follow logical concerns and architectural boundaries.
baseline.summary: Restore headroom under the 800-LOC module-size cap (6 uncovered files at 786-800)

# Context

Discovered while fixing 79d6 (financial-maroon-toucan, Gerrit 1658), which unguarded the region env so every live-LLM matrix arm resolves a Bedrock region.

`tests/external/test_completion_banking_behavior_0707.py` sets `_live_llm_ready = _live_llm.live_llm_ready()` — a probe that answers "is the credential present for the provider THIS ARM resolves from the standard model class". But the module bypasses model-class resolution and pins `_MODEL = "bedrock:us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6"`. On the anthropic and openai arms the probe says READY (an Anthropic/OpenAI key exists) while every cell actually calls Bedrock — an arm that carries no AWS credential, because the OIDC step is gated `if: matrix.provider == 'bedrock'`.

A module's readiness sentinel must agree with the model it pins. Here it cannot.

It is the ONLY bedrock-pinned module in the `llm_live` lane: `test_bedrock_cache_live.py` is also bedrock-pinned but carries no `_live_llm_ready` sentinel (plain `external` + its own `REBAR_LIVE_BEDROCK` opt-in), so it runs in the complement job and is unaffected.

# Disposition — option (b) is REJECTED; do not re-litigate

**Un-gating the OIDC step to all arms is rejected**: it hands AWS credentials to arms holding third-party API keys (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` / `OPENAI_API_KEY`), widening the blast radius of the scoped Bedrock CI role for ZERO coverage gain — it would call the same model from three arms and learn the same fact three times. The OIDC step stays gated to `matrix.provider == 'bedrock'`.

Also rejected: un-pinning `_MODEL` so the eval follows each arm. The pin exists to hold the model fixed while reproducing bug 0707; unpinning turns a single-model regression reproduction into a 3x-spend cross-provider eval, which is a different test with a different purpose.

**Approved: option (a) — a provider-aware readiness sentinel.** Test-harness correctness with zero credential-surface change.

# Plan

1. `tests/external/_live_llm.py`: give `live_llm_ready()` an optional `required_provider`
   argument. When supplied, readiness additionally requires the arm's `configured_provider()`
   to MATCH it, so a module that pins a provider is ready only on the arm that runs it.
   Add a `skip_unless_provider(provider)` mark factory whose reason names the mismatch
   (module pins X, arm resolves Y) so the skip is VISIBLE, not silent. Purely additive:
   the no-argument call and the module-level `skip_without_live_llm` are unchanged, so the
   seven modules that do not pin a provider keep their exact current behaviour.
2. `tests/external/test_completion_banking_behavior_0707.py`: pass the pinned provider to the
   sentinel and apply `skip_unless_provider("bedrock")` on both tests.
3. Regression test for the invariant.

Canary-safe: the all-skip canary fires only when collected>=1 and executed==0. On a non-bedrock arm the other `llm_live` modules still execute, so the arm stays green for the right reason.

# Acceptance criteria

- [x] AC1 — A module that pins a provider is `_live_llm_ready` only on the arm that resolves
  that provider; on other arms it skips with a reason naming both the pinned provider and the
  arm's resolved provider.
- [x] AC2 — `tests/external/test_completion_banking_behavior_0707.py` uses that gate for
  `bedrock`, and modules that pin nothing are behaviourally unchanged.
- [x] AC3 — A test pins the invariant (a pinned-provider module is not ready on a mismatched
  arm, and is ready on the matching arm when its credential is present), and the rejection of
  option (b) is recorded on this ticket.
baseline.summary: Bedrock-pinned live-LLM modules lack AWS credentials on non-bedrock arms

## Summary
The store's `git commit` path (`_git_commit`, `_git_commit_paths`, and the UU-recovery commit in `src/rebar/_store/event_append.py`) lacked the object-DB transient retry that `_git_add` has. A `git commit` WRITES new tree + commit loose objects via git's same `create_tmpfile` path as `git add`; on a CI-runner FS that intermittently fails ("unable to create temporary file"). `_git_commit` retried only index.lock + "could not parse HEAD", so this transient surfaced as a hard StoreError, dropping a concurrent locked `append_event` write.

This is the intermittent failure of `tests/interfaces/store/test_enrich_drain_prune_concurrency.py::test_enrich_queue_prune_never_drops_concurrent_locked_writes` (swallowed_write_raises=1, lost=1). ~4% reproduce rate locally; seen on CI ubuntu py3.12.

## Root Cause (proven)
`_git_add` composed an object-DB retry (`_TRANSIENT_ADD_MARKERS` loop); `_git_commit` / `_git_commit_paths` / UU-recovery commit did not — asymmetric coverage left when the object-DB add retry was added (edf7/vocal-dip-robin). Proven by injection: injecting the object-DB signature into the FIRST `git commit` makes `stage_and_commit` RAISE (no retry) and lose the event; the same signature into `git add` self-heals; index.lock into `git commit` self-heals.

## Fix
Factor the object-DB retry into a shared `_with_transient_add_retry(run_once)` helper and apply it to `_git_commit`, `_git_commit_paths`, and the UU-recovery commit (and refactor `_git_add` to use it). Add a live RED test (`test_single_write_retries_transient_commit_odb_failure`) that injects the object-DB signature on the first commit and asserts self-heal.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `_git_commit`, `_git_commit_paths`, and the UU-recovery commit retry the object-DB
  transient (via `_with_transient_add_retry`). Proof: `pytest tests/interfaces/store/test_event_append_transient_retry.py`.
- [ ] A RED test asserts a commit object-DB transient self-heals; it fails if the retry is
  removed from `_git_commit` (mutation-checked).
- [ ] The concurrency test passes across repeated runs (post-fix failure rate ~0 vs ~4% pre-fix).
- [ ] make lint + typecheck pass; no existing test weakened.
baseline.summary: Store git commit drops a concurrent locked write on an unretried object-DB FS transient (enrich-prune flake)

baseline.description:
## Context

A plan-review attestation must stay valid exactly as long as the thing it certifies — the plan, reviewed against the code it reasons about — is unchanged. Two facets of the current binding are wrong, and this epic fixes both (decomposition + full rationale: session log `rich-keel-pen`, ADR `docs/adr/0002-code-drift-invalidation.md`):

- **Over-invalidation (the LIVE bug — `worm-folly-barge`/a36b).** `attest.py::claim_gate_check`
  binds freshness to the exact code HEAD sha, so ANY commit — even an unrelated file or a docs
  typo — invalidates a freshly-earned, still-correct attestation, forcing a slow, billable
  re-review for no semantic reason. (So code drift is NOT "silent" today — the binding is simply
  too COARSE; the original framing of this epic as a pure under-invalidation problem was wrong and
  is corrected here.)
- **Under-invalidation (precision goal).** Because the binding is whole-HEAD rather than scoped to
  the code the review depended on, once we narrow it we must NOT lose the ability to detect that the
  relevant code actually changed.

Both share one root cause: the code-binding is whole-HEAD instead of scoped to the review's dependency set. The material-fingerprint binding (problem-2, already shipped in `dead-stalk-chasm`: invalidate on description/AC/file_impact/decomposition edits, not on tags/comments/links/assignee) is correct and stays; this epic adds a SEPARATE, independent code-drift check ANDed with it.

## Chosen approach (and why)

**Content-addressed, dependency-scoped, no attribution.** Invalidate on *what the review depended on*, not *who/what changed the rest of the tree*. This is the consensus of every sound incremental-staleness system (Gerrit `copyCondition` `has:unchanged-files`, Bazel input-hashing, proof-caching dependency checksums) — none decide staleness by attributing a change to an author, so the "sibling exemption" concern dissolves: a sibling's edit to a shared file is treated like any edit. Concretely:

- **Dependency set** = the ticket's declared `file_impact` ∪ the files cited in its `REVIEW_RESULT`
  findings (whole-file granularity in v1; region/AST narrowing is a possible future, not configured
  now).
- **Binding** = a per-path `{path: content-hash}` map stored INSIDE the signed manifest (so drift
  detection is itself tamper-evident; today `head_sha` is unsigned audit metadata). Content-
  addressing is ancestry-independent — immune to rebases and shared-checkout HEAD moves.
- **Decision = INVALIDATE (hard block), not flag-stale.** A drifted dependency blocks the claim and
  prompts re-review, consistent with the existing gate (absent/stale signature already blocks). We do
  NOT ship a soft warning for drift.
- **Empty dependency set** (no `file_impact`, no citations) → conservative fallback: invalidate on
  any commit (today's safe behavior, now only for unscopable tickets). A new DET-floor check (`P9`)
  emits an advisory nudge to populate `file_impact` so scoping works.
- **Re-review may be narrowed (Story 2).** On pure code drift, re-running only the enforced
  code-grounded criteria (`CODEBASE_GROUNDED`) is sound and cheaper than a full re-review; the
  full re-review is the fallback.

## Hot-path budget

The drift check runs on the **claim path** (the fast, no-LLM, no-network HMAC verify; target p95 < ~50ms). Hashing the handful of dependency files is sub-millisecond, so it stays well within that budget; the check must add no LLM/network call to claim.

## Rollout / back-out

The check lives behind the existing `verify.require_plan_review_for_claim` gate. Attestations signed *before* this lands carry no `{path: hash}` map in their manifest; on first claim under the new code they are treated as needing re-review (re-run `review-plan` to earn a map-bearing attestation) — acceptable because re-review is the normal recovery. Back-out = revert the drift check; the material-fingerprint binding is untouched, so reverting cannot corrupt existing attestations.

## Decomposition

- **Story 1 — `jerky-vista-amok` (22bf):** drift detection + invalidation (full re-review on drift)
  + the `P9` empty-`file_impact` DET warning. Fixes `worm-folly-barge`.
- **Story 2 — `grace-thud-feint` (5a6c, depends_on Story 1):** narrowed delta-re-review over the
  enforced code-grounded set + chained attestation; measured before default-on.
- **Bug — `worm-folly-barge` (a36b):** the over-invalidation failing-case report; its remedy is
  owned and implemented by Story 1 and it closes when Story 1 lands.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A mechanism detects material drift in the review's dependency set (`file_impact` ∪ cited
      files), via a per-path content-hash map signed into the attestation manifest.
- [ ] Drift **invalidates** the attestation (hard block, prompting re-review); an unrelated change
      does NOT invalidate (fixes `worm-folly-barge`). Empty dependency set → conservative fallback.
- [ ] The check runs on the claim path within its latency budget (no LLM/network; sub-ms hashing).
- [ ] The novel decision is documented (ADR `0002-code-drift-invalidation.md`) and the manifest
      payload shape is pinned so Story 2's per-finding code-hash vintage composes on it.
- [ ] Tested: code drift in a dependency file after a signed review → attestation invalid; an
      unrelated commit → attestation stays valid.
- [ ] An attestation is invalidated when the code it was grounded against (its dependency set) drifts
- [ ] The drift check is content-addressed and cheap enough to run on the claim hot path.
baseline.summary: Code-drift invalidation for plan-review attestations

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem
The READ-ONLY, S3-backed live **Jira Cloud** multi-project bridge rehearsal was dropped when the effort pivoted to Jira Data Center. Sibling story 368f landed the DC harness (git/file-backed, throwaway low-volume projects). Two dimensions DC cannot exercise remain uncovered: the **S3 store backend** and **real Cloud ticket volume/diversity** across the two real Cloud projects **REB** and **DIG**. This story restores that coverage — strictly read-only against Cloud.

## Approach
Add a new opt-in live suite `tests/external/live_jira_cloud_s3/` that drives the reconciler against REB + DIG over an ISOLATED, S3-backed copy of the ticket store, using ONLY read paths proven non-mutating on Jira:
- **Inbound fetch** via `rebar_reconciler.fetcher.compute_snapshot(...)` — the
  read-only counterpart of `fetch_snapshot` (writes nothing; only issues JQL
  searches). The store's `projects.json` mapping drives a per-project JQL fan-out
  (`fetcher._build_snapshot`), so a REB+DIG mapping fetches both projects.
- **`rebar.bridge_preview(...)`** — dry-run (`Mode.DRY_RUN` → `MODE_CAPS=0` →
  `persist=False`), so no leaf applier runs and nothing is written to Jira or the
  store.
Structural read-only enforcement: an autouse fixture monkeypatches every mutating method on the Cloud transport class (`AcliClient.create_issue/update_issue/ add_comment/add_label/remove_label/set_entity_property/delete_issue/ transition_issue_by_name/unassign_issue/set_parent/update_priority/ update_issuetype/update_comment/delete_comment/delete_issue_link`) to raise, so the suite is STRUCTURALLY unable to invoke an outbound Jira mutation; read methods are untouched. Every Jira-touching scenario also asserts per-project issue counts are identical before and after (belt-and-braces). The store is a FRESH, isolated store (never the production remote): its ONLY git remote is a throwaway `s3://<bucket>/<unique-prefix>` wired via `git-remote-s3`, with `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off`. Store CONTENT is irrelevant to a read-only fetch (volume comes from live Jira), so a minimal store is the correct, lighter isolation boundary — it cannot reach production. The prefix is deleted in teardown. Avoiding the prior failure: map ONLY real, reachable projects (REB, DIG). One negative-control scenario maps an UNKNOWN key and asserts the fetch FAILS CLOSED (raises), never silently succeeds — the documented correct behaviour.

## Scope
- `tests/external/live_jira_cloud_s3/conftest.py` (new) — gating sentinel
  `_live_jira_ready` (earns `jira_live`), the isolated S3 store fixture, the
  structural read-only guard fixture, and the throwaway-prefix teardown.
- `tests/external/live_jira_cloud_s3/test_multi_project_rehearsal.py` (new) — the
  read-only scenarios below.
- `tests/external/live_jira_cloud_s3/README.md` (new) — runbook + env vars.
- `.github/workflows/external-integration.yml` (edit) — a new manually-dispatched
  `jira-cloud-s3-rehearsal` job running `pytest -m external
  tests/external/live_jira_cloud_s3 -q -rA`, plus `--ignore=tests/external/
  live_jira_cloud_s3` on the existing `external` job so it is not double-collected.
This is a test/CI-only change; no `src/rebar` runtime code changes.

## Testing
This ticket IS a live test suite. Scenarios (all read-only):
1. `test_one_store_maps_both_projects` — the S3 store maps REB and DIG with the
   expected repo lists; its only remote is the throwaway S3 prefix.
2. `test_inbound_fetch_pulls_both_projects` — `compute_snapshot` with REB+DIG mapped
   yields keys from BOTH projects at real volume (each project > 0; total in the
   thousands), every key ∈ {REB,DIG} (per-project attribution via key prefix).
3. `test_fetch_is_scoped_per_project` — REB-only mapping → snapshot ⊆ REB and zero
   DIG; DIG-only → ⊆ DIG and zero REB (mapping scopes the fetch; no contamination).
4. `test_bridge_preview_read_only_and_scoped` — `bridge_preview` plan targets only
   REB/DIG; per-project Jira counts identical before/after.
5. `test_s3_store_roundtrips_with_mapping_intact` — push the store's `tickets`
   branch to the S3 prefix, clone it back, assert the REB+DIG mapping survives.
6. `test_unknown_project_fails_closed` — an unknown mapped key makes `compute_snapshot`
   RAISE (fail-closed), never a silent empty fetch.
7. `test_read_only_guard_is_real` — calling a patched mutator raises, proving the

Local validation: `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy` on the new files; `pytest --collect-only`; then a real green `REBAR_RUN_EXTERNAL=1 pytest -m external tests/external/live_jira_cloud_s3 -q -rA` against live REB+DIG+S3.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] The new suite exists under `tests/external/live_jira_cloud_s3/`, is gated by
      `REBAR_RUN_EXTERNAL` + Jira/AWS creds, and enforces the read-only invariant

      fixture is autouse on every Jira-touching test).

      `.github/workflows/external-integration.yml`, and the `external` job ignores

      fetched into one S3 store, correct per-project resolution, read-only preview
      scoping, S3 round-trip, and ZERO Jira writes (verified: the captured
      `-rA` run output is attached as a ticket comment, showing before/after Jira
      counts equal and the guard active).
- [x] The throwaway S3 prefix is deleted after the run (verified: an `aws s3 ls`
      of the prefix returns empty, recorded on the ticket).
- [x] `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, and `mypy` pass on the new files.

## Summary

Found by the Step 7 (Axis 1 construct) sibling sweep while fixing `satiated-activated-aardwolf` (5524-e353-2e2d-4dbe). Same detect-only drift class as `CONFIG_PATHS`, but on the gerrit deploy-key materializer, which was overlooked when `materialize-g2p-config.sh` was added to `CONFIG_PATHS`.

`infra/gerrit/materialize-deploy-key.sh` is an SSM→file materializer (it puts the replication deploy key into the gerrit user's dir), a direct sibling of `infra/gerrit/materialize-g2p-config.sh`. `materialize-g2p-config.sh` IS enumerated in `CONFIG_PATHS` (detect-only, `reason=config_manual`); `materialize-deploy-key.sh` is in **no** manifest. So a merged change to the deploy-key materializer rsyncs to `/opt/rebar` and silently does nothing — the same drift class `CONFIG_PATHS` detect-only was created to make visible.

## Class-level plan (PRIMARY ticket for the manifest-omission class)

This ticket is the primary for a ONE class-level change fixing both confirmed instances of the class "an infra SOURCE that affects the running environment is absent from every path manifest in `infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh`, so a merged change to it drifts silently". The change touches ONLY `infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh` (two manifest additions) plus the new/extended regression tests. Sibling ticket `5d4c-a25b-b612-4aca` (broke-choleric-hound) is fixed in the same change.

Both instances proven at runtime with a discriminating contrast against the sibling source that IS in the manifest (see RCA comments on each ticket).

## Acceptance criteria (both instances are criteria)

- [ ] **Instance 1 (this ticket, DETECT-ONLY):** `infra/gerrit/materialize-deploy-key.sh` is enumerated in `CONFIG_PATHS` in `infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh`, so a deploy-key-materializer-only change emits `AUTODEPLOY_ERROR reason=config_manual` (parity with `materialize-g2p-config.sh`). Applying it touches gerrit — the same operator-judgement boundary as the rest of `CONFIG_PATHS` — so signal only, no auto-reload.
- [ ] **Instance 2 (sibling 5d4c, APPLY-PARITY):** `infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh` is enumerated in `MCP_PATHS`, so an entrypoint-source-only change rebuilds the MCP image via the EXISTING blue-green mcp deploy path (ADR 0079 v1 mcp auto-apply scope; reuse the existing path exactly — no new apply semantics).
- [ ] RED→GREEN regression test per instance (held out from the fixer), mirroring `tests/scripts/test_autodeploy_signals_gerrit_config.py` (instance 1) and `tests/scripts/test_autodeploy_mcp_bluegreen.py` (instance 2), each shown RED first and with mutation teeth (empty the manifest entry → back to RED).
- [ ] `observability.sh` already counts the `config_manual` signal (it counts every `AUTODEPLOY_ERROR {` regardless of reason) — verified, no observability change needed.
- [ ] `make lint` (incl. shellcheck) + full `tests/scripts` suite green.

## Structural guard (decided separately — NOT in this change)

A structural manifest-completeness guard for this class is being evaluated separately and is intentionally out of scope here. This change closes the two confirmed instances; any further same-class instances found are enumerated in the final report, not filed, per the sweep-containment directive.

## Evidence

- `CONFIG_PATHS='… infra/gerrit/materialize-g2p-config.sh …'` includes the g2p materializer but NOT `materialize-deploy-key.sh`.
- `grep -oE "^[A-Z_]+_PATHS='[^']*'" infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh | grep materialize-deploy-key` → no match.
- Runtime: deploy-key-materializer-only change → NO signal; g2p-materializer-only change → `config_manual` fires.

# Six tickets carry a FORCE_CLOSE audit record AND a certified completion attestation

## Observation, NOT a diagnosis

Found while verifying that bug 738a's fix does not make a force-close signable (it does not — that guard runs first and is now mutation-checked). Scanning the whole store for force-close audit records turned up a population I could not fully explain, so it is filed rather than folded into 738a.

```
tickets carrying a FORCE_CLOSE audit record:  146
of those, completion-verifier == certified:     6
   119f (epic)   145e (story)  93d0 (story)
   9447 (story)  e879 (story)  e95e (story)
```

All six are epics/stories, not bugs, and none carries a `close_class`. **No force-closed BUG is certified**, which is why this did not surface through 738a's own investigation.

## Why this may well be benign

A `FORCE_CLOSE` comment is a permanent audit record; it does not disappear when a ticket is later re-closed properly. So "has a force-close record AND is certified" is consistent with the documented remedy having been applied. Five of the six were signed AFTER their last force-close:

```
119f  signed 1785223166  last force 1785223127   signature AFTER force
145e  signed 1784801284  last force 1784795114   signature AFTER force
93d0  signed 1785268444  last force 1785268436   signature AFTER force
9447  signed 1785221502  last force 1785219250   signature AFTER force
e879  signed 1785665032  last force 1785625021   signature AFTER force
e95e  signed 1784248078  last force 1784346923   signature BEFORE force
```

**But none of them records `last_reopened_at`**, and the documented remedy is reopen → in_progress → re-close. A signature appearing after a force-close *without* a reopen needs an explanation.

## The leading candidate, explicitly UNVERIFIED

`sign_completion_verdict`'s docstring names a SECOND producer: "the trusted op-cert gate service's worker on a PASS verdict", which points `REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH` / `REBAR_OPCERT_ENV_ID` at the provisioned environment key and calls the same seam. That service can mint a completion cert independently of the close path, which would explain a signature landing after a force-close with no reopen — and would be entirely correct behaviour.

**I have not traced any of the six to that service.** Do not treat the above as diagnosed; it is the hypothesis a reader should test first.

## `e95e` is the odd one out

Its signature PREDATES its last force-close by ~28 hours. So whatever certifies it today was minted before the force-close, not after. That ordering is not explained by the op-cert-service hypothesis and is the most interesting single case here.

## Why it matters even if benign

`child_closure_findings` treats a valid completion attestation as sufficient for a child's closure to count as certified. If any of these six is a direct child of a parent that later closed, that parent's certification rested on an attestation whose provenance relative to a force-close is unclear. Worth settling, because the whole point of the attestation chain is that certification propagates only from verified state.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] each of the six is traced to the producer that minted its attestation (close path vs the trusted
      op-cert gate service), with the evidence recorded here
- [x] `e95e`'s signature-before-force-close ordering is explained, or confirmed as a defect
- [x] it is determined whether any of the six is a direct child whose parent's certification depended
      on it, and if so whether that parent's signature should stand
- [x] if the op-cert service can mint a completion cert for a ticket whose close was FORCED, a
      decision is recorded on whether that is intended

## Method note

Three scans returned wrong answers before this one: two pointed at a tracker copy that had none of these records, and a third used `subprocess` `grep`, which disagreed with the shell's `grep` (193 matching files vs 0). Only the pure-Python scan is trustworthy, and the numbers above come from it. An empty result from a scan is not evidence of absence until the scan itself is verified.
baseline.summary: Six tickets carry a FORCE_CLOSE audit record and a certified completion attestation

## Context / Problem

Observed in the DEPLOYED review-bot's logs (2026-08-28), once per run:

```
current gate-ref snapshot unavailable; hashing the working tree
  File "/app/src/rebar/llm/plan_review/manifest.py", line 254, in _hash_basis
    sha = resolve_ref(gate_source.default_ref(root), root, fetch=False)
  File "/app/src/rebar/_snapshot/repo_snapshot.py", line 292, in resolve_ref
rebar._snapshot.git_fetch.SnapshotRefError: cannot resolve ref 'origin/main' to a commit in '/tmp/reviewbot-cjb9jh6c'.
```

## Proven mechanism

`_hash_basis(repo_root, *, at_current_gate_ref=True)` (`src/rebar/llm/plan_review/manifest.py:246-260`) wraps the gate-ref resolution in a bare `except Exception`, logs a WARNING, and returns `_config.repo_root(repo_root)` — the in-place working tree — as the hashing basis.

Its sole production caller is the CLAIM-GATE freshness re-check (`src/rebar/llm/plan_review/attest.py:605-613`, inside `compute_validity` for `kind == plan-review`), which re-hashes the attestation's SIGNED dependency paths against that basis to decide `stale-code`.

Signing-time hashing (`manifest.py:398 dependency_hashes`, `attest.py:237 _rehash`) uses the OTHER branch (`current_code_root()`), so **no signed attestation's `verified_at_sha` or manifest hashes are affected**. The defect is entirely on the VERIFY side.

### The fallback is fail-OPEN, contrary to its own stated rationale

The docstring claims the degradation is "the conservative direction, since the checkout normally contains the drift". A runtime experiment falsifies this. With one signed attestation and a genuinely drifted `origin/main`, toggling ONLY whether the gate ref resolves:

* gate ref resolvable  -> `{'ok': False, 'verdict': 'stale-code'}`  (claim BLOCKED)
* gate ref unresolvable -> `{'ok': True,  'verdict': 'certified'}`  (claim ALLOWED)

Whenever the working tree happens to match the reviewed content while the gate ref has moved (a worktree not yet fast-forwarded; a checkout pinned at the reviewed SHA), the substituted basis reports NO drift and the gate certifies a stale attestation.

### Violated authority

`docs/plan-review-gate.md:1566-1574`:

    | Claim gate | **fail-closed** | a missing/stale plan-review attestation BLOCKS the claim |
    ... reserve fail-closed for the claim gate.

and ADR 0002 (`docs/adr/0002-code-drift-invalidation.md:46`) "keeping the fallback fail-closed". `verify.require_plan_review_for_claim = true` in this project's `rebar.toml`, so the gate is live.

### Reachability

The `except Exception` catches far more than a missing ref: any failure of `resolve_ref` OR `_cache.acquire` (snapshot materialization) — disk pressure, a corrupt/evicted cache entry, a lock timeout, a transient git fault — degrades the same way, on the on-box MCP server (`REBAR_ROOT=/var/gerrit/site/mcp-code`) where claims are actually decided. The only trace is a WARNING line.

In the review-bot's own clone (`gerrit_client.py:396 clone_change_ref` does `git init` + `git fetch <url> <patchset-ref>` with NO `origin` remote) the ref can NEVER resolve, so the fallback fires on 100% of runs. There the consumer is the bugfix-size gate, whose `ACCEPTED_VERDICTS = {certified, stale-code, stale-head}` absorbs both outcomes — so the observed log line does not change the review-bot's vote. The review-bot is the messenger, not the victim.

## What is NOT the defect

The fallback's EXISTENCE is intended and documented (ADR 0002 "Shared ref-resolution boundary"; the operator-approved decision on ticket 72d9-8fbd-3a9e-48a6 — "source=local config or an unresolvable ref degrades to the working tree"; and the existing test `tests/interfaces/lifecycle/test_ref_coherence.py::test_hash_basis_resolution` asserts "an unresolvable ref -> degrade to the working tree (never crash)"). The fix must NOT remove it. The defect is that the substitution is invisible to the consumer, so the fail-closed claim gate silently becomes fail-open.

## Expected Behavior

When the claim gate's drift check cannot obtain the configured ATTESTED basis, it must not certify. The substitution must be visible to the verdict consumer, and the claim must be blocked with a reason naming the unobtainable basis. A configured `source=local` gate is UNCHANGED: there the working tree is the correct, documented basis, not a degradation.

## Approach

1. Keep `_hash_basis`'s public behaviour and signature exactly as today (the tested,
   ADR-documented contract). Extract the gate-ref resolution into a sibling that also
   reports whether it degraded, and have `_hash_basis` delegate to it — preserving the
   ADR 0002 "ONE shared ref-resolution boundary" invariant.
2. In `compute_validity`'s plan-review drift arm, consume the degradation signal: when
   the gate is configured ATTESTED and the basis degraded, return the existing
   `stale-code` verdict with a reason naming the unobtainable gate ref, instead of
   comparing hashes against a substituted tree.
3. Reuse the EXISTING `stale-code` literal deliberately: it is already in
   `bugfix_size_gate.ACCEPTED_VERDICTS`, so the review-bot's vote is unchanged (it
   already lands on `stale-code` for most runs today), while the claim gate blocks.
   No new verdict literal, no change to `KNOWN_VERDICTS`.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/manifest.py`
- `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/attest.py`
- `tests/interfaces/lifecycle/test_ref_coherence.py`

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] With an attested gate config, a signed attestation whose dependency drifted on the
      gate ref, and a working tree still matching the signed content: the claim gate
      returns `ok=False` / `verdict=stale-code` when the gate ref CANNOT be resolved
      (today it returns `ok=True` / `certified`).
- [x] The denial reason names the unobtainable gate ref rather than claiming the files
      drifted.
- [x] With the gate ref RESOLVABLE, every existing behaviour is unchanged: committed
      drift in a signed dependency still invalidates; an unrelated committed change and an
      uncommitted working-tree edit still do NOT.
- [x] A configured `source=local` gate is unchanged (working-tree basis on both sides; no
      degradation reported).
- [x] `_hash_basis(..., at_current_gate_ref=True)` still returns the working-tree path on
      an unresolvable ref (never raises) — `test_hash_basis_resolution` stays green.
- [x] No new verdict literal: `bugfix_size_gate.KNOWN_VERDICTS` is untouched and the
      review-bot's bucket for these runs is unchanged.
- [x] `make lint`, `make typecheck`, and the default pytest suite exit zero.
baseline.summary: Claim gate fails OPEN when the current gate ref cannot be resolved: _hash_basis silently substitutes the working tree

## Context / Problem

A rebar ticket carries no record of which tracker project it syncs into, nor which repos it belongs to. The current ticket state fields are seeded in `src/rebar/reducer/_state.py:29-81` and declared in `src/rebar/schemas/ticket_state.schema.json`; neither includes a project. Today the project is only implicit — recoverable from a bound issue's key prefix in `bindings.json`, and absent entirely for a ticket that has never been bound. Epic `0e68-41eb-5782-4336` needs it explicit, because a ticket that is deliberately not synced has no binding to infer from.

## Approach

Add two ticket state fields together, in one edit set: `bridge_project` (string) and `repos` (list of strings). They are one story rather than two because a field is not usable without its write path, and splitting them would put two children on `src/rebar/_commands/composer.py`.

`bridge_project` is **tri-state**, mirroring the established `file_impact_scope` undeclared/none/paths pattern (`docs/ticket-model.md:210-212`): absent means legacy, an explicit empty string means never sync, and a key means sync there. The three states are distinguished so a pre-feature store is not read as "every ticket is unsynced". Resolution of the absent state is not implemented here — it belongs to `resolve_project` in the mapping module.

Both fields are written into the CREATE event data by `create_core` (`src/rebar/_commands/composer.py:169-220`), projected by the reducer, and seeded in `make_initial_state`. Create-time arguments `--bridge-project` and `--repos` are added to all three write surfaces — CLI (`composer.create_cli`), library (`src/rebar/_lib_writes.py:79-135`), and MCP (`src/rebar/_mcp_writes.py:47-70`). Note the CLI flag loop rejects unknown options strictly (`composer.py:287-291`), so the new flags must be registered there or they are hard errors.

`bridge_project` is **promote-only**: setting it on a ticket with no binding is allowed, changing it on a ticket that already holds one is refused. That keeps the change free of any issue-move or unbind/rebind machinery. `repos` stays freely editable — it never reaches the tracker, so there is no binding to invalidate.

No schema version bump: `docs/event-schema.md:124-150` states additive fields on an existing event type do not require one. Types are generated from the schemas (`reducer/_state.py:11-13`), so the generator is re-run.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/schemas/ticket_state.schema.json`
- `src/rebar/reducer/_state.py`
- `src/rebar/reducer/_processors.py`
- `src/rebar/_commands/composer.py`
- `src/rebar/_lib_writes.py`
- `src/rebar/_mcp_writes.py`
- tests under `tests/`

## Testing

Tier per the shared standard: a producer/consumer contract test for the event→state path (real CREATE event fed through the real reducer, no stubbing), plus a real CLI subprocess test for the argument parsing, since the strict unknown-option rejection is itself part of the mechanism.

- Happy path: `create task "t" --bridge-project REB --repos rebar,api` produces a ticket whose state
  shows `bridge_project == "REB"` and `repos == ["rebar", "api"]` after a full replay.
- Three-state coverage: a ticket created without the flag replays with the field **absent**; one
  created with an explicit empty value replays with `""`. These must be distinguishable — asserting
  the absent case is not merely falsy is the point of the test.
- Cross-surface parity: the same ticket shape results from the CLI, the library, and MCP.
- Failure path: an edit setting `bridge_project` on a ticket that already holds a binding is refused
  with a non-zero exit and the stored value is unchanged; the same edit on an unbound ticket succeeds.
- Collateral invariant: replaying a ticket created before this change yields identical state apart
  from the two new keys.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `bridge_project` and `repos` are declared in the ticket state schema, seeded in
      `make_initial_state`, and projected by the reducer; checked by a replay test asserting both on
      a freshly created ticket.
- [ ] `--bridge-project` and `--repos` exist on the CLI, library and MCP create paths and produce
      identical state; checked by a per-surface test comparing the resulting ticket state.
- [ ] The absent, explicit-empty, and set states are distinguishable after replay; checked by a
      parameterized test asserting each of the three separately.
- [ ] Setting `bridge_project` on a bound ticket is refused while setting it on an unbound ticket
      succeeds; checked by a paired test covering both directions.
- [ ] A ticket created before this change replays to the same state apart from the new keys; checked
      by a fixture-based regression test.
baseline.summary: Ticket fields: tri-state bridge_project and repos, with create-time arguments on all three write surfaces

## Why

The cross-cutting requirement is ONE shared registry consumed by all gates. The risky core is
already shared (`review_kernel/` verify/decide/coach — both gates consume it). But the
registry/descriptor layer is duplicated: plan-review has `load_criteria()` (a merged descriptor);
code-review (`b744`) has only `routing_index()` (raw routing, no descriptor loader, no
`facet/checklist`, and a **deliberately divergent** `blocking_enabled` vs `default_posture`). This story unifies them into `rebar.llm.criteria`. **b744 has LANDED on `main`** (PR #102), so
`code_review/` is available and this capstone is now workable.

## What

- Introduce `rebar.llm.criteria`: the shared merged-descriptor abstraction + loader both gates
  consume (generalize plan-review's `load_criteria`; give code-review the descriptor it lacks).
- Reconcile the **deliberate** posture divergence in one `threshold_for` that honors BOTH
  `default_posture` (plan-review) and `blocking_enabled` (code-review) — do NOT "fix" the
  divergence away.
- Exec-tier-polymorphic criteria: LLM overlays (prompt+contract+routing) AND prompt-less DET
  invariants (the 2 security keys live only in code-review's `criteria_routing.json` today).
- Route code-review's `OVERLAY_IDS` / `routing_index` / `threshold_for` through the shared
  `effective_criteria` so code-review also gets project criteria + the `.rebar/` overlay.
- **Preserve `review_code` / `code_review/shim.py`'s `review_result` return shape** — a
  back-compat surface consumed by MCP `review_code`, CLI `rebar review-code`, and the Gerrit
  `review_bot/adapter.py`.
- Docs/ADR: the how-to for authoring/activating/eval'ing/blocking on a criterion across gates.

## Scope

- Files: new `src/rebar/llm/criteria/` (shared); `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/registry.py` +
  `code_review/registry.py` (delegate to it); `code_review/` attestation port.
- Migration is expand-contract; rollback = fail-open to packaged (overlay absent ⇒ both gates
  behave as today). A misbehaving unified registry falls back per-gate.
- BLOCKED ON `b744` (epic `3156` already `depends_on b744`).

## Scope-narrowing + threshold_for design (remediation, run 1)

### Coherent single concern (clears G5 — no child decomposition)
This story is the **shared registry layer + posture reconciliation + docs** — ONE concern. The
cross-gate **attestation port** (`attest.py` → code-review + code-review `registry_version`) is
explicitly OWNED BY STORY `08af` (the attestation/invalidation story), NOT duplicated here; and
the DET-invariant consumer generalization is story `7f0d`. So the AC set below is the unification
core only (≤6 ACs, one architectural seam), not an epic-of-epics.

### `threshold_for` gate-dispatch (clears E2)
The unified `threshold_for(criteria, *, gate)` takes a **`gate` argument** (`"plan_review"` |
`"code_review"`) and applies that gate's OWN blocking convention over the SAME shared routing
records — it does NOT collapse the divergence:
- `gate="plan_review"` → a criterion blocks when its `default_posture == "blocking"`;
- `gate="code_review"` → a criterion blocks when its explicit `blocking_enabled` is true.
Both read `block_threshold` the same way (min over the criteria). Each gate's existing call site
passes its own `gate`, so neither gate's behaviour changes; the shared function just hosts both
conventions side-by-side (the deliberate posture divergence is preserved, per design).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A shared `rebar.llm.criteria` layer that both plan-review and code-review consume, replacing
      the two parallel registries.
- [ ] `threshold_for` honors BOTH posture conventions (`default_posture` + `blocking_enabled`)
      without collapsing the divergence.
- [ ] The shared descriptor is exec-tier-polymorphic (LLM overlay + prompt-less DET).
- [ ] Code-review consumes `effective_criteria` (project criteria + `.rebar/` overlay work in
      code-review too).
- [ ] `review_code` / `shim.py` `review_result` return shape is preserved (MCP + CLI + Gerrit).
- [ ] An ADR + `CLAUDE.md`/`docs/` how-to documents the unified registry across gates.
baseline.summary: Unify plan-review + code-review into shared rebar.llm.criteria (blocked on b744)

## Context

`tests/interfaces/store/test_event_append_index_lock.py::test_contended_index_lock_cleared_during_backoff_succeeds` failed on the `pytest (macos-latest, py3.13)` leg of the Gerrit Verified gate (run 31338947918, change 1575), and was reported on change 1574 in the same hour. Neither change touches `src/rebar/_store`. On run 31338947918 the three Linux legs passed the identical tree; only macOS failed, and that leg took 23m24s against ~12m for each Linux leg.

    rebar._store.event_append.StoreError: Error: git commit failed while holding lock:
    fatal: unable to write new index file

## ROOT CAUSE — PROVEN (test-timing; reproduced locally with the exact CI error string)

The test deletes **git's own real `index.lock`** out from under the `git commit` it is testing.

`stage_and_commit` runs under the exclusive store write lock, so `_git_add`/`_git_commit` (`src/rebar/_store/event_append.py`) pass `force_reclaim=True` into `gitutil._with_index_lock_retry`. Under `force=True` the age gate is bypassed, so the planted young lock is force-reclaimed on the FIRST retry rather than blocking for long:

- t=0    the test plants a young `index.lock` and arms `threading.Timer(0.4, ...)`
- t≈0    `git add` attempt 1 fails on the lock; `_reclaim_if_stale_index_lock(force=True)` removes the planted lock
- t≈0.2  `git add` attempt 2 succeeds
- t≈0.2+ `git commit` runs and creates git's OWN REAL `index.lock`
- t=0.4  the Timer fires and unlinks **whatever lock exists** — on a slow runner, git's real one, mid-commit
- git's `commit_locked_index` rename fails: `fatal: unable to write new index file`

The timer body is `lambda: lock.exists() and lock.unlink()` — no identity check, so it cannot distinguish the planted lock from git's. On a fast machine `git commit` finishes before t=0.4; on the slow macOS leg it is still holding its lock.

Local reproduction (test shape preserved, backoff widened so the timer lands inside `git commit`):

    FAIL StoreError: Error: git commit failed while holding lock:
         fatal: unable to write new index file   timer_deleted_at=[0.4314896250143647]

RULED OUT:
- **Runner resource exhaustion** — all failing job logs across the cited runs grep clean for
  `No space` / `ENOSPC` / `Cannot allocate` / runner warnings (zero hits). Slowness is real but
  is an amplifier of the window above, not the cause.
- **A real backoff race** — the production path is correct throughout: it force-reclaims the
  orphan, retries, and succeeds. No product change is warranted.
- **Lock-retry classification** — `unable to write new index file` is correctly absent from
  `_is_git_lock_error`; it is a genuine write failure and must not be retried blindly.

## Plan

Replace the wall-clock `threading.Timer` release with the seam `gitutil` already ships for exactly this purpose: `_retry_probe`, documented as "a deterministic alternative to timer-based lock release". It fires after every attempt inside `_with_index_lock_retry`, so the test can release the planted lock **only after the first failure is confirmed** — no wall clock, and no way to delete a lock git owns. Test-only change; no production behavior is modified.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `test_contended_index_lock_cleared_during_backoff_succeeds` no longer uses a wall-clock
      timer to release the planted lock, so it can never unlink a lock held by the `git add`/
      `git commit` under test.
- [x] The test still proves what it did before: a CONTENDED (young, live-peer) `index.lock`
      that is released mid-retry is ridden out and the write succeeds (`rc == 0` and the
      COMMENT event is committed).
- [x] The lock release is driven by an observed retry attempt (`gitutil._retry_probe`), not by
      elapsed time, so the test is insensitive to runner speed.
- [x] The test passes repeatedly under load locally (>= 50 consecutive runs, and under `-n 4`
      xdist) with no timing-dependent failures.
- [x] No file under `src/rebar/` is modified by this change.

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem

`caused_by` auto-derivation falls back to best-effort `git blame` over a bug's impacted paths when no `--caused-by` is supplied (`derive_caused_by`, invoked from `_commands/transition_close.py::_resolve_caused_by_culprit` only when the bug carries no `caused_by` edge yet). The edge feeds `rebar metrics`' escape-rate lenses and the epic-close `caused_by` floor, and a WRONG edge is worse than an absent one: it silently charges an escaped defect to a ticket whose reviewers could not plausibly have caught it.

Whether the file-level auto-derivation is accurate for this codebase's dominant defect shapes is an OPEN QUESTION with no direct evidence either way — see the two correction comments below. The proven part is only that the dominant defect shapes here (unmet obligations, carrier commits, omissions) are structurally hard for blame. This ticket measures rather than asserts.

## Approach

Measure the actual mechanism (`derive_caused_by`) against the actual store, read-only:

1. **Enumerate the population.** Reduce every ticket in the tracker; select closed `bug` tickets
   whose reduced state carries at least one active `caused_by` edge. Report the population size.
2. **Re-run the real deriver on each.** For every sampled bug, call
   `rebar.metrics.blame.derive_caused_by(bug_id, repo_root, tracker)` in this worktree (full
   git history, current HEAD) and compare its output to the recorded edge target:
   agreement / disagreement / abstention (`None`). Because the recorded edge carries NO
   derived-vs-explicit marker (`_apply_caused_by` writes via `_write_link_event` with no
   provenance field — verified at src/rebar/_commands/transition_close.py), this
   classification BOUNDS rather than identifies the blame-derived population, and the
   findings must say so: agreement means only "consistent with blame-derivation";
   disagreement/abstention means "not reproducible by the deriver TODAY", which is evidence
   of explicit supply but not proof, since the deriver also abstains or diverges for reasons
   unrelated to supply (fixing commit no longer resolving, `file_impact` paths renamed or
   deleted, majority dissolved by later reformat/move carriers, culprit trailer no longer
   resolving). Each non-agreement case is annotated with the deriver's observable failure
   reason (no-fixing-commit / no-file-impact / no-majority / unresolvable-culprit /
   different-target) and reported as a bound with those caveats.
3. **Score accuracy against proven origins.** For the subsample of bugs whose ticket record
   independently establishes the true origin (a root-cause comment or description naming the
   introducing ticket — the `/rebar-debug` protocol writes these), compare the deriver's output
   to that proven origin and classify each case: correct / wrong-target / abstained. Classify
   each wrong/abstained case by defect shape (unmet obligation / carrier commit / omission /
   other) so the rate connects to the shapes hypothesis.
4. **Record the two decisions** the measurement informs, with reasoning, as a findings comment:
   (a) should a blame-derived edge be distinguishable on read from a supplied one;
   (b) should the fallback decline to attribute for shapes it cannot get right.
   Any resulting schema change or review-time criterion is FILED as its own ticket linked
   `discovered_from` this one — gate/criterion changes are operator-adjudicated, so those
   tickets are proposals for the operator, not work performed here.

Default assumptions (stated so no executor question remains): the sample is the WHOLE population of closed bugs with `caused_by` edges; a proven origin exists only where the ticket record names one explicitly; history drift counts as a named limitation, not an error, when the deriver abstains for lack of the fixing commit.

## Scope

No repository file changes: measurement scripts run ad-hoc in the worktree interpreter against the store and git history; results, methodology, and decisions are recorded on this ticket. Follow-up implementation work (schema marker, deriver behaviour change, review criterion) is filed as separate tickets, not done here.

## Testing / Verification

The deliverable is a measurement, so verification is reproducibility: the findings comment must quote the exact probe snippets run (Python importing `rebar.metrics.blame.derive_caused_by` and `rebar.reducer.reduce_ticket`, executed with this worktree's `.venv` interpreter against the live tracker and git history) together with their raw counts, so any reader can re-run the same snippet and reproduce the agreement/disagreement/abstention table. The proving command for each numeric claim is that quoted snippet; the proving evidence for each decision is its recorded reasoning referencing those numbers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] [non-codebase] The rate is measured, not estimated: the population of closed bugs with
      `caused_by` edges is enumerated (size reported), the real `derive_caused_by` is re-run on
      each, and the agreement/disagreement/abstention counts are reported in a findings comment
      on this ticket, with the method stated — checked by reading the comment.
      provenance: environment=work-50e3 worktree venv, live tracker and full git history at origin/main; principal=RebarBotNava analysis agent; privilege_posture=production-equivalent; instrument=live-call — the real derive_caused_by ran on all 88 population bugs; the findings comment quotes the snippet and raw counts (agree 38 / disagree 6 / abstain 44).
- [x] [non-codebase] For every bug in the subsample with an independently proven origin, the
      deriver's output is scored correct / wrong-target / abstained and classified by defect
      shape; the proportion of blame-derivable edges naming a defensibly wrong origin is
      reported with the subsample size — checked by reading the comment.
      provenance: environment=work-50e3 worktree venv, ground truth from the store's root-cause records; principal=RebarBotNava analysis agent; privilege_posture=production-equivalent; instrument=live-call — the deriver's real output on each of the 8 proven-origin bugs was scored: correct 0 / wrong-target 1 / abstained 7, each shape-classified in the findings table.
- [x] [non-codebase] A decision is recorded on whether a blame-derived edge should be
      distinguishable from an explicitly supplied one on read, with reasoning — checked by
      reading the comment.
      provenance: environment=work-50e3 worktree; principal=RebarBotNava analysis agent; privilege_posture=production-equivalent; instrument=static-analysis — the YES decision follows from the verified absence of a provenance field at the _write_link_event call sites in transition_close.py plus the measured 38/6/44 bound; recorded in the findings comment.
- [x] [non-codebase] A decision is recorded on whether the fallback should decline to attribute
      for the shapes it cannot get right, rather than guessing, with reasoning — checked by
      reading the comment.
      provenance: environment=work-50e3 worktree; principal=RebarBotNava analysis agent; privilege_posture=production-equivalent; instrument=static-analysis — the decision (keep fail-closed as-is; shape is unobservable to the mechanism; discount via the provenance marker) is recorded in the findings comment with the 50% population and 7/8 subsample abstention figures.
- [x] [non-codebase] Any proposed review-time criterion or schema change is filed as its own
      ticket linked `discovered_from` this one rather than implemented here — checked by the
      links on this ticket.
      provenance: environment=work-50e3 worktree, live tracker; principal=RebarBotNava analysis agent; privilege_posture=production-equivalent; instrument=live-call — proposal ticket highborn-gabardine-dairycow (6536-367c-e358-424d) was created and linked discovered_from this ticket; nothing was implemented (operator-adjudicated).
baseline.summary: Measure whether caused_by blame auto-derivation is reliable for this codebase's dominant defect shapes
