## Context / Problem

At the audited snapshot, `src/rebar/llm/config.py` was 799 lines and `LLMConfig.from_env` occupied lines 566-768. ADR 0056 and closed ticket `candied-senseless-squirrel` anticipated this next headroom breach.

## Approach

Keep `LLMConfig.from_env` as the sole precedence and composition facade. Extract cohesive table-driven readers for model/provider, budgets, tracing, web, and path settings into focused sibling modules. Preserve current precedence, validation, defaults, and patch-visible exports during this extraction; the separately ADR-gated internal-shim work may later migrate private compatibility paths.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/llm/config.py`
- focused LLM configuration reader siblings
- `tests/unit/test_config_llm.py` and config precedence/patch tests

Cascade flag: true. Recensus semantic, string, dynamic-import, environment, and monkeypatch references.

## Testing

Use table-driven cases for config-file, environment, explicit override, malformed value, missing value, and cross-field precedence.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Model/provider, budget, tracing, web, and path parsing are owned by cohesive readers without duplicating precedence logic.
- [x] `LLMConfig.from_env` remains the only composition/precedence facade.
- [x] Existing defaults, validation failures, environment/config precedence, and patch-visible behavior are byte/value equivalent.
- [x] Focused config tests plus module-size, complexity, lint, and typecheck gates pass.
baseline.summary: Extract cohesive table-driven LLM configuration readers

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem

The plan-review attestation currency check `rebar review-plan <id> --status` is a read-only, no-LLM, no-network query that answers "should I re-gate before I implement?". It is exported from the library (`rebar.llm.plan_review_status`) and exposed on the CLI, but there is NO MCP tool for it. An MCP-only agent can therefore never ASK whether its attestation is current — it only discovers staleness by attempting a `claim` or a `transition ... closed` and reading the resulting error.

Found while sweeping every attestation refusal surface for bug 94a3-1323-3497-4f59, which made the refusal messages name what changed. That sweep helps a CLI agent immediately; an MCP agent still has to provoke a refusal to learn anything, which is the parity gap.

## Approach

Add a read-only MCP tool `plan_review_status` alongside the existing read tools in `src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py`, registered by `register_read_tools` with the `READ_ONLY` annotation preset (so it is present under `REBAR_MCP_READONLY` and absent from the write registrar). Its body is a thin delegation to `rebar.llm.plan_review_status(ticket_id)` — the SAME function the CLI's `--status` branch calls — imported lazily inside the tool body so the `[agents]`-extra import cost is not paid at read-registrar import time and so the delegation is observable (patching `rebar.llm.plan_review_status` changes the tool's answer).

Its return annotation is a new `PlanReviewStatusOut` pydantic model in `src/rebar/_mcp_models.py` (where every other MCP output model lives — the ticket's original scope guessed `src/rebar/schemas/`, but the JSON-Schema files there are only needed for the subset of models listed in `check_mcp_models.MODEL_SCHEMAS`, which this additive model does not join). The model declares the documented `{ok, verdict, reason, verified_at_sha, signed_at}` shape and inherits the permissive `extra="allow"` base, following `VerifySignatureResultOut`.

`docs/mcp-reference.md` is GENERATED by `scripts/gen_mcp_reference.py` from the server's own registrars and is guarded by a CI drift gate, so the doc row is produced by regenerating the file, not by hand-editing it.

Why this rather than widening an existing tool: `show_ticket` already carries a derived `plan_review_health` payload, but that is relationship/phase health, not the claim-gate currency verdict — overloading it would conflate two different questions and change an existing tool's contract. A dedicated read-only tool is additive and matches how the CLI already separates the two.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py` — the new read-only `plan_review_status` tool.
- `src/rebar/_mcp_models.py` — the `PlanReviewStatusOut` output model.
- `docs/mcp-reference.md` — regenerated so the read-tool inventory lists the tool.
- `tests/unit/test_mcp_plan_review_status.py` — the new tests.

Behaviour-preserving for every existing surface: no existing tool, model, CLI verb, or library function is modified; this change is purely additive.

## Testing

- Happy path: a ticket with a current attestation returns `ok: true`, `verdict: "certified"`.
- Failure path: a ticket with no attestation returns `ok: false`, `verdict: "unsigned"`.
- Delegation: patching `rebar.llm.plan_review_status` changes the tool's output.
- The tool is registered in the MCP read-tool set and is absent from the write set (it must
  not be gated by readonly mode).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC1 — A read-only MCP tool named `plan_review_status` is registered by
      `register_read_tools` and is NOT registered by `register_write_tools`.
      Verify: `python -m pytest tests/unit/test_mcp_plan_review_status.py -q -k inventory`
- [x] AC2 — For a ticket whose plan-review attestation is current the tool returns
      `ok: true` and `verdict: "certified"`.
      Verify: `python -m pytest tests/unit/test_mcp_plan_review_status.py -q -k certified`
- [x] AC3 — For a ticket with no plan-review attestation the tool returns `ok: false` and
      `verdict: "unsigned"`.
      Verify: `python -m pytest tests/unit/test_mcp_plan_review_status.py -q -k unsigned`
- [x] AC4 — The tool delegates to `rebar.llm.plan_review_status` rather than reimplementing
      the check; patching that function changes the tool's output.
      Verify: `python -m pytest tests/unit/test_mcp_plan_review_status.py -q -k delegat`
- [x] AC5 — `docs/mcp-reference.md` lists `plan_review_status` in its Read-only section and
      is not stale with respect to its generator.
      Verify: `grep -q '`plan_review_status`' docs/mcp-reference.md && python scripts/gen_mcp_reference.py --check`
- [x] AC6 — No existing behaviour regresses: lint, typecheck, and the MCP + doc-generator
      unit tests pass.
      Verify: `make lint && make typecheck && python -m pytest tests/unit -q -k "mcp"`
baseline.summary: No MCP tool for `review-plan --status`: MCP agents cannot ask if an attestation is current

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem
Both review gates execute criterion work through runners whose return values cannot distinguish clean execution from failed, cancelled, skipped, budget-shed, or resumed work. Plan-review failures can become empty successful checkpoints; code review loses earlier work when a later criterion raises. An effective-policy snapshot cannot fix those execution facts.

## Approach
Add a narrow shared discovery kernel as a NEW `discovery` submodule under `rebar.llm.review_kernel`, independent of that package's four-pass DECISION kernel (find/verify/decide/coach): it neither imports nor modifies `verify`/`decide`/`coach`/`verify_models`, and `__init__` gains additive exports only.

Define immutable `DiscoveryStagePlan`/`DiscoveryUnitPlan` inputs plus `DiscoveryStageResult` and typed per-unit outcomes (`success`, `resumed`, `skipped`, `shed`, `failed`, `cancelled`). A plan carries stable unit ids, dependencies, prompt/contract/model/mode identities, context/policy digests, blocking capability, budget estimate, and gate-supplied execution callbacks.

The executor owns dependency-aware scheduling, explicit positive-budget shedding, usage accumulation, cancellation observation, and success-only checkpoint envelope creation. Shedding order is deterministic — ascending dependency rank, then stable unit id; shedding a unit also sheds its unmet dependents as `skipped`, and the loop re-evaluates projected spend against the cap after each shed-plus-cascade, stopping once the kept set fits (minimal, identical across runs). After RP-01 exhausts a local operation it preserves successful independent results and continues; a dependent of missing work becomes `skipped` with a dependency reason. Systemic config/provider-init failures and cancellation abort remaining work with exact completed-so-far accounting. Verdicts remain outside the executor.

Define a new versioned, digest-complete checkpoint/trace envelope whose identity covers material, code/ref, effective-policy snapshot, prompt and contract, model/mode, topology, input context, dependencies, and a namespace version — the discovery contract/schema version, a constant in `discovery` bumped when the envelope schema changes, so identity is deterministic and a mismatched-or-absent namespace version is legacy and missing. Only `success` and content-identical `resumed` units commit as reusable successes; failed, cancelled, skipped, and shed units remain missing.

The typed trace is safe stored diagnostic data — normalized ids, outcomes, reason codes, usage, lineage only; it excludes raw prompts, ticket/context bodies, provider responses, and secrets. No per-unit trace is added to review/review-status contracts.

## Boundaries and Rationale
Keep policy selection, gate context construction, YAML/BPMN topology, provider-turn retry/output, checkpoint persistence, and final verdicts in their current owners.

Prior-art reconciliation — the kernel defines unified typed successors that RP-06's migration stories move the gates onto; current implementations stay unchanged until then:
- Budget: `sizing.shed_to_budget` treats `cap_override=None` as the centrality-scaled COMPUTED cap (not uncapped), `0.0` as a valid "shed everything" cap, and never sheds container (G3/G4) criteria. The kernel deliberately defines the simpler AC4 contract; S3 owns mapping `REBAR_PLAN_REVIEW_BUDGET`/`cap_override` and container-never-shed on explicitly, so no cost posture changes silently here.
- Checkpoint/resume: `sizing.load_checkpoint`/`save_checkpoint`/`_checkpoint_key` and `pass1.run_pass1` are chunk-keyed and can round-trip an empty-but-"successful" checkpoint; the versioned digest-complete envelope supersedes that keying (existing functions remaining until S3), and `run_pass1`'s independent finding-extension + usage aggregation is restated as typed outcomes so a later-raising unit cannot erase earlier successes.
- Cancellation: the cut point is reused verbatim from `generation.review_cancelled()` (observed BEFORE dispatch; an already-dispatched non-interruptible call is sunk cost and commits as its true `success`/`failed` outcome with real usage; a not-yet-dispatched unit is `cancelled`), so no new mechanism and AC3's accounting is total.
- Scheduling vs `workflow/executor.py`: the discovery kernel is a thin linear SYNCHRONOUS pass ordering review-criterion units by `graphlib.static_order` — the SAME primitive and the same no-asyncio/threads/retry discipline ADR 0065's Burr tripwire protects — not a second scheduler. It does not reuse that executor because the domains differ (workflow steps carry `${{ steps.x.outputs }}` templating, registry dispatch, WORKFLOW_RUN/STEP RunState/RunRecorder; discovery units carry typed outcomes, shedding, the envelope). Shared primitive reused, interpreter not forked; no ADR 0065 trigger fires.

The per-unit dependency graph and `skipped`-with-dependency-reason are the shared-substrate contract, NOT a current gate edge: today plan-review Pass-1 chunks/agent criteria fan out INDEPENDENTLY (a failed chunk merely counted in `chunk_errors`) and code-review runs each criterion independently — so for both current gates the graph is EMPTY and scheduling is independent fan-out. The typed edge exists so a migration story composing a unit that consumes another's result expresses a skip-on-missing dependency as a first-class `skipped` outcome, not a silently-emptied success. Introducing it now, empty-graph path tested, keeps the envelope's dependency digest stable across migrations.

## Testing
In-process contract tests with the real plan/result/envelope codecs and an injected stateful fake only at the model-call boundary, asserting exact call order, outcomes, usage, checkpoint eligibility, collateral state, and a clean retry after injected local failure. Negative controls prove a systemic failure aborts and a failed/shed/cancelled result never round trips as success. Covered: the empty-graph fan-out path; a cancellation where an in-flight call completing after the signal commits as its true outcome while a not-yet-dispatched sibling is `cancelled`; a budget case with an identical shed set across runs, zero rejected, omission uncapped.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] `DiscoveryStagePlan` and `DiscoveryStageResult` represent stable unit identity, dependencies, blocking capability, usage, and all six outcome kinds without gate-specific verdict fields.
- [x] The discovery contracts live in a new `rebar.llm.review_kernel.discovery` submodule with additive `__init__` exports and no change to the existing `verify`/`decide`/`coach`/`verify_models` symbols.
- [x] Given one exhausted local failure, the real executor retains earlier successes, executes later independent units, and marks dependent units skipped with the missing dependency id.
- [x] Given a systemic initialization/configuration failure or cancellation, the executor stops scheduling new work and returns exact completed, failed, and cancelled accounting without fabricating usage or findings; a unit whose non-interruptible call was already dispatched when cancellation is observed commits as its true `success`/`failed` outcome with real usage; a not-yet-dispatched unit is `cancelled`.
- [x] A positive explicit budget deterministically sheds work that does not fit — in ascending (dependency rank, unit id) order so the shed set is identical across runs; omission is uncapped and zero is rejected rather than interpreted as disablement.
- [x] The versioned envelope round-trips only digest-complete, content-identical success/resume records; injected failed, cancelled, skipped, shed, corrupt, and legacy envelopes stay missing.
- [x] Stored trace serialization contains normalized outcome metadata and lineage but no raw prompt, ticket/context body, provider payload, or secret, and public review result schemas remain unchanged.
- [x] Fault-injection tests prove restoration plus a clean rerun succeeds and unrelated success state is unchanged.
baseline.summary: RP-06 S2 — Build typed discovery execution and trace contracts

baseline.description:
# Committed store compatibility record with a fail-closed capability gate

Introduce a committed store-level compatibility record (`format_version` + `required_capabilities`) that a v1.0 binary reads before any mutating or externally-publishing operation, failing closed on an unknown version or required capability while keeping reads and diagnostics available. (Readiness Finding 2 — verified VALID against `src/rebar/_store/ensures.py`, `src/rebar/reducer/_version.py`, `src/rebar/_commands/{compact,fsck,init}.py`, `docs/migrations.md`.)

## Why

rebar's migration mechanism is an idempotent desired-state ensure-registry, not an ordered ledger: `run_ensures` runs every unit under the write lock, converts exceptions to `failed`, and **returns normally** (`src/rebar/_store/ensures.py` docstring "Never raises"; init/boot never abort). Event compatibility is preserve-and-ignore: unknown event types are skipped in replay (`reducer/_replay.py:195-196`) and omitted from the compaction fold but kept on disk (`_commands/compact.py:179-195`), and `fsck` emits an informational WARN that does not increment `issue_count` or stop operation (`_commands/fsck.py:229-252`, which itself notes "a reconcile host on an old binary may push stale state").

This forward-compat is correct for *optional additive* data — it prevents an old compactor from deleting new bytes. But there is **no committed store-format-version or required-capability record** (confirmed absent; `SCHEMA_VERSION` is a stamp, never compared to fail closed). So an old binary computes state that omits the unknown event and can then emit a new event, compact, evaluate close/verify policy, or push a stale field to Jira from that incomplete state. `docs/migrations.md` explicitly files the "A-tier ledger + committed store-format version that fails closed" under future work. **The reader must ship in v1.0**: an already-installed v1.0 binary cannot be taught later to inspect a record whose existence and semantics were not defined in v1.0 — so to ever mark a store as requiring a post-v1.0 capability, v1.0 must already know how to detect and refuse unknown required capabilities.

## What

Adopt git's repository-format-version pattern (`core.repositoryformatversion` + `extensions.*`: an implementation that does not understand the advertised format or a required extension must not operate, because continuing can produce incorrect results or lose data), and git's staged rollout (teach readers first, make writing opt-in, default later):

- **The record.** Add a committed store-level record, minimally
  `{"format_version": 1, "required_capabilities": []}`, at a fixed store path (e.g.
  `.store-compat.json`). It is **committed to the `tickets` branch** (not
  git-ignored) — it is the shared fact the gate reads. Write it with the store's
  standard write-to-tempfile-then-atomic-rename pattern so a partial/interrupted
  write never leaves a truncated file.
- **Recognised-capability vocabulary.** The new module exports
  `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES: frozenset[str] = frozenset()` — the set of capability strings
  **this** binary understands. The gate blocks when any entry in a record's
  `required_capabilities` is not in `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES`. Future capabilities are
  added to this set only when the feature that consumes them ships (git
  `extensions.*` semantics).
- **The gate error.** The module exports `StoreIncompatibleError(Exception)`, raised
  by the gate; entry-point callers convert it to the existing `CommandError` /
  non-zero exit path (as other gate errors do), with a message naming the
  unsupported version/capability.
- **Four record states (explicit).** (1) **Absent** → implicit legacy format
  version 0, compatible / pass-through, NOT blocked. (2) **Present + compatible** →
  pass. (3) **Present + incompatible** (unknown `format_version` or a
  `required_capabilities` entry ∉ `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES`) → **fail-closed**. (4)
  **Present + unreadable/corrupt** (JSON parse error, truncation, permission denied)
  → **fail-closed** with a diagnostic message naming the parse error and the record
  path (a corrupt record is NOT treated as absent — that would silently bypass the
  gate).
- **Expand phase (writing the record into pre-v1.0 stores).** Every store created by
  a pre-v1.0 build is state (1). An idempotent ensure unit (School B) writes the
  record at the current version when absent, at init / fsck-repair / MCP-boot.
  **Because `run_ensures` is fail-silent** (a `LockTimeout` silently skips the whole
  sweep; exceptions become `failed` and it returns normally), the covered-write path
  must not *depend* on the ensure sweep having run: the gate treats absent as
  pass-through regardless, and the record is written opportunistically. So a missed
  sweep never blocks writes — it only defers stamping the record to a later covered
  operation. **absent = legacy/needs-migration, not blocked; present-incompatible or
  corrupt = blocked.**
- **Gate at the true structural choke point, NOT by enumerating call-sites.** "No
  mutation without the gate" must not rest on a hand-maintained list a future path can
  bypass. The single convergence point for **all lock-based store mutations** is
  **`lock.acquire()` in `src/rebar/_store/lock.py`** — both the `write_lock()` context
  manager AND the direct callers that bypass it (`txn.py`'s `_acquire_write_lock` for
  claim/transition, `compact.py:167`/`:415`, `fsck.py:419`) call `acquire()`. Insert
  the `check_store_compat()` gate **inside `lock.acquire()`**, after `canonical_tracker()`
  resolves the path and before the fcntl/mkdir legs — so every lock-holding path
  (context-manager and raw-handle) is covered by one insertion point, with no
  enumeration. **Gate ALL `lock.acquire()` unconditionally — no `read_only` parameter
  needed.** The diagnostic exemption is already **structural**: `fsck`'s diagnostic
  path reads ticket data **without acquiring the lock at all**, so it is inherently
  ungated and stays available; only `fsck`'s **repair** path (which *does* call
  `lock.acquire()` at `fsck.py:419`), and `compact.py`/`txn.py`, hold the lock and are
  therefore gated. This is simpler and less error-prone than a read/write-intent flag.
- **Two paths do NOT go through `lock.acquire()` and each gets its own explicit gate:**
  1. **`fsck_recover.py`** performs raw `git cherry-pick`/`rebase --continue`/`merge
     --abort` via its `_git()` helper with **no locking at all** — so it is genuinely
     un-gated by the lock choke point. Add an explicit `check_store_compat(tracker_dir)`
     at the top of `fsck_recover_cli` before any mutation. (Wrapping the mutation block
     in `write_lock` too would additionally close a real pre-existing concurrency gap,
     but at minimum the explicit gate is required.)
  2. **Outbound Jira publish** — the push/reconcile side effect is a **remote API
     call**, not a lock-held write. Jira writes are scattered
     (`create_issue`/`update_issue`/`delete_issue`/`add_comment` across
     `apply_outbound.py` + `dispatch_one.py`), but they all funnel once per pass
     through **`reconcile._apply_mutations()`** (`src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/reconcile.py`,
     which calls `applier.apply(...)`). Gate there, **after the `persist=True` check**
     (so dry-run / reconcile-check / cap-0 no-write passes are excluded) and before
     `applier.apply()` — mirroring the existing fail-closed cross-project guard
     precedent at `applier.py:637-652` ("refuse BEFORE issuing any Jira write … abort
     the whole pass, no partial writes"). **Use the reconciler's own tracker path**
     (`repo_root / ".tickets-tracker"`, hardcoded at `reconcile.py:133/670`), NOT
     `config.tracker_dir()`, since the reconciler resolves the store directly.
- **Completeness is CI-enforced.** A coverage test/lint greps the tree for **both**
  `lock.acquire(` and `write_lock(` (and asserts each routes through the gate) plus
  asserts `fsck_recover_cli` calls `check_store_compat` — so a new un-gated write path,
  in any of the acquisition forms, fails CI rather than relying on this prose list.
- **Read/diagnostic allowance.** Under an incompatible/corrupt record, the read-only
  commands — `fsck` (diagnostic mode), `show`, `list`, `search` — stay available
  (exit 0) and report the unsupported version/capability (structured, machine-checkable
  output). `fsck`'s **repair** mode (write-intent) is gated like any other mutation.
- **Rollback safety (decided, then proven).** Post-rollback the committed
  `.store-compat.json` remains on the `tickets` branch unchanged, and a pre-v1.0 binary
  **ignores it** (ignored-unknown → rollback-safe): `.store-compat.json` is a *new*
  file at a path no pre-v1.0 code reads — pre-v1.0 replay/compaction/fsck open only
  event files and the known metadata files (`.env-id`, `.gitignore`, etc.), never this
  name — so there is no parse-and-error path. This is the committed design position
  (not a deferral), and the **hard rollback test below is its empirical proof** (git-
  stash the gate code, run `rebar fsck` against a store containing `.store-compat.json`,
  assert operable + file byte-unchanged). The delete-`.store-compat.json` recovery is
  documented as belt-and-suspenders only.
- **Scope boundary.** Keep the ensure-registry for convergent check-then-act repairs.
  Do **not** build the ordered ledger here — only the record + reader gate. Clarify
  the relationship to `SCHEMA_VERSION` in `reducer/_version.py` (it stays the
  event-schema discriminator; `format_version` is the new store-format gate — state
  whether they move together or independently).

## Scope

- New module under `src/rebar/_store/` for the compatibility record + gate, exporting
  `StoreIncompatibleError`, `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES`, and `check_store_compat()`.
- `src/rebar/_store/lock.py` — insert the gate inside `lock.acquire()` (the single
  convergence point for `write_lock()` + all direct `lock.acquire()` callers:
  `txn.py`, `compact.py:167`/`:415`, `fsck.py:419`), gating every acquisition
  unconditionally (fsck diagnostic holds no lock → structurally exempt).
- `src/rebar/_commands/fsck_recover.py` — explicit `check_store_compat()` before its
  raw-git mutation (it holds no lock, so the `lock.acquire()` gate does not cover it).
- `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/reconcile.py` — `check_store_compat(repo_root/".tickets-tracker")`
  at the top of `_apply_mutations()` after the `persist=True` check (the single
  per-pass chokepoint for both write paths; excludes dry-run/cap-0 passes).
- A coverage test/lint grepping `lock.acquire(` + `write_lock(` + `fsck_recover`'s check.
- `src/rebar/reducer/_version.py` — relate `format_version` to the existing
  preserve-and-ignore `KNOWN_EVENT_TYPES` machinery and to `SCHEMA_VERSION`
  (optional-additive events stay preserve-and-ignore; a required capability is the
  new fail-closed path).
- `src/rebar/_commands/init.py` — the ensure unit that writes the record when absent.
- `docs/migrations.md` — document the record, the four states, the fail-closed
  semantics, the absent-record upgrade path, and the concrete rollback state.
- Interface tests extending `tests/interfaces/contracts/test_event_schema_forward_compat.py`.
- Out of scope: the ordered migration ledger; changing any existing event-replay
  behaviour for currently-known types.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A committed store compatibility record (`format_version` +
  `required_capabilities`) is created at init at a fixed path, written atomically
  (tempfile + rename), and read by a gate function that raises
  `StoreIncompatibleError`; the module exports `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES: frozenset[str]`.
- [ ] An **absent** record (pre-v1.0 store) is treated as legacy format version 0 /
  compatible (pass-through, not blocked), and the ensure unit idempotently writes the
  record on the next init / fsck-repair / MCP-boot — verified by a test that opens a
  record-less store with a v1.0 build, confirms it operates, and confirms the record
  is then present (upgrade-in-place, no manual step); the test also confirms a missed
  ensure sweep does not block writes — by monkeypatching `run_ensures` to raise
  `LockTimeout` (or return a `failed` outcome) and asserting a subsequent write still
  succeeds (the gate treats the still-absent record as pass-through).
- [ ] The gate is inserted inside `lock.acquire()` (`src/rebar/_store/lock.py`, after
  path resolution, before fcntl/mkdir) and gates **every** acquisition unconditionally
  — `write_lock()` context-manager callers AND direct `lock.acquire()` callers
  (`txn.py`, `compact.py`, `fsck.py:419` repair) — by one insertion point; `fsck`
  diagnostic holds no lock so it is structurally exempt. Plus an explicit
  `check_store_compat()` at the top of `fsck_recover_cli` (raw-git, no-lock mutation)
  and at the top of `reconcile._apply_mutations()` after the `persist=True` check
  (before `applier.apply()`, using `repo_root/".tickets-tracker"`) for the outbound
  Jira push. It raises `StoreIncompatibleError` (→ non-zero exit) before any side
  effect when the record is **present but incompatible**. Verified by (a) a test in
  `tests/interfaces/contracts/test_event_schema_forward_compat.py` writing a record
  with a `required_capabilities` entry ∉ `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES` (e.g. `["unknown-v99"]`)
  and driving a lock-held mutation (store files byte-unchanged), an `fsck_recover`
  invocation, and a reconcile pass (mock Jira adapter records zero calls); and (b) a
  coverage test/lint that greps the tree for **both** `lock.acquire(` and `write_lock(`
  and for `fsck_recover_cli`'s + `_apply_mutations`'s `check_store_compat` call,
  asserting each routes through the
  gate — so a new un-gated write path in any acquisition form fails CI.
- [ ] A **corrupt/unreadable** record (truncated JSON / parse error) is treated as
  fail-closed (NOT as absent) with a diagnostic naming the parse error and path —
  verified by a test writing a truncated record and asserting a mutating entry point
  is blocked.
- [ ] A rollback **test** (hard requirement) simulates a pre-v1.0 binary by invoking
  the store layer with the gate patched out (monkeypatch `check_store_compat` to a
  no-op, emulating code that predates it) against a store carrying the committed
  `.store-compat.json`, and asserts **operable** = `rebar list`/`fsck` exit 0 AND a
  normal write (e.g. `comment`) succeeds, and the `.store-compat.json` file is
  byte-unchanged afterward (proving upgrade-in-place won't brick a pre-v1.0 clone). The
  ignored-unknown guarantee and the delete-`.store-compat.json` compensating path are
  also documented in `docs/migrations.md`.
- [ ] Under an incompatible/corrupt record, the read-only commands `fsck` (diagnostic
  mode), `show`, `list`, and `search` exit with the read-allowed code (0) and their
  structured output / stderr (WARNING+) contains the unsupported version/capability
  identifier — while `fsck` **repair** mode (write-intent) exits non-zero — verified by
  a test asserting the exact field via `jq -e` / an anchored regex and the repair-mode
  non-zero exit.
- [ ] Optional additive (unknown-but-not-*required*) events retain today's
  preserve-and-ignore behaviour — the existing forward-compat contract tests still
  pass, and a new test proves a *required* capability fails closed while an *optional*
  additive event does not.
- [ ] `docs/migrations.md` documents the record, the four states, the fail-closed
  gate, the deployment-order rationale (why the reader ships in v1.0), and the
  concrete rollback state.
- [ ] `make lint && make typecheck && make test` pass, and the change lands via the
  Gerrit two-vote gate.
baseline.summary: Committed store compatibility record with a fail-closed capability gate

# `plan_review/passes.py` is now at the hard cap with zero headroom

## Context

Discovered while landing c6c9 (the `attest.py` split). With `attest.py` brought down to 656, the largest file in `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/` is now `passes.py` at **exactly 800** lines — the hard cap enforced by `tests/unit/test_module_size_contract.py::test_no_src_module_over_the_hard_cap` (limit single-sourced in `.github/module-size-limit.txt`, gate is `> limit`).

This is the identical failure mode c6c9 was raised for: the file passes only because the comparison is strictly-greater. **Any** next edit to `passes.py` — including a one-line bug fix — cannot land without first splitting it, and that cost lands on whoever next needs to fix a bug there, under time pressure, as an unrelated blocker.

Current top of the package (post-c6c9):

    800  passes.py          <- at the cap, zero headroom
    784  __init__.py
    776  pass1.py
    769  registry.py
    759  det_floor.py
    726  sizing.py
    702  orchestrator.py

Note this is a *cluster* problem, not a single-file one: seven files in this one package sit between 700 and 800. `passes.py` is the urgent one; the rest are a standing risk worth a broader look.

## Approach

Same discipline as c6c9 and 2682 — split ONLY along a seam that already exists in the call graph, never mechanically to hit a number, and never creating a sub-100-LOC file.

The c6c9 split is the worked reference for the two things that make this safe:

1. **Find the reference set with BOTH tools.** Serena `find_referencing_symbols` AND a repo-wide string `grep` for each moved symbol — the LSP cannot see `monkeypatch.setattr` / `getattr` / `importlib` targets, and an empty semantic result is not trustworthy.
2. **Watch for patch seams.** In c6c9 the moved code called two helpers that the suite monkeypatches ON the source module object; a module-level `from .x import y` in the new module would have bound the pre-patch objects and silently ignored the patches (verified: it turns 4 tests RED). Function-local imports preserve the semantics. Expect the same class of hazard here.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/passes.py` is under 700 LOC
- [x] any extracted module is at least 100 LOC
- [x] the split follows a pre-existing call-graph seam, with the caller analysis recorded in the commit message
- [x] zero test edits are required by the move, or each required edit is justified in the commit message
- [x] [operator-attested] the full suite passes with a test count equal to the pre-split count, evidenced by the two pytest summary lines quoted in a comment
baseline.summary: passes.py sits at exactly 800/800 LOC — the next file at the cap

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem

`.bridge_state/bindings.json` keeps two indexes that must stay in lock-step: forward `bindings[local_id] = {jira_key, …}` and reverse `reverse[jira_key] = local_id`. A `reverse` entry that survives removal of its forward entry is reported by `rebar bridge fsck` forever as `store_integrity` / kind `reverse_missing_forward`, and **no supported surface can clean it up** — so the binding-drift canary alerts indefinitely on a benign fault, masking any genuine future integrity problem behind a constant non-zero count.

Already happened: 13 orphaned reverse keys (REB-410…REB-422) sat in the store until repaired under nonliteral-spangly-fly (now closed), where the repair had to reach past the public API into `BindingStore._data["reverse"]` because nothing else could express it.

## The defect (verified on current origin/main @ cc69cc1179)

`BindingStore.unbind()` — `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/binding_store.py:426-430`:

    def unbind(self, local_id: str) -> None:
        """Remove binding (for cleanup/rollback)."""
        entry = self._data["bindings"].pop(local_id, None)
        if entry is not None and entry.get("jira_key"):
            self._data["reverse"].pop(entry["jira_key"], None)

It unconditionally pops the forward entry but pops the reverse entry **only if the forward entry still carries a `jira_key`** — cleanup of index B made conditional on index A, which it just destroyed. `_retire()` (`:591-592`) is the correct model: it pops both unconditionally.

**Reachability, measured not assumed.** In *current* code the guard happens to hold: `reverse` is written only where a `jira_key` exists (`:422` `bind_confirm`, `:564-565` `note_absent_or_rekey`), so `reverse[K] = L` implies `bindings[L].jira_key == K`. `unbind()` is **incidentally** safe today — safe by a whole-file invariant, not by its own logic.

**The already-realised hole:** only `unbind()` (`:428`) and `_retire()` (`:592`) remove a forward entry. Any *other* route leaks the reverse key permanently — an out-of-band prune, a manual edit, or a merge artifact. The tickets branch resolves `bindings.json` as `merge=ours` (`docs/concurrency.md:414`), so a concurrent divergence can drop forward entries wholesale with no reverse pop. That produced the 13 repaired keys.

## Approach

Two independent changes; either alone is an improvement, both close the hole.

**1. Make `unbind()` self-contained** (`binding_store.py:426-430`). Keep the O(1) keyed pop as a fast path, then sweep the reverse index for any residual key still pointing at `local_id`, so the method is correct regardless of the forward entry's contents:

    entry = self._data["bindings"].pop(local_id, None)
    reverse = self._data["reverse"]
    if entry is not None and entry.get("jira_key"):
        reverse.pop(entry["jira_key"], None)
    for key in [k for k, v in reverse.items() if v == local_id]:
        reverse.pop(key, None)

The leverage: after this, `unbind(L)` also clears a *stranded* reverse key — the forward pop no-ops and the sweep removes every `reverse[K] == L`. So fix 1 makes the orphan class expressible through the existing public API and fix 2 needs **no new `BindingStore` method** — which matters, as `binding_store.py` is 785/800 LOC.

**2. Add a supported prune verb.** New module `src/rebar/_commands/bridge_repair.py` holding `prune_orphan_reverse_bindings(tracker_dir, *, force_reason) -> int`. `bridge_fsck.main()` (`bridge_fsck.py:590`, argparse at `:606-618`) gains a `--repair` flag that delegates to it — the audit functions stay pure, preserving the L9 audit boundary (`bridge_fsck.py:199,342`). `rebar bridge fsck` already forwards REMAINDER args to `main()` (`_cli/_bridge_commands.py:117-122,201-202`), so no new CLI plumbing; only `_bridge_commands.py:59` (metavar) and `:216-220` (help text) mention the flag.

Deletion runs as `store.unbind(local_id)` per audited orphan, then one `store.save()` (atomic tempfile + `os.replace`, `binding_store.py:292`) — never a raw rewrite, never a `_data` reach.

The verb takes its finding set from the existing `audit_store_integrity()` (`bridge_fsck.py:198`) rather than re-deriving orphans — the repair-consumes-the-detector discipline of `tracker_maintenance.py:93` — and applies four guards, each aborting before any write:

1. every `store_integrity` finding must be kind `reverse_missing_forward` — refuse if another
   kind is present (never repair a store carrying an unaudited fault);
2. no orphan key may appear in `bindings-retired.json` (retired means tombstone, not delete);
3. no orphan key may have a forward binding under any spelling;
4. post-deletion the forward map must be unchanged and no orphan may remain.

A durable audit line follows the `tracker_maintenance.py:100-118` model — one `json.dumps` line in the tracker's **git dir**, not the worktree, so it never becomes merge-conflicting store content — recording timestamp, actor, argv, deleted keys, and before/after counts.

**Exit codes:** `0` healed or nothing to do, `1` a guard refused, `2` operational failure.

## Scope

See the recorded `file_impact` for the exact path set.

**Out of scope (deliberate, minimal surface):** exposing the prune through the library facade or MCP — it is an operator break-glass, not an agent-callable write. Follow-up if wanted.

## Testing

Fixtures follow the existing local helpers — `BindingStore(tmp_path / ".tickets-tracker")` + `bind_confirm` (`tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/test_binding_walk.py:58-63`) and the raw-JSON tracker builders in `tests/scripts/bridge/test_bridge_fsck_binding_drift.py`.

- **RED (pins fix 1):** store with `reverse[K] = L` where `bindings[L]` exists but carries no
  `jira_key`; `unbind(L)`; assert `K` is gone from `reverse`. Fails today.
- **Regression:** `unbind()` on a normally-confirmed binding still removes both indexes.
- **Prune:** happy path, refusal on a foreign integrity kind, refusal on a retired orphan key,
  and no-op on a healthy store — one test each, as enumerated in the criteria below.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `unbind()` removes the reverse entry without reading the forward entry's `jira_key`.
      Verified by the RED test: it fails on `cc69cc1179` and passes after the change.
- [x] `unbind()` on a normally-confirmed binding still clears both indexes. Verified by the
      regression test above.
- [x] `rebar bridge fsck --repair` reduces `store_integrity` from N to 0 on a store seeded
      with N `reverse_missing_forward` orphans. Verified by the prune happy-path test.
- [x] The prune mutates no forward entry: `bindings` is byte-identical before and after.
      Verified by comparing the serialised forward map in the happy-path test.
- [x] The prune leaves `bindings-retired.json` byte-identical. Verified by a sha256 compare
      in the happy-path test.
- [x] The prune exits 1 and writes nothing when any non-`reverse_missing_forward`
      `store_integrity` kind is present. Verified by the refusal test.
- [x] The prune exits 1 and writes nothing when an orphan `jira_key` is present in
      `bindings-retired.json`. Verified by the retired-guard test.
- [x] The prune exits 0 and mutates no file on a healthy store. Verified by the no-op test
      asserting the `bindings.json` mtime and bytes are unchanged.
- [x] The prune performs deletion via `BindingStore.unbind()` + `save()`. Verified by
      `grep -n "_data" src/rebar/_commands/bridge_repair.py` returning no match.
- [x] `bridge_fsck.py`'s audit functions are unchanged apart from `main()`'s flag dispatch.
      Verified by `git diff` touching only `main()` in that file.
- [x] `make lint` passes.
- [x] `make typecheck` passes.
- [x] `pytest tests/scripts/bridge tests/unit/rebar_reconciler` passes.
- [x] No `src/rebar` file exceeds 800 LOC (the CI module-size gate).
baseline.summary: unbind() leaks reverse bindings when the forward entry lacks a jira_key, and no supported surface can clean them up

## Context / Problem

`7e9e-07f7-8fe1-4e38` delivered gateway correlation headers but explicitly deferred the run-level root span. The consequence is stated in that epic's Out-of-scope and is real: rebar opens no span per gate run, so `tracing.py`'s per-candidate spans are each their own trace root. A plan-review that fans out across chunk, container and verify calls therefore appears in Langfuse as many traces rather than one, and the gateway header id (minted at the boundary when nothing is recording) does not match any of them.

Prior-art review of the header design flagged this as the idiomatic end state — Langfuse's own model is one trace per unit of work — and the epic's own plan-review confirmed the shipped behaviour does not achieve it.

## Approach

Open one rebar-owned span at each gate run boundary in `workflow/gate_dispatch.py`, so every agent call in the run nests beneath it and the run is one trace. `run_identity.mint_run_identity` already prefers an active recording span's trace id over minting, so the correlation header and the exported spans then carry the same value with no further change — that read exists precisely to make this cheap.

**The span must ENCLOSE the `gate_config(...)` statement, not sit inside it.** Both sites read `gate_config(with_identity(cfg, ...))` (`:174`, `:706`), and `with_identity` is evaluated as an ARGUMENT — it runs before the `with` body opens. A span opened inside that block would therefore not be the active recording span when `mint_run_identity` fires, and it would mint anyway, silently defeating the whole change. This ordering is the load-bearing fact.

**Three boundaries, not two.** `produce_code_review_verdict` (`:372`) is the third gate-run boundary, with its own multi-pass fan-out whose per-candidate spans are equally separate trace roots. It is IN scope: it opens no `gate_config`/`with_identity`, so it gains the one-trace- per-run grouping but not header correlation — which is the right outcome, since `review-code` has no ticket and its `${run:...}` headers are omitted by design.

Contextvar propagation into the parallel fan-out already works (`generation._submit_ctx` runs each pool task under `copy_context()`), so no threading work is required.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/llm/workflow/gate_dispatch.py` — open the run span ENCLOSING all three
  boundaries (`:174` plan-review, `:706` completion, `:372` code-review).
- `src/rebar/llm/tracing.py` — the span factory, alongside the existing `candidate_span`.
- `tests/unit/test_run_span.py` (new).

## Testing

Tier: in-process unit tests against the real tracer — span parentage runs for real in-process.

- Happy path: candidate spans opened inside a gate run share the run span's trace id.
- Parallel path: a candidate span opened inside a `_submit_ctx`-submitted pool task shares it
  too — the fan-out is the whole point, so a main-context-only assertion proves nothing.
- Edge: with no tracer configured, behaviour is unchanged and nothing raises.
- Fail-open: a configured tracer that raises on span open does not abort the run — the same
  best-effort discipline `candidate_span` follows.
- Correlation: `mint_run_identity` inside the run returns the run span's trace id, so the
  gateway header and the exported spans agree.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Two candidate spans opened within one gate run share a trace id; checked by asserting both
      against the run span's context.
- [x] A candidate span opened INSIDE a `generation._submit_ctx` pool task shares the run span's
      trace id; checked by submitting the span-opening work through the real `_submit_ctx` and
      comparing. This is the load-bearing case: the criterion above passes even if both spans
      open on the main context, leaving the parallel-propagation path — which is the entire
      reason a fanned-out run is currently many traces — unexercised.
- [x] Inside a gate run with a recording tracer, `mint_run_identity` returns that run span's
      trace id rather than a minted value — the assertion that fails if the span is opened
      inside rather than around the `gate_config(with_identity(...))` statement.
- [x] A code-review run's candidate spans share one trace id; checked by asserting two of them
      against each other, proving the third boundary is covered.
- [x] With no tracer configured the gate run behaves exactly as before; checked by asserting no
      exception and an unchanged verdict shape.
- [x] With a tracer CONFIGURED that raises on span open, the gate run still completes with an
      unchanged verdict shape — the failure is swallowed and logged, never propagated; checked
      by a test whose tracer raises, mirroring the guard `candidate_span` already uses. This is
      a new failure point whose blast radius is the whole run, and `tracing.py`'s standing rule
      is that tracing must never break an operation.
- [x] `gate_dispatch.py` stays at or under the 800-line module cap.
baseline.summary: Open a rebar-owned root span per gate run so one run is one trace

## Why
Rec 1 + Rec 9 of session-logs/2026-06-09-architecture-review.md (risks R3/R4/R5/R8/R9). 14.9k LOC of bash with ~140 embedded python3 heredocs (27 in ticket-lib-api.sh, 20 in ticket-lib.sh) is the dominant maintenance liability for agent-driven development. The hard-won lessons live in the I1-I9 doctrine, the already-Python critical sections (ticket_txn.py, reducer, graph), and the 1,400+ test corpus — not in the bash itself. The regression-safe playbook is already proven in-repo: REBAR_NATIVE_READS (commits 7d53bc5 -> a93885e): port behind a kill-switch, pin parity, soak, remove the switch.

## What
Tiered strangler-fig port; each tier spawns its own child tickets when started; the relevant bash suite is the per-command characterization gate, run against BOTH impls until byte-identical before any default flips:
- Tier A: read shims (show/list/ready/search/deps) -> dispatcher calls _reads.py (story rich-glare-sake).
- Tier B: leaf writes (comment, tag/untag, set-file-impact, set-verify-commands, archive, scratch) -> rebar._commands; may temporarily shell to the bash write core.
- Tier C: compute-heavy bash (ticket-next-batch.sh 944 LOC, validate-issues.sh 945, ticket-list-epics.sh 449).
- Tier D: the write/sync core (_flock_stage_commit, _push_tickets_branch, _reconverge_tickets) LAST, behind REBAR_WRITE_CORE=bash|python, soaked one full release on this repo's own store.
- Tier E: delete the dispatcher; cli.py becomes a real argparse CLI over the same _commands functions as the library. Unpacked-disk constraint, jq prerequisite, and flock fallback all retire here.
Test consolidation rides along (Rec 9): each ported command's bash suite is translated to pytest and retired only after the default flips and soaks; parity tests are deleted as each duplication collapses.

## Scope
The full bash engine over multiple releases; one tier (and within tiers, one command) at a time. NOT in scope: any change to the store/locking design (ratified sound) or the event schema.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Tier ordering + kill-switch discipline documented in docs/architecture.md and followed (default stays bash until parity green + dogfood soak)
- [ ] Each port ticket carries its bash suite as the characterization gate (byte-identical before flip)
- [ ] End state: one implementation + three facades; zero standalone shell test harness; no embedded heredocs
baseline.summary: Bash-to-Python strangler-fig migration (Tiers A-E, kill-switch per tier)

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem

Stores that already exist — including client deployments, not just this one — have no `.bridge_state/projects.json` and no `bridge_project` on any ticket. Without a migration those stores would read every ticket as having an absent project, and there would be no recorded legacy default for the resolver to fall back to, so a store that syncs perfectly today would stop syncing on upgrade.

## Approach

Ship the migration as ensure units on the existing idempotent registry (`src/rebar/_store/ensures.py`, `REGISTRY_IDS` at `:66`, `_registry()` at `:82`), which is rebar's sanctioned seam: `docs/migrations.md:40-56` describes adding a unit, and the ordered School-A ledger is explicitly not built (`docs/migrations.md:14-16`). Units run at init/re-init, `fsck --repair`, and MCP boot (`docs/migrations.md:57-65`), so a client store converges without any operator action.

**The migration writes no ticket events.** A unit emitting an EDIT per ticket would be a four-figure event write under the store write lock on a store this size, and the MCP-boot entry point runs the sweep on a deliberately short lock budget and skips when contended (`docs/migrations.md:63-65`) — so an event-writing migration would silently skip at one of its three entry points and converge unpredictably. Instead the unit records `legacy_default` once in the mapping, and the tri-state resolver treats every ticket with an absent field as belonging to it. One small write migrates the whole store.

Two units, both check-then-act and both safe to re-run:

1. **Seed the mapping.** If `.bridge_state/projects.json` is absent, write it with `legacy_default`
   and a single `projects` entry taken from the backend's configured project
   (`Backend.project`, documented as the effective write/create scope at `_backend.py:610-632`). If
   the record already exists, return `ok` and write nothing. Tree-check before committing so a
   converged store makes zero git commits, as `docs/migrations.md:45-46` requires of commit units.
2. **Stamp the capability.** When — and only when — the mapping holds more than one project, add
   `multi-project-bridge` to `.store-compat.json`'s `required_capabilities`. A single-project store is
   never stamped and stays usable by older binaries.

Ids are new and never reused, per `docs/migrations.md:50-51`.

**Where the unit bodies live.** The existing six units are implemented in `src/rebar/_commands/init.py` (for example `_store_compat_unit` at `:528`) and referenced from `_registry()` (`src/rebar/_store/ensures.py:93`). This story deliberately does **not** follow that placement: at the time of writing `_commands/init.py` measures 799 lines against the repository's hard 800-line module-size gate (`.github/module-size-limit.txt`), so adding two unit bodies there would fail CI on a limit that has no allowlist escape hatch. Because `_registry()` maps an id to any callable, the two new units live in their own `src/rebar/_store/project_ensures.py` and are referenced from `ensures.py` — which is 253 lines and gains only its two registry entries. This keeps the change inside the gate without refactoring an unrelated 799-line module as a precondition.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/_store/project_ensures.py` (new) — both unit bodies
- `src/rebar/_store/ensures.py` — two `REGISTRY_IDS` entries and two `_registry()` mappings
- tests under `tests/`

## Testing

Tier per the shared standard's git row — real temporary git repositories and refs — because the units commit to the `tickets` branch and the zero-commit-when-converged property is only observable against real refs.

- Happy path: sweeping a store with no mapping creates one whose `legacy_default` equals the
  configured backend project, and every existing ticket resolves to it.
- The load-bearing assertion: the sweep writes **zero ticket events**. Assert the store's event count
  and the set of event files are identical before and after — this is what distinguishes this design
  from an EDIT-per-ticket migration.
- Idempotence: a second sweep on a converged store returns `ok` for both units and makes zero new git
  commits (assert the branch tip SHA is unchanged, not merely that no error was raised).
- Conditional stamp, as a contrast pair: a one-project mapping leaves `required_capabilities` empty; a
  two-project mapping adds exactly `multi-project-bridge`. The one-project half proves the stamp is
  genuinely conditional rather than unconditional.
- Failure path: a unit raising is recorded as `failed` and does not abort the sweep or the caller, per
  the registry's skip-and-continue contract.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A store with no mapping gains one whose legacy default is the configured backend project, and
      every pre-existing ticket resolves to it; checked by a real-git test asserting the record and
      the resolution.
- [ ] The sweep writes zero ticket events; checked by asserting the event file set is identical
      before and after.
- [ ] A second sweep returns `ok` for both units and leaves the tickets-branch tip SHA unchanged;
      checked by comparing the SHA across two sweeps.
- [ ] The capability is stamped only when the mapping holds more than one project; checked by a
      paired test over a one-project and a two-project mapping.
- [ ] Both unit ids are registered in `REGISTRY_IDS` and mapped in `_registry()`; checked by the
      existing registry-agreement test, which fails if they disagree.
baseline.summary: Legacy-store migration: ensure units seeding the project mapping without writing ticket events

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem
Split out of `d26a-8ffa-97cd-4b2a` (`dire-expectable-terrapin`), where these were carried as its DEFERRED AC5 and AC6. That bug fixed the key-path DIVERGENCE that made the deployed MCP server sign op-certs it could never verify (Gerrit 2337, merged as `83edf9972728ae1e0729a39098ec70e4fab4617a`): verification now resolves the public half from the same ordered chain the signing side resolves the private half.

What that fix did NOT add is any GUARD. `sign_manifest` still mints a certificate without checking that the environment can resolve a public counterpart for the key it just signed under, and nothing at deploy/startup surfaces it when it cannot. So the CLASS of defect — a silently uncertifiable attestation — can regress the moment a new deployment shape puts the signing key somewhere the resolution chain does not reach. Signing succeeds; only a later `verify_signature` (or a refused claim) reveals the problem, potentially long after the certificates were minted.

## Approach
Two independent, additive guards, neither of which changes an existing success path:

1. At MINT: after `ensure_opcert_key` resolves the SPECIFIC signing key path used for this
   mint, read THAT key's own public line with `_read_opcert_pub(key_path)` and check whether it
   is a MEMBER of the verify-side resolvable set `_opcert_own_public_keys`
   (`src/rebar/_opcert_signing.py`). Matching is on the key TYPE+BASE64 BODY (comment-
   insensitive), mirroring ssh `allowed_signers`. The check is membership of the specific
   signing key's public counterpart, NOT merely the non-emptiness of the aggregate chain — a
   chain where a DIFFERENT key resolves a pub must NOT satisfy the guard for the key actually
   signed under. When the specific key's counterpart is absent, emit an explicit WARNING naming
   the resolved key path and the principal. It must NOT refuse — refusing would break every
   existing sign flow and is a behaviour change beyond this bug's scope.

   Worked example (specification by example). Own-key chain = [binding-key `K_b`, genesis
   `K_g`]. `ensure_opcert_key` selects `K_g` for this mint (binding absent), but only `K_b`'s
   `.pub` is derivable (K_g lives on a path the resolver cannot reach). Aggregate
   `_opcert_own_public_keys` = {body(K_b)} — NON-EMPTY. A non-emptiness check would stay
   SILENT (wrong). The specified membership check computes `body(_read_opcert_pub(path_of
   K_g))` ∉ {body(K_b)} → WARNS (correct), naming `path_of K_g` and the principal.

2. At STARTUP/DEPLOY: the MCP server's existing health surface (`src/rebar/_mcp_health.py`)
   reports a DEGRADED field and logs a boot WARNING when the bound startup signer's public key
   is not the pinned trusted-environment key for its principal — the ONE same-environment
   failure the (derivative) public key cannot otherwise catch. SERVE-DEGRADED, never abort
   boot (operator ruling; ADR 0104 decision 3 makes required-environment binding advisory
   today), mirroring `store_status` / `run_startup_store_sweep`.

Both are in-process checks driven by an operation and by server startup, with no dependency on any particular CI provider.

### AC3 reframing (operator ruling, recorded here)
The op-cert public key is DERIVATIVE (`_derive_opcert_pub` = `ssh-keygen -y`, re-derivable on demand from the private key), and `compose_startup_opcert_binding` already fails closed on a bad/missing/encrypted/non-Ed25519 private key. So a "can we resolve/derive a public cert?" startup probe would be REDUNDANT. The one genuinely non-redundant condition is whether the bound signer's public key MATCHES the environment's pinned/published trusted-environment key (`rebar.attest.trusted_env`) — the key required-environment verify checks against. Even that is non-blocking: those are still valid signed attestations that only fail an advisory environment-binding check, so AC3 emits a degraded health field + a warning and does NOT refuse to serve or abort boot.

## Scope
- In scope: the mint-time warning and the startup/health serve-degraded surface.
- Out of scope: the key-resolution chain itself (already fixed by 2337); any change to the
  cross-environment `foreign_key` verdict, which is documented intended behaviour (ADR 0104),
  not a defect; extending `compose_startup_opcert_binding` to abort; a redundant derive probe.

## Testing
Unit tests: a mint under a key whose SPECIFIC public half cannot be resolved (even when another chain key's pub resolves) emits the warning and still returns a signature; a mint under a resolvable key emits no warning; the startup/health check reports degraded (and warns) for a bound signer whose public key is not the pinned key, and is quiet/non-degraded for a matched key, for an unbound signer, and for a deployment that has not opted into pinning; key matching is on the key type+base64 body (comment-insensitive); a resolution fault is surfaced as degraded (not swallowed); a `RemovedInputError` fails hard.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] AC1: `sign_manifest` emits an explicit WARNING — naming the resolved signing key path and the principal — when the SPECIFIC key it just signed under has no public counterpart in the verify-side resolvable set (`_read_opcert_pub(key_path)` body ∉ `_opcert_own_public_keys`), even if a different chain key's pub resolves; it still returns the signature (no refusal, no existing sign flow broken).
- [x] AC2: `sign_manifest` emits no such warning when the specific signing key's public counterpart IS resolvable.
- [x] AC3: the MCP server's startup/health surface reports a DEGRADED `opcert` field and logs a boot WARNING when the bound signer's public key is not the pinned trusted-environment key for its principal, and is non-degraded/quiet when it matches (or when unbound / pinning not configured). Non-blocking: it NEVER aborts boot (serve-degraded; ADR 0104 decision 3).
- [x] AC4: both guards are in-process and operation-linked, with no dependency on a specific CI provider.

## Definition of Done
- [x] DD1: AC1 and AC2 covered by a test that is RED before the change and GREEN after it, including the specific-key case where a different chain key's pub resolves (aggregate non-empty) yet the signed key's own counterpart is absent.
- [x] DD2: AC3 covered by a test over the startup/health check (degraded, matched, unbound, and not-pinned cases).
- [x] DD3: AC4 verified by the observable proxy that both guards execute with no CI-provider environment present — the unit tests exercise mint and startup/health with no CI env vars set and assert the warning/degraded behaviour purely from in-process log/dict output (no network, no CI API), confirming operation/startup-linked triggers.
baseline.summary: No guard surfaces a signing key with no usable public counterpart: sign_manifest stays silent and startup does not fail

## Context / Problem
Four authoritative-looking doc/comment entry points have drifted from current contracts (audit ae1b). Premises RE-VERIFIED against HEAD 641ba8bed1 — all four still present:
- **Bare `--assignee <handle>` teaches a Jira-UNRESOLVABLE value.** `README.md:44` (`rebar claim "$tid" --assignee alice`) and `README.md:50` (the adjacent library block, `rebar.claim(tid, assignee="alice")`), `docs/user-guide.md:115` (`rebar claim <ticket-id> --assignee alice`), `docs/user-guide.md:234` (`rebar edit <id> --priority=1 --assignee=bob --add-tag=urgent`). Yet `docs/config.md:461-467` documents `ticket.default_assignee` and requires a Jira-resolvable identity — a bare handle is silently cleared by the next reconcile.
- **MCP navigation mis-route**: `docs/README.md:25` routes "Drive rebar over MCP" → `llm-framework.md`, while the complete generated tool reference is `docs/mcp-reference.md` (itself indexed at `docs/README.md:77`).
- **Removed config surface**: `docs/README.md:91` still describes `config.md` as covering the flat `.rebar/config.conf` keys; `docs/config.md:13,519` already record that reader as REMOVED in favour of `rebar.toml` / a `[tool.rebar]` pyproject table.

## Approach
Correct each drifted example/label/comment against the CURRENT contract; no behavior change.

- `docs/README.md:91` → describe `config.md` as `rebar.toml` / `[tool.rebar]` keys, precedence, and design of record.
- `pyproject.toml:488-490` → state that mypy is gated over the whole library and `scripts/`, with `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]` layering the extra `disallow_untyped_defs` ratchet on the promoted packages.

## Scope (docs + one TOML comment only)
- `README.md` — quickstart claim example (44) and the adjacent library example (50).
- `docs/user-guide.md` — claim example (115) and `edit` example (234) + one clause of surrounding prose.
- `docs/README.md` — MCP route (25) and the `config.md` description (91).
- `pyproject.toml` — the `[tool.mypy]` header comment (488-490). No `[tool.mypy]` VALUES change; the ratchet-flip is explicitly out of scope (pyproject.toml is contended, per the epic).

Dropping only the `--assignee alice` argument keeps all four needles and keeps the block runnable (`claim` without `--assignee` is the documented default path), so both stay green. ## Why

A kernel is only reusable if a SECOND gate can plug in without copying, and only honest if reuse
is enforced by mechanisms that don't make the workflow system brittle. This story defines the
consumer SEAM (what a gate plugs in) and the ENFORCEMENT strategy — deliberately enforcing
STRUCTURE mechanically and BEHAVIOR via evals, and explicitly REJECTING a prompt-text lint
(an anti-pattern: mature projects — DSPy, Guardrails, Instructor, promptfoo — enforce typed
contracts + output/behavior, never prompt-string greps). This is the contract `b744` (code
review) builds on.

## What

- **Consumer seam (doc + API):** a kernel doc enumerating the per-gate plug-points — criteria +
  routing, finder prompts, the domain-context assembler, the verify-prompt preamble, and the
  move-catalog — and the kernel's public Pass-2/3/4 entry points. Plan-review is the worked
  reference; `b744` is the named second consumer (this epic `blocks` b744).
- **Soft-rule discoverability:** a canonical verifier-rules SCAFFOLD/snippet (atomicity;
  independence — don't show the finding's own conclusion; allow "insufficient";
  verdict-with-citation-NOT-fix) that a gate's verify-prompt preamble embeds.
- **Behavioral enforcement (NOT a lint):** an eval that asserts the rules are OBEYED — a
  deterministic FakeRunner assertion suite on the gate path (runs in CI) + a small GATED live
  eval kept OFF the blocking CI path (multi-run, lenient threshold). Reuse the existing contract/
  derived-prompt-index drift gate for vocabulary drift. Add NO prompt-marker lint.
- Record the enforcement rationale (structure-mechanical, behavior-via-evals, no text-lint) in the
  doc so consumers don't reach for the rejected mechanism.

## Scope

In scope: the kernel consumer-seam doc + the rules scaffold + the behavioral-eval enforcement
(offline + gated-live) + reusing the contract-drift gate. Out of scope: the pass extractions
themselves (WS1/WS2/WS3, on which this depends), building b744's code-review gate, and any
prompt-marker lint (explicitly rejected). Touches the kernel module's public surface, docs
(a new kernel doc + `reuse-surface.md`), and the eval seam (Inspect-AI / FakeRunner suites).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A kernel doc enumerates the consumer seam (criteria, finder prompts, domain-context
      assembler, verify preamble, move-catalog) + the public Pass-2/3/4 entry points, with
      plan-review as the worked reference; the epic `blocks` b744.
- [ ] A canonical verifier-rules scaffold records the soft rules (atomicity, independence,
      allow-insufficient, verdict-with-citation-not-fix) for a gate's verify preamble to embed.
- [ ] A BEHAVIORAL eval verifies the rules are obeyed: a deterministic FakeRunner suite on the
      gate path runs in CI; a small live eval is GATED and kept off the blocking path (multi-run,
      lenient threshold).
- [ ] Vocabulary/contract drift is caught by the existing contract / derived-prompt-index drift
      gate; NO prompt-marker (text-grep) lint is added, and the rationale is recorded.
- [ ] `make lint` + `make check` + the full test suite pass.
baseline.summary: WS4: Kernel consumer seam + behavior-based enforcement (evals, no prompt-text lint) + docs

## Why
The engine must execute workflows deterministically and survive crashes/concurrency on an event-sourced, auto-pushing store, identically across library/CLI/MCP.

## What
- Thin linear executor (graphlib.static_order) running scripted + agent steps.
- Persist run-state as new WORKFLOW_RUN/WORKFLOW_STEP event types (per-key LWW map), read back
  via replay for the async status tools.
- Idempotency: WORKFLOW_STEP marker committed AFTER the effect; forward-only recovery;
  (run_id, step_id) handed to downstream APIs as their idempotency token.
- Async over MCP: run_workflow returns a run_id; add get_workflow_status / get_workflow_result.

## Scope
- In: executor, run-state events, idempotency, async MCP entrypoints, TTL orphan-tmpdir sweep.
- Out: agent-step internals + snapshot creation/teardown (WS-D); scripted steps (WS-E).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Linear executor; Burr-tripwire CI test scoped to executor.py ONLY (not the package) asserting none of asyncio/concurrent.futures/threading/multiprocessing/retry-libs is imported; carries the written Burr-adoption trigger list; executor state pre-shaped toward an immutable Burr-style State.
- [ ] WORKFLOW_RUN/WORKFLOW_STEP event types wired (KNOWN_EVENT_TYPES, EVENT_TYPES, per-key LWW processor, compaction preserve, replay read-back).
- [ ] Globally-unique run_id; marker-after-effect idempotency; forward-only recovery.
- [ ] now()/uuid4()/random()/live reads captured once and persisted in the WORKFLOW_STEP record for deterministic replay.
- [ ] WS-C owns the TTL orphan-tmpdir sweep (snapshot create + finally-teardown belong to WS-D).

## The gap

`tests/unit/workflow/test_terraform_plan_review_tools.py::test_terraform_call_gets_tools_and_finalizer` hard-requires the OPTIONAL `grounding-terraform` extra (`python-hcl2==8.1.3`) but carries **no `importorskip` guard**. Every CI lane that deliberately installs without that extra therefore fails this test.

This is breaking `main` NOW. Run 33905162633 (test.yml on branch main, sha ee2c54f881d6):

```
FAILED tests/unit/workflow/test_terraform_plan_review_tools.py::test_terraform_call_gets_tools_and_finalizer
AssertionError: assert 'abstain' == 'refuted'
1 failed, 15435 passed, 92 skipped in 415.78s
```

at `test_terraform_plan_review_tools.py:118`:
```
result = lookup("aws_instance.web", module_path="infra")
assert result["evidence"]["outcome"] == "refuted"   # got 'abstain'
```

## Root cause — VERIFIED by controlled experiment

The install step SUCCEEDS; this is not a resolution failure. `src/rebar/grounding/terraform_tools.py::open_session` does `if not available(): pending = "missing_extra"`, and every query then returns a closed ABSTENTION rather than a verdict. `available()` is `_capabilities.is_available("grounding_terraform")`, whose probe is `hcl2`. So without the extra the tool abstains, and the test asserting `refuted` fails.

Experiment in a throwaway worktree at ee2c54f881d6:
- hcl2 absent -> `1 failed, 15 passed`, identical assertion. Reproduced.
- `uv pip install python-hcl2==8.1.3`, NO other change -> `16 passed`. Confirmed.

## Why it appeared now, and why only on some lanes

`6dde7dffe6b2` ("Add optional Terraform structural grounding") added this test module. Its two sibling modules from the SAME commit — `tests/unit/grounding/test_terraform_tools.py` and `test_terraform_index.py` — each carry a module-scope `pytest.importorskip("hcl2")`. This module got none. That inconsistency sat latent.

`c57057f41` ("Enable the grounding-terraform extra") then added `--extra grounding-terraform` to `.github/workflows/_build-and-test.yml` (the gating Verified lane) and `_optionality.yml` — but NOT to `test.yml`. So the gating lane installs the extra and passes, while every `test.yml` sweep lane installs without it (`uv pip install --resolution lowest-direct '.[dev,agents]'` at line 413; `.[dev,reviewbot,ui]` at 320/352/380) and fails.

Confirmed in the same run: `build-and-test / pytest (macos-latest, py3.13)` PASSED with `uv sync --locked ... --extra grounding-terraform` and `+ python-hcl2==8.1.3` in its log, while `sweep (declared lower-bound resolution)` and `sweep (py3.14)` both failed with the byte-identical assertion.

## Regression, not pre-existing — VERIFIED

`sweep (declared lower-bound resolution)` had NEVER failed before this run. Earlier red main-health runs failed on DIFFERENT jobs:
```
33875177644 (09-04 12:54, 1af450654) success — sweep (windows) only
33846424069 (06:55) failure — sweep (windows), sweep (macos, full suite)
33840948374 (05:33) failure — sweep (windows), scanner-integration
33824556786 (01:07) failure — sweep (windows), pytest (ubuntu, py3.13)
33792688019 (09-03 18:48) success — sweep (windows) only
```
Introduced between `1af450654` (green) and `ee2c54f881d6`.

## Approach

Add a **FUNCTION-SCOPE** `pytest.importorskip("hcl2")` immediately before the real-parse query in `test_terraform_call_gets_tools_and_finalizer`, just before the `lookup = next(...)` call around line 117.

**Function scope, not module scope.** This is the only test in the file that needs a real HCL parse; the other 15 exercise routing, the extra-less contract, and read-set freshness. A module-scope guard would over-skip and discard exactly the coverage the lean lanes SHOULD keep — including the tests that verify correct behaviour when the extra is absent, which are the most valuable ones to run on an extra-less lane.

**Guard the test; do NOT widen the sweep lanes' installs.** The lower-bound lane's own header states its contract: "The floorless optional web extras (ui/reviewbot/pricing) are out of scope — their tests self-skip via importorskip". The repo already has the sanctioned TWO-SIDED mechanism (`tests/_extra_guard.py`, bug 599e-77da-29dd-482d): tests guard with `importorskip`, and the gating lane sets `REBAR_REQUIRE_EXTRAS=1` — which DOES install grounding-terraform — so the guard becomes a hard error there if the extra ever silently disappears. That gives skip-on-lean and fail-loudly-on-gating from one mechanism. Adding the extra to every sweep lane would instead make the lean lanes not lean, defeating their purpose.

**No dependency floor should be raised.** `python-hcl2==8.1.3` is an EXACT pin, so there is no floor to fail. Any floor change here would be aimed at the wrong cause.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC1 — `test_terraform_call_gets_tools_and_finalizer` calls `pytest.importorskip("hcl2")`
      before its real-parse query, and the module's other 15 tests still RUN (not skip) without
      the extra installed.
- [ ] AC2 — In an install WITHOUT `grounding-terraform`, `pytest tests/unit/workflow/test_terraform_plan_review_tools.py`
      reports `15 passed, 1 skipped`. Demonstrate with actual output.
- [ ] AC3 — In an install WITH the extra, all 16 tests run and pass. Demonstrate with actual output.
- [ ] AC4 — Under the gating lane's configuration (`REBAR_REQUIRE_EXTRAS=1`), the guard is a HARD
      ERROR rather than a silent skip, so a silently-vanished extra cannot hide as a skip on the
      lane that is supposed to prove it. Verify against `tests/_extra_guard.py`'s existing
      mechanism rather than inventing a second one.

## Non-goals

Not changing `terraform_tools.py`'s abstention behaviour — abstaining without the extra is CORRECT and is what the other 15 tests pin. Not adding `grounding-terraform` to any `test.yml` sweep lane. Not raising any dependency floor. Not touching `sweep (windows)`, which is a separate long-standing failure with its own ticket (`unsuited-locustal-incatern`) blocked on an operator scope decision.

## File impact

`tests/unit/workflow/test_terraform_plan_review_tools.py`
baseline.summary: test_terraform_call_gets_tools_and_finalizer lacks an importorskip guard, so it fails on every CI lane without the optional grounding-terraform extra: main is red across the sweep lanes
