## Context
ADR 0100 makes the immutable route registry and parser factories authoritative for command identity, grammar, and committed help. Twenty-one visible pure-intercept routes support `rebar <command> --help` but remain absent from overview help and fail under `rebar help <command>`. The `identity` child parsers disable their own help actions, so `rebar identity create --help` reaches top-level usage and exits with an error.

## Plan
- Make the help-backed predicate exactly `not route.hidden and not route.retired` in `scripts/gen_cli_help.py`, `src/rebar/_cli/_help_route.py`, `tests/interfaces/contracts/test_help_overview_coverage.py`, and `tests/interfaces/contracts/test_create_help_no_write_b8de.py`. Do not add route metadata.
- Add nonblank parser descriptions to `reconcile.build`, `enrich.build`, `identity.build`, and `certs.build_trusted_env` so route-owned summaries populate overview help.
- Move `_unwrap_usage` and `_collapse_metavars` from `scripts/gen_cli_reference.py` into `scripts/gen_cli_help.py`. Apply usage unwrapping only to intercept routes without explicit parser usage. Apply metavar normalization to intercept option lines before byte normalization. Preserve the explicit multiline `trusted-env` usage.
- Expand the generator census through its public entry point. Do not test the private `_expected` helper. Generate one committed artifact for each newly help-backed route and regenerate `overview.txt`.
- Widen top-level help pre-scan to every live visible route. Keep `_NESTED_INTERCEPTS` exactly `audit`, `config`, `identity`, `llm`, `prompt`, `criteria`, and `workflow` so nonleading child help reaches the owning parser or handler.
- Enable help on the `identity create`, `identity use`, and `identity key` child parsers. Prove that each child returns child usage and exits successfully.
- Keep the explicit `config validate --help` contract because `config validate` is handler-dispatched and has no populated argparse subparser action.
- Keep parser-introspective nested-family coverage for argparse-backed families. Assert that the derived family set matches runtime ownership, then exercise each child-help path. Keep the 42-subprocess all-route contract in the held-out outer oracle.
- Delete `_render_intercept` from `scripts/gen_cli_reference.py`. Make CLI reference generation consume `subcommand_help(route.name)` for every documented route. Update the two legacy expectations in `tests/unit/test_gen_cli_reference.py`.
- Correct comments and docstrings that claim intercept routes lack committed help. The affected paths include `scripts/gen_cli_help.py`, `scripts/gen_cli_reference.py`, `src/rebar/_cli/_help_route.py`, `src/rebar/_cli/__init__.py`, `src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py`, `src/rebar/_cli/_llm_eval_commands.py`, `src/rebar/_cli/_workflow_commands.py`, `src/rebar/_cli/_jira_onboard.py`, `src/rebar/_commands/verify_commit.py`, `src/rebar/_commands/verify_authorship.py`, `tests/interfaces/contracts/test_help_overview_coverage.py`, `tests/interfaces/contracts/test_create_help_no_write_b8de.py`, `tests/interfaces/contracts/test_parser_formatter_pinned.py`, `tests/interfaces/facades/test_central_mount_gate_ad9f.py`, `tests/unit/test_cli_registry_cutover_s6.py`, and `tests/unit/test_gen_cli_reference.py`.
- Update affected expectations in `tests/interfaces/lifecycle/test_plan_review_gate.py` and `tests/interfaces/facades/test_intercept_registry_cutover_s6_heldout.py`.
- Retain `_OVERVIEW_OMIT` as exactly `bridge-fsck` and `bridge-probe`. Retain the test allowlist as exactly `help`, `bridge-fsck`, and `bridge-probe`.
- Keep `tests/interfaces/contracts/test_parser_formatter_pinned.py` scoped away from pure-intercept parsers because generator normalization permits those parsers to retain the standard library formatter.
- Regenerate package help and the CLI reference through their existing generators. The Python 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13 CI cells must pass the help drift check against the same committed bytes.
- Do not add another router, parser, help source, mechanical writing-policy gate, or change to the Markdown-only reduced test policy.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] Every live visible route outside the documented omit set appears exactly once in overview help.
- [x] `rebar help <command>` succeeds for every canonical pure-intercept route returned by the registry.
- [x] The pure-intercept help contract proves that no command handler executes.
- [x] The pure-intercept help contract proves that no ticket store is mounted or created.
- [x] `rebar help <command>` returns the matching committed artifact bytes.
- [x] Top-level `rebar <command> --help` returns the matching committed artifact bytes.
- [x] Every pure-intercept parser factory supplies a nonblank overview description.
- [x] The committed `trusted-env` usage banner preserves separate `add` and `revoke` lines.
- [x] Each CLI-reference pure-intercept syntax block equals the matching committed artifact.
- [x] A repository-wide semantic and string search reports zero `_render_intercept` references.
- [x] All four help-backed census sites use the live-visible predicate.
- [x] The exact overview exemptions remain `help`, `bridge-fsck`, and `bridge-probe`.
- [x] Hidden aliases and retired spellings remain absent from overview discovery.
- [x] `_NESTED_INTERCEPTS` equals `audit`, `config`, `identity`, `llm`, `prompt`, `criteria`, and `workflow`.
- [x] Every parser-introspectable nested family returns child-parser usage for each child.
- [x] `rebar identity create --help`, `rebar identity use --help`, and `rebar identity key --help` return their child usage and exit successfully.
- [x] `rebar config validate --help` reaches `build_validate` and returns validate child help.
- [x] Comments and test docstrings describe committed help ownership accurately.
- [x] The help drift check passes on supported Python versions.
- [x] The CLI-reference drift check passes.
- [x] No competing routing, parser, or help mechanism is introduced.
- [x] No mechanical writing enforcement is introduced.
- [x] The Markdown-only reduced test policy remains unchanged.

## CI gate remediation
- Classify the generated `jira-onboard` artifact and overview entry as compatibility surfaces. ADR 0100 records `jira-onboard` as a compatibility shim with a distinct historical invocation. The approved F12 acceptance criteria require the overview omit set to remain unchanged.
- Register the existing `review_result` schema for `scan-spec`.
- Add JSON schemas for the stable `config` and `sign-review` output contracts.
- Extend the CLI output contract test with offline drivers for `config` and `sign-review`.
- Add a reason-bearing CLI driver exemption map in `tests/interfaces/contracts/test_schema_coverage.py` for `review-code`, `review-plan`, `scan-spec`, and `verify-completion` because they invoke model operations. Wire the map into driver classification, require a nonblank reason for every entry, reject stale entries, and reject overlap with offline drivers. The guard documentation permits explicit exemptions, but the current CLI guard does not implement this facility.
- Correct schema registry comments that depend on intercept routes lacking committed help.
- Document the added schemas in the external output catalog.

## Additional acceptance criteria
- [x] Retained compatibility spellings are categorized without removing them from generated help.
- [x] Every newly discovered output advertiser has a registered schema.
- [x] Offline output advertisers are exercised against their registered schemas.
- [x] Every model-backed driver exemption has a nonblank reason.
- [x] The fixture-store contract test does not invoke model-backed output advertisers.
- [x] The three CI regressions reproduce red before remediation and pass afterward.

# Provision AWS-hosted Gerrit + rebar MCP; lock rebar's GitHub `main` to Gerrit

## Context
We are adopting Gerrit as the gatekeeper for all code merged to rebar's `main`, self-hosted on AWS alongside the rebar MCP server, with GitHub as a downstream read-only mirror (the Go-project topology). This epic stands up that environment and locks the rebar GitHub repo so `main` only advances via commits Gerrit replicates after its submit requirements pass. It is the prerequisite that enables dogfooding the agentic code-review capability on rebar itself.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AWS instance (~8 GB; e.g. t4g.large) provisioned; Gerrit + rebar MCP each containerized; Gerrit heap pinned (~2 GB); reverse proxy on 443; Gerrit HTTP 8080 + SSH 29418.
- [ ] Gerrit rebar project configured: `change.submitWholeTopic=true`; custom `LLM-Review` label; submit requirement = the SINGLE deterministic vote `label:LLM-Review=MAX AND -has:unresolved` (the LLM-Review label is voted by the deterministic pass-3 blocker based on thresholds; there is exactly ONE code-review vote, with no separate human Code-Review or CI Verified votes); `copyCondition` carrying the vote across trivial rebases.
- [ ] Gerrit replication plugin pushes `main` -> GitHub (non-force), authenticated by a dedicated single-repo write **deploy key** as the replication identity (see S5). (Supersedes the earlier 'GitHub App / service account' phrasing: a deploy key is the simpler fit for one repo, and is the sole ruleset bypass actor in S6.)
- [ ] GitHub rebar repo locked: ruleset restricts `main` updates to the replication identity only (block force-push + deletions); repo write limited to that identity; no human/admin bypass.
- [ ] rebar MCP server reachable by Gerrit (stream-events/webhook) and can vote `LLM-Review` via REST.
- [ ] End-to-end proof: a test change is reviewed + submitted in Gerrit and appears on GitHub `main`; a direct GitHub push / PR-merge to `main` is rejected.
- [ ] A single AWS instance hosts Gerrit (NoteDb, no external DB) + the rebar MCP server.
- [ ] rebar's GitHub `main` can only be updated by Gerrit's replication identity; all other pushes / PR-merges / force-pushes are rejected.
- [ ] An `LLM-Review` label + submit requirement are wired to the rebar MCP server, and a change flows end-to-end (push to Gerrit -> review -> submit -> replicate to GitHub).


## Decomposition & resolved design questions (2026-06-28 brainstorm + derisk + peer review)
Decomposed into **9 stories**: S1 (TF base), S2 (Gerrit + review-bot receiver + nginx/TLS), S3
(project/label/submit-req/topic), S4a (bot identity + event plumbing), S4b (receiver review/vote
logic + backfill), S5 (replication), S6-pre (mirror-lock pre-work), S6 (apply mirror lock), S7
(e2e + backup/restore + monitoring). The plan-review gaps on the original ACs are resolved as:
- **IaC tooling + remote state:** Terraform with an S3 backend (`use_lockfile`, TF >= 1.10) + a
  one-time state-bucket bootstrap — S1.
- **Secrets management:** AWS SSM Parameter Store SecureString + a least-privilege instance-role
  policy, pulled to a `chmod 600` `.env` at boot — S1/S2 (scoping reinforced in S4a).
- **rebar MCP is stdio-only -> Gerrit can't reach it:** S2 stands up a thin **webhook->review->vote
  RECEIVER** (a plain HTTP service that IMPORTS the review kernel as a library) behind nginx at
  `/review/`; the stdio MCP is NOT exposed over HTTP (Gerrit POSTs webhooks, not MCP — an MCP HTTP
  transport would reject the webhook). S4a wires the bot identity/plugins/inbound auth; S4b the
  review/vote logic.
- **Gerrit event mechanism:** the `webhooks` plugin (push) + the `events-log` plugin with a
  reconciler poller for backfill — S4a/S4b. (Not SSH stream-events.) NOTE: the `webhooks` plugin
  has NO native HMAC, so inbound auth is a secret-token URL + network ACL (S4a), not a signature.
- **NoteDb persistence + backup:** NoteDb on a dedicated gp3 EBS volume at `/var/gerrit` with
  `prevent_destroy` + DLM daily snapshots (S1) and a non-destructive restore drill (S7); merged
  code is always safe on the GitHub mirror.
- **gate verdict -> `LLM-Review` integer mapping:** the gate's `finalize_verdict` emits
  `PASS`/`BLOCK`/`INDETERMINATE`; the voter maps `PASS`=+MAX, `BLOCK`/`INDETERMINATE`=-1
  (fail-closed), config-driven — S4b.

**AC4 refinement:** the lockdown is a REPO-LEVEL ruleset (navapbc is a `free` org; admin-proof
org-level rulesets need a paid plan). So "no human/admin bypass" means no direct/accidental
pushes + force-push/deletion blocked (proven empirically: an active deploy-key-only ruleset
rejects an admin push); TRUSTED repo admins can deliberately edit/disable the rule — an
explicitly accepted PoC risk. The existing `main-protection` ruleset (PR + status-checks) is
replaced by the mirror lock (S6).

**Peer-review corrections (folded into the children):** (a) S6 uses `terraform-provider-github`
>= 6.8.0's NATIVE DeployKey bypass (the prior `null_resource`/`gh api`/two-phase dance is
dropped); `actor_id:null` is canonical (empirically confirmed). (b) S4 split into S4a/S4b and
reframed to a webhook receiver (not MCP-over-HTTP); inbound auth via secret-URL + ACL (the
plugin has no HMAC); async ACK + idempotency vs `webhooks` retries. (c) S3 copyCondition is
`changekind:NO_CODE_CHANGE` only (dropping `TRIVIAL_REBASE`, which would certify a moved-base
tree). (d) S5 adds a `projects=` single-repo binding (a functional bug otherwise) + a crash-safe
`replication.eventsDirectory`.

## Plan-review remediation notes (recalibrated gate)
- **Rollback / availability (T4):** replacing `main-protection` is reversible — S6 documents a <15-min rollback (ruleset `enforcement=disabled`, restore `main-protection` from the S6-pre snapshot, re-enable PRs/Issues/Actions). Outage posture is the locked **freeze-and-restore** (no break-glass v1): if Gerrit/the receiver/LLM is down, `main` freezes until restored; merged code is always safe on the GitHub mirror.
- **Architecture decisions captured (T5e):** recorded as ADRs in the children — 0007-review-bot-receiver + 0008-secrets-source-ssm (S2), 0009-review-bot-pipe (S4b), 0010-gerrit-github-replication (S5), 0011-github-mirror-lock (S6-pre), 0012-iac-foundations (S1). CLAUDE.md is updated when d251 lands.
- **Integration de-risked up-front, not only at S7 (G5):** the two riskiest seams were validated empirically before build (session_log vivid-mull-need): (a) an active repo-level ruleset with deploy-key-only bypass REJECTS a non-bypass admin push (proven on the real repo, GH013); (b) the DeployKey bypass `actor_id:null` is accepted + canonical; (c) Gerrit 3.14.1 boots on arm64 and the submit-requirement predicate + nginx %2F config validate. S7 remains the full e2e proof, but the high-risk mechanisms are already de-risked.
- **What S4b's "proven pipe" actually reviews (G6 seam):** the d251 receiver casts the `LLM-Review` vote by invoking the EXISTING `rebar.llm.review_code(...)` (single-pass, ships today) — clean->label MAX, issues/error->-1 fail-closed — proving the webhook->review->vote->submit->replicate plumbing. The REAL four-pass code-review gate (criteria/prompts/context via `gate_dispatch.produce_code_review_verdict`) is **b744-WS6**, which swaps into the same seam for the dogfood. d251 proves the pipe; b744 supplies the review depth. (Note: this is CODE review — verdict PASS|BLOCK — not the plan-review gate's `finalize_verdict`.)

## Round-7 remediation
- **Proven-pipe decision rule (G6):** `rebar.llm.review_code()` returns a `review_result` (a `findings` list), NOT a verdict string. The receiver derives a binary decision: **BLOCK if any finding is at/above a configured blocking severity (default critical/high), else PASS** -> PASS->label MAX, BLOCK or error/no-result->-1 (fail-closed); the threshold is config-driven. b744-WS6 will ADD a code-review verdict producer to `gate_dispatch` (planned — e.g. `produce_code_review_verdict` returning a typed `code_review_verdict {verdict: PASS|BLOCK, ...}`); it does NOT exist yet (today `gate_dispatch` exports only `produce_plan_review_verdict` / `produce_completion_verdict`), so until b744 lands the pipe uses `review_code`'s findings + the decision rule above.

## Round-9 remediation
- **Formal d251->b744 seam contract (T5e):** the receiver depends on a stable ADAPTER interface — `code_review_decision(diff_text) -> {decision: PASS|BLOCK}` (name TBD) — NOT on `review_code`/`produce_*` directly. d251 implements the adapter over `review_code()`'s findings (the severity-threshold rule); b744-WS6 reimplements the SAME adapter over its four-pass verdict producer. The swap is drop-in with no receiver change. That interface IS the formal seam.


## Round-11 remediation (2026-06-29 — derisk experiment + coherence)
Derisk evidence: session_log a7e2-381c-6dc6-4d0c (EXPERIMENT 2 — live REST contract against gerrit-review.googlesource.com).

- **Adapter seam reconciled (supersedes Round-9's `diff_text`-only contract — G4 critical):** the
  formal seam is `code_review_decision(diff_text: str, repo_root: Path, ref: str) -> {decision: PASS|BLOCK}`
  (concrete name, module `src/rebar/review_bot/adapter.py` — no longer "TBD"). The adapter passes **`source="local"`** to `review_code()` — the receiver has already cloned the Gerrit change ref into `repo_root`, so `review_code` must read that checkout directly; `attested` mode is WRONG here (it would `git fetch origin` against Gerrit and try to resolve the change ref as an origin branch). The third/fourth
  args are REQUIRED because `review_code()` needs a repo context (`resolve_gate_handle`), which
  `diff_text` alone cannot supply — this is exactly S4b's Round-10 reality, so Round-9 and
  Round-10 are now consistent. **Error/fallback rule co-located with the schema:** any
  error / no-result / unparseable verdict → `decision: BLOCK` (fail-closed → `-1`). The adapter return is `{decision: PASS|BLOCK, message: str, findings: [...]}` — NOT decision-only — so the receiver assembles the Gerrit vote COMMENT uniformly from `message`/`findings`; d251 fills them from `review_code()`'s findings, b744-WS6 from `produce_code_review_verdict`, preserving 'no receiver change' for the comment dimension too. d251-S4b
  (918c) implements the adapter over `review_code()`'s findings + the severity-threshold rule;
  b744-WS6 (4119) reimplements the SAME signature over `produce_code_review_verdict` — drop-in,
  no receiver change. A covering AC for the adapter is added to S4b.
- **Webhook carries NO diff (T3 critical — PROVEN):** the `webhooks`-plugin payload (and the
  change-metadata JSON) carry no diff/patch field; the receiver fetches it via a separate
  authenticated REST call `GET /a/changes/{id}/revisions/{rev}/patch` which returns a
  **base64-encoded** git format-patch (must be base64-decoded), or the JSON
  `/files/{f}/diff` (XSSI-guarded). S4b's Round-9 AC ("fetch diff via Gerrit REST as
  `diff_text=`") is clarified to require the base64 decode. The `events-log` REST backfill
  query (`GET /a/plugins/events-log/events`) was not in the named E1–E5 derisk set but IS an
  S4a AC — flagged for an explicit smoke-check there before S4b's reconciler depends on it. The reconciler is RESUMABLE+IDEMPOTENT via a persisted cursor (last-processed events-log event id) + the per-(change,revision) vote-existence check, so webhook and backfill converge to one vote; FALLBACK if events-log is absent/errors/malformed: log + trip the voter alarm + rely on webhook (degraded), NEVER mark a missed change submittable-but-unreviewed (fail-safe).
- **Outbound READ credential provisioned (G3/G4 critical):** the bot's Gerrit HTTP token
  (S4a, SSM `/rebar/prod/gerrit-bot-token`) is the SAME credential used for both the REST
  `/a/` calls (diff fetch + vote) AND git-over-HTTPS clone of the change ref into `repo_root`.
  S1 scaffolds the param; S4a generates+stores it; documented that its scope covers both. No
  separate SSH deploy key is needed for the receiver's read path — and a per-`(change_id, revision)` SINGLE-FLIGHT lock guards the review+vote critical section so a webhook retry or backfill firing mid-review cannot spawn a second review or cast a conflicting vote against Gerrit's last-write-wins Set Review (receipt-time dedup alone is insufficient; detail on S4b) (the replication deploy key
  in S5 is write-only to GitHub, a different identity).
- **SSM scaffolding completeness (G3 major):** S1's SSM SecureString scaffolding adds
  `/rebar/prod/alert-endpoint` (consumed by S7 `monitoring.tf`) and `/rebar/prod/gerrit-bot-token`
  (consumed by S4a) to the enumerated set, so no downstream `data.aws_ssm_parameter` lookup
  fails on a missing param.
- **IAM-role ownership contract (G4 major):** S1 CREATES the single EC2 instance role; S2 and
  S4a ADD separately-named scoped inline policies (`aws_iam_role_policy` attachments) — they
  never re-declare the role. Documented so two applies can't clobber each other's grants.
- **`gerrit.config` ownership contract (G4 major):** S2 owns the base `gerrit.config`; S3
  patches ONLY the `[change]` section via documented read-modify-write (not a full-file
  overwrite), mirroring S4a's `refs/meta/config` RMW. No story rewrites the whole file.
- **DLM lifecycle-policy ownership (G4 major):** S1 OWNS the DLM service role + the
  `aws_dlm_lifecycle_policy` (retain count=7); S7 only ASSERTS/monitors it (no second DLM
  resource) — resolves the S1/S7 double-management risk.
- **Replication-plugin BSL scope (T1 critical):** the claim that GerritForge's 2025-09-30 BSL
  re-license touches only pull-replication/multi-site (not the core Apache-2.0 `replication`
  push plugin) must be CITED in S5's ADR-0010 against GerritForge's published scope, OR
  reframed as an assumption verified by inspecting the plugin LICENSE in the pinned 3.14.1
  image before S5 builds. S5 AC updated.
- **`terraform plan`-before-`apply` discipline (T10 major):** reaffirmed as a cross-story
  rule, especially for the high-stakes S6 apply that replaces the live `main-protection`
  ruleset; already in S7's runbook AC, now stated at the epic level.
baseline.summary: Provision AWS Gerrit + rebar MCP; lock rebar GitHub main to Gerrit (code-review dogfood prerequisite)

## Why
The contract HOME and the safe authoring substrate. Front-matter carries each prompt's contract; the writer must round-trip without corruption (item-4 requirement), validated by spike E1.

## What
- Define the CLOSED front-matter key set (Prompty spellings): `schema_version, title, description,
  inputs, outputs, execution_mode, category, model, tags, dimension, applies_to, langfuse_prompt,
  default`. Heavy JSON Schemas referenced BY NAME (not inlined). `inputs`/`outputs` are the prompt's
  contract surface (see the epic Terminology note).
- Build the parse-split-rejoin canonical writer over PyYAML in `src/rebar/llm/prompts.py` (extend
  `parse_front_matter`; add `write_front_matter`): split on `---`, canonical key order, unknown-key
  WARN+PRESERVE (appended deterministically), LF + single trailing newline, no BOM, body byte-for-byte,
  idempotent (`wb(wb(x))==wb(x)`). Stamp `schema_version`.
- READ-SIDE version coexistence: when a file's `schema_version` is HIGHER than the running binary
  understands, the reader emits a clear WARNING and skips/refuses THAT prompt gracefully (never renders
  unknown front-matter into the body) — mixed-fleet safety, upgrade-reconcile-hosts-first (like TAG_DELTA).
- Ship `.gitattributes` pinning prompt/index files to `eol=lf`.

## Scope
In: format + reader/writer + version-coexistence + golden tests. Out: migrating the reviewers (S3), resolver (S3).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Canonical writer is idempotent, preserves the body byte-for-byte (incl. no-trailing-NL / CRLF / body-starting-with---), warns+preserves unknown keys, rejects BOM.
- [ ] Golden round-trip tests over fixtures including the three boundary corruptors (port spike E1).
- [ ] A file with a higher `schema_version` than the binary triggers a graceful warn+skip (read-side), tested.
- [ ] `.gitattributes` pins the prompt/index file globs to `eol=lf`.
- [ ] WRITE-side version policy: a writer bumps `schema_version` ONLY when it emits a key the prior version lacked; the documented deploy order is readers-before-writers (the read-side refuse is the safety net, not the primary gate).
baseline.summary: Prompt front-matter format + canonical writer (parse-split-rejoin over PyYAML)

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem
The deployed MCP server mints op-cert signatures it can never verify. Every attestation it produces — the plan-review cert at claim and the completion-verifier cert at close — is permanently uncertifiable on the same box, so `claim` through the deployed server is refused for every ticket.

Observed 2026-08-27 against the LIVE MCP server (`https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/mcp`), signing and then immediately verifying on the same server:

```
sign_manifest {"ticket_id": "ruby-griffinish-goitered", "manifest": ["probe: ..."]}
  -> {"algorithm": "sshsig", "key_id": "9f1c8e42-...", "envelope": "{...}"}   # SUCCEEDS

verify_signature {"ticket_id": "ruby-griffinish-goitered"}
  -> {"verified": false, "verdict": "foreign_key",
      "reason": "this environment has no op-cert public key; it cannot certify any signature"}
```

`claim_gate_check` (`src/rebar/llm/plan_review/attest_gate.py:113-133`) reads a non-`verified` result as "no certified plan-review attestation" and denies the claim. That is the P1.

## Mechanism — sign and verify resolve the key from two DIFFERENT places
This is a path mismatch, not a missing file. The signing and verifying halves do not share a key-resolution chain.

SIGN side — `ensure_opcert_key` (`src/rebar/_opcert_signing.py:155-206`) resolves, in order: the context-local startup binding's process-owned key copy; else `REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH`; else the `<tracker>/.opcert-key` genesis. The deployed server takes the FIRST branch: `compose_startup_opcert_binding` (`src/rebar/mcp_server.py:717-746`) composes a signer from `REBAR_OPCERT_ENV_ID` + `REBAR_IDENTITY_SIGNING_KEY` (`/run/secrets/opcert-ed25519-key`), and `run_mcp` binds it around the serving loop (`src/rebar/_mcp_health.py:325-329`), so every tool call signs under a process-owned copy of the MOUNTED key.

VERIFY side — `_opcert_own_public_key` (`src/rebar/_opcert_signing.py:238-258`) consults NEITHER the binding NOR `REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH`. It reads `<tracker>/.opcert-key.pub`, and its self-healing branch re-derives that `.pub` only from `<tracker>/.opcert-key`. On this box the tracker holds NEITHER file (verified in-container: only `.env-id` and `.ensure-applied`), so the self-heal cannot fire and the function returns `None`. `verify_opcert_record` (`:528-535`) then answers `foreign_key`.

The tracker re-clone (`7be0edb7132d`) is context, not the cause: even with a tracker-local keypair present, it would be a DIFFERENT keypair from the mounted signing key, so verification would still fail (as `mismatch` rather than `foreign_key`). Regenerating tracker-local key material is therefore NOT a fix.

`REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH` is likewise not a fix: it is read only by the SIGN-side `ensure_opcert_key`, which the bound server does not even reach, and the verify-side reader never consults it.

## Impact
rebar mints exactly two op-cert kinds (ADR 0049). On this server both are signed-but-uncertifiable: the claim gate refuses every ticket, and a close records a `completion_signature` that `verify_signature` cannot certify. A project that later enables `verify.require_environment` + `verify.opcert_enforce_since` would find every attestation this server produced rejected. Signing succeeds while verification is structurally impossible, so nothing surfaces the problem when the certificate is minted.

## Reproduction
1. Against the deployed MCP server, call `sign_manifest` on any ticket with a one-item manifest.
2. Observe it succeeds and returns an `sshsig` envelope.
3. Call `verify_signature` on the same ticket.
4. Observe `verdict: "foreign_key"`, reason "this environment has no op-cert public key".

## Fix
Make the verify side resolve the public half from the SAME ordered chain the sign side resolves the private half (binding, then `REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH`, then tracker genesis), deriving the public line in-process from the resolved private key with `ssh-keygen -y`. Deriving — rather than shipping a second secret — is required because the deployment key is bind-mounted READ-ONLY, so no `.pub` cache can be written beside it; the derived text, not a file, is the authority. No new secret, mount, or deploy change.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] [non-codebase] AC1: On the deployed MCP server, a `sign_manifest` immediately followed by `verify_signature` on the same ticket returns `verdict: "certified"`, `verified: true`.
      provenance: environment=deployed rebar MCP server https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/mcp (box i-00880b2c7f13527c5); principal=9f1c8e42-7a3b-4d5e-b6c1-2f0a9d8e7c65; privilege_posture=production-equivalent; instrument=live-call — the defect exists only in the deployed server's own key-resolution environment, so the proof is a live sign-then-verify round trip on that server, which no repository fact can supply.
- [x] AC2: `_opcert_own_public_key`'s successor resolves the public key from the same ordered
  chain as `ensure_opcert_key` — bound startup signer, then `REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH`, then
  `<tracker>/.opcert-key` — deriving the public line in-process from the resolved private key.
  The deployment ships no additional key material.
- [x] AC3: Deriving the public line never requires writing beside the private key: a key whose
  directory is read-only (the bind-mounted secret) still certifies.
- [x] AC4: The unbound tracker-genesis path is unchanged, including its `.pub` cache write, and
  verification still never creates a private key.

AC5 and AC6 (the deferred mint-time WARNING and the deploy/startup health check) are SPLIT OUT to `879b-9bf0-86fd-4a6b` (`weaponless-textile-cutworm`), linked `discovered_from` this bug. They are additive guards against the class regressing, not part of this key-resolution fix, and are out of scope here.

## Definition of Done
- [x] DD1: AC2, AC3 and AC4 covered by a regression test that is RED before the fix and GREEN
  after it — `pytest tests/unit/test_opcert_own_pub_resolution_d26a.py`.
- [x] [non-codebase] DD2: AC1 demonstrated against the deployed MCP server after the change is deployed.
      provenance: environment=deployed rebar MCP server https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/mcp (box i-00880b2c7f13527c5); principal=9f1c8e42-7a3b-4d5e-b6c1-2f0a9d8e7c65; privilege_posture=production-equivalent; instrument=live-call — a post-deploy demonstration is an outside-world event on the running server, not a repository fact.
baseline.summary: Deployed MCP server signs op-certs it cannot verify: the signing key has no public counterpart, so every attestation is foreign_key

## Suspected sibling of 7dea-2f00-db57-4a96 (completion-cache shared-tmp collision)

`src/rebar/llm/plan_review/sizing.py::save_checkpoint` writes `tmp = d / f".tmp-{envelope.digest}.json"` then `tmp.replace(path)`, where `_checkpoint_dir` is `.rebar/cache/plan-review/<ticket_id>` — keyed by ticket only, NOT run-scoped. Two concurrent plan-review workers saving a checkpoint for the SAME (ticket, digest) therefore target the SAME temp file: both write it, both call `tmp.replace(path)`, and the second raises `FileNotFoundError` (the first replace consumed the temp), which the outer `except Exception: return False` swallows — a silently lost checkpoint. This is the exact construct proven in 7dea (shared deterministic temp name + concurrent writers), in a different subsystem.

## Mandatory reproduction before remediation
Mirror 7dea's experiment: drive two concurrent save_checkpoint writers for the same ticket+digest with a barrier forcing both temp writes before either replace; capture each writer's return value, suppressed exceptions, final JSON validity, and orphaned temp files. Include a cross-process case.

## Remediation if reproduced
Same fix shape as 7dea: unique same-directory temp via a stdlib tempfile primitive (tempfile.mkstemp(dir=d, ...)), retain atomic replace onto the shared final <digest>.json, and bounded cleanup of only the writer's own temp on failure. No contract/output change.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] A deterministic two-writer experiment proves or falsifies the collision (thread + cross-process). — PROVEN/REPRODUCED: barrier-forced thread repro lost writer A ({'B': True, 'A': False}); instrumentation caught the losing writer's `tmp.replace()` raising FileNotFoundError (winner consumed the shared `.tmp-<digest>.json` inode); cross-process repro reproduced identically ({'A': 'FileNotFoundError', 'B': 'True'}).
- [x] If reproduced, a RED regression test fails against the shared .tmp-<digest>.json implementation before the fix. — `test_concurrent_save_checkpoint_same_digest_loses_no_writer` was RED ({'A': True, 'B': False}) against the shared-tmp implementation; GREEN after the fix; mutation-checked in an OS sandbox (re-seeding the shared-tmp defect returns it to RED — the test has teeth).
- [x] If reproduced, writers use unique same-directory temp paths and atomically replace the shared final key; concurrent stress leaves one valid record, no partial, no residue. — fix uses `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=d, prefix=f".tmp-{digest}-", suffix=".tmp")` per writer, atomic `Path(tmp).replace(<digest>.json)`, and `Path(tmp).unlink(missing_ok=True)` of only the writer's own temp on failure; replication shows both writers persist ({'A': True, 'B': True}) with no `.tmp` residue.
- [x] If falsified, no production change; close with the falsifying evidence. — N/A: the collision was REPRODUCED, not falsified, so the reproduced-branch criteria above are the operative ones; a production change landed (Gerrit change 2334, commit f135b84d1188).
baseline.summary: plan-review save_checkpoint shares a .tmp-<digest>.json path across concurrent same-ticket writers

baseline.description:
## Defect

`rebar review-plan` crashes on the attestation-persistence path with:

```
TypeError: _with_index_lock_retry() got an unexpected keyword argument 'force_reclaim'
```

(observed exit code 11) when two or more `review-plan` runs race the ticket-index lock concurrently — e.g. several plan reviews launched in parallel. The signing/persist step calls `_with_index_lock_retry(..., force_reclaim=...)` but the retry helper does not accept that keyword, so the attestation write aborts.

## Impact

- The review body completes and `signature.signed` may be reported `true` on stdout, but the
  attestation is **not persisted** to the store — `rebar audit show <id>` shows no signature.
  So stdout `signed=true` is not a reliable indicator of a durable signature under contention.
- Forces plan-review gating to be run strictly serially to avoid the crash; parallel review of
  an epic + its children (the natural batch operation) is unsafe.

## Repro (observed)

1. Launch >=2 `rebar review-plan <id>` runs concurrently against tickets sharing the index lock.
2. One or more crash with the `force_reclaim` TypeError (EXIT=11) on the persist step.

## Suggested fix direction

Reconcile the caller/callee signatures on the index-lock retry path (`_with_index_lock_retry` and the attestation-persist caller in the workflow/orchestrator layer): either add/accept the `force_reclaim` parameter on `_with_index_lock_retry` or stop passing it. Add a regression test that persists an attestation while the index lock is contended.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Concurrent `review-plan` runs contending the index lock persist their attestations
  without raising `TypeError: ... force_reclaim`.
- [ ] `rebar audit show <id>` reflects the persisted signature after a contended review.
- [ ] A regression test exercises the contended-persist path.

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem

Once a store actually syncs more than one tracker project, an older rebar binary reading it is dangerous rather than merely limited: it would fetch only its single configured project, see every other project's bound tickets as having no corresponding remote issue, and create duplicate issues in the wrong project. There is a shipped mechanism for exactly this — `.store-compat.json` with a fail-closed read (`src/rebar/_store/compat.py`) — but `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES` is still an empty frozenset (`compat.py:60`), so no capability has ever been declared through it.

## Approach

Register `multi-project-bridge` in `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES`. That single addition is what makes a binary able to *recognise* the capability; a binary that predates it hits the "required capability this binary does not provide" branch and raises `StoreIncompatibleError`, refusing writes rather than corrupting the store (`docs/migrations.md:158-165`).

This is the expand half of the expand/contract rollout `docs/migrations.md:138-149` describes: teach binaries to read and fail closed **before** anything writes the requirement. Registering the name here is inert on its own — nothing stamps it in this story, so shipping it changes no behaviour for any existing store. The conditional stamp lands separately, which is why the two are ordered rather than combined.

Reads deliberately stay available: the gate is on the write lock only (`docs/migrations.md:174-178`), so `list`/`show`/`search` keep working against a store an old binary may not write, and `fsck` surfaces the condition as a structured `compat_error` without changing its exit code.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/_store/compat.py`
- tests under `tests/`

## Testing

Tier per the shared standard's pure-branch row: an in-process unit test against the real classification function, since the mechanism is entirely a validation branch with no I/O of its own — plus one real-store test for the write-gate, because the gate fires inside lock acquisition and a unit test would not cross that component.

- Happy path: a record declaring `multi-project-bridge` classifies as compatible on a binary that
  registers it.
- Contrast case: a record declaring an unregistered capability name still raises
  `StoreIncompatibleError` — proving the registration widened the known set by exactly one entry and
  did not disable the check.
- Absent-record regression: a store with no `.store-compat.json` still passes through as implicit
  legacy, so pre-feature stores are unaffected.
- Write-gate path: a store whose record declares an unknown capability refuses a write through the
  real lock acquisition, while `list`/`show` against the same store still succeed. The read half is
  the contrast case that proves the gate is scoped to writes.
- Corrupt-record path: a malformed record still raises rather than being treated as absent, which is
  the bypass the gate is designed to prevent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `multi-project-bridge` is in `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES` and a record declaring it classifies as
      compatible; checked by a unit test over the classification function.
- [ ] A record declaring an unregistered capability still raises `StoreIncompatibleError`; checked by
      the paired negative case.
- [ ] A store with no compat record still passes through as implicit legacy; checked by an
      absent-record regression test.
- [ ] A store declaring an unknown capability refuses writes while reads still succeed; checked by a
      real-store test exercising the write lock and a read command against the same store.
- [ ] A corrupt record raises rather than being treated as absent; checked by a malformed-record test.
baseline.summary: Register the multi-project-bridge store-compat capability (expand half)

# The project's authoritative config never got the Bedrock switch — only a per-developer opt-in was shipped

## Context / Problem

Epic 061c was tracked as having THREE permanent production switches: the repo config / local env, the AWS review bot, and the CI external suite. The review bot is now cut over [rebar:eb6e-f43a-e86b-443a] and CI selects a provider through `REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE`. **The repo config half was never done**, so every local gate run on this project still resolves to direct Anthropic.

MEASURED, in a clean worktree at `gerrit/main` with no `REBAR_LLM_*` env set:

    merged [llm] file table keys: (EMPTY)
    model_classes present: False
      frontier -> anthropic:claude-opus-4-8
      standard -> anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6
      trivial  -> anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5

`rebar.toml` IS this project's authoritative config — `src/rebar/config.py` discovers `rebar.toml` then `pyproject.toml`, and `read_reserved_section("llm", root)` reads a top-level `[llm]` table from it. But `rebar.toml`'s only sections are `[verify]`, `[ticket]`, `[mcp]`, `[jira]` and `[identity]`. There is no `[llm]` table, so the built-in class defaults apply and those are unqualified names that infer provider `anthropic`.

**What WAS shipped, and why the tracking drifted.** [rebar:1aa2-37cf-5cdf-48b7] closed legitimately against its own criteria: its Scope allowed "local LLM configuration only (the config file AND/OR documented env for a developer machine)" and it chose the documented-env route — `docs/local-dev-env.md:142-182` tells a developer to `export REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE="/Users/joeoakhart/rebar-wt-provider-seam/.github/llm-providers/bedrock.toml"`, explicitly labelled "opt in", with a documented revert. So 1aa2 is not a false close; the epic-level summary that read it as "repo config / local env — DONE" is what overstated it. Nobody has to opt in, and by default nobody does.

**Why it matters rather than being cosmetic.** The epic's founding premise is that the path rebar develops against is not the path rebar's users run, and that dogfooding closes the gap. A per-developer opt-in that defaults OFF leaves that gap open for the local gates — which are the gates a developer and every coding agent hit constantly. Observed while working eb6e: a local `rebar review-plan` ran on `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6` minutes after the production bot was verified on Bedrock.

## Scope

- `rebar.toml` — add an `[llm.model_classes]` table (the file is the project's authoritative config).
- `docs/local-dev-env.md` — the opt-in section becomes an OPT-OUT section, since the default inverts.
- possibly a pinning test, so the ids cannot drift from `.github/llm-providers/bedrock.toml` (the same
  two-sided pin `tests/unit/test_reviewbot_bedrock_cutover.py` applies to the compose block).

## Approach — and the decision this ticket actually needs

The mechanical change is small; the DECISION is not, and should be made explicitly rather than by committing a default:

* **Precedence makes it safe to try.** `REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE` OUTRANKS the project file, and env
  class slots outrank both, so CI arms that name a provider overlay (the external matrix, prompt-eval)
  are unaffected by a project default. The offline unit lanes make no LLM calls at all.
* **The cost is that every local gate then needs working AWS credentials.** A contributor without
  Bedrock access, or offline, would find their local gates failing where they used to work with an
  Anthropic key. That is a real onboarding regression and is the reason this is a decision, not a
  chore. Mitigation is a documented one-line opt-out (`REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE=…/anthropic.toml`),
  which is the mirror of what is documented today.
* Alternative considered: leave the default as Anthropic and instead make the opt-in loud (a
  `make` target, or a doctor warning). Cheaper, keeps onboarding intact, but does not close the
  dogfooding gap — it only advertises it.

Do NOT set `[llm] model` as a scalar; use `[llm.model_classes]`, or the per-pass frontier/standard split collapses (the same trap [rebar:eb58-e71d-ec90-4b00] deprecated `REBAR_LLM_MODEL` for).

## Testing

- assert that in a clean checkout with no `REBAR_LLM_*` env and no `REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE`, the three
  classes resolve to `bedrock:` ids — i.e. the exact measurement above, inverted. Verify RED by
  removing the table.
- assert the ids are byte-equal to `.github/llm-providers/bedrock.toml`, two-sided, so editing either
  file alone fails.
- assert the documented OPT-OUT works: with `REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE` pointed at the anthropic overlay,
  resolution returns to `anthropic:` — otherwise the escape hatch is unproven.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] the decision is recorded (project default Bedrock vs loud opt-in), with the onboarding cost
      stated, so it is a choice rather than a drift.
- [x] if the default flips: `rebar.toml` carries an `[llm.model_classes]` table whose three ids are
      byte-equal to `.github/llm-providers/bedrock.toml`, pinned two-sided by a test.
- [x] a clean checkout with no LLM env resolves all three classes to `bedrock:` ids — recorded as
      observed output, since the current state was only discovered by measuring rather than reading.
- [x] `docs/local-dev-env.md` documents the OPT-OUT (and no longer presents Bedrock as opt-in), and
      the opt-out is exercised once.
- [x] the epic-level claim that the 'repo config / local env' switch is complete is corrected wherever
      it appears, so the next reader is not misled the way this was discovered.
baseline.summary: Local dev still defaults to Anthropic: rebar.toml has no [llm] table, so the repo-config half of the Bedrock switch was never done

# Land the completion-verifier runaway diagnostic artifacts on main

## Context / Problem
This ticket's own findings — and its ACCEPTANCE clause — cite `docs/experiments/diag-runaway-transcript.md`, `docs/experiments/diag_runaway_transcript.py` and `docs/experiments/diag_runaway_matrix.py` as the durable record of the measurement. Those three files were committed in `556708771e` on the branch `impl-10ae-verifier-ctx`, which is NOT an ancestor of `origin/main`. So on main the cited paths do not exist and a reviewer checking this ticket's evidence concludes the measurement was never produced. The ticket is currently unverifiable against main through no fault of the measurement itself.

## Approach
Land the three artifacts on main, unchanged, as their own change — nothing else from `556708771e` (that commit also carries the 2948 implementation: `completion_banking.py`, the scaled step floor, the read memo, schema and test changes, all of which belong to 2948's own review, not here).

Landing rather than de-citing is the right call on the evidence:
- `docs/experiments/` on main already holds exactly this artifact shape — paired live-diagnostic
  driver + findings write-up (`ed6d_live_recovery.py` + `ed6d-live-recovery.md`,
  `f6fc_live_memo_nudge.py` + `f6fc-live-memo-nudge.md`). These match that established
  convention.
- Both scripts are reusable, not throwaway: they are parameterised over ticket / ref / step
  floors / trial count, and they depend only on surfaces that still exist on main —
  `rebar.llm.pai_tools.{filesystem_tools,grounding_tools,rebar_tools}` and
  `rebar.llm.completion._VERIFY_MIN_STEPS` (`completion.py:84`). The budget-anchoring matrix is
  re-runnable against any future change to the verifier's step floor.
- They are content-free by construction: raw transcripts are written outside the repo and are
  never committed, which is why the findings doc records only aggregates.

`docs/` is outside the `ruff check src tests` / `ruff format --check src tests` lint gate, so the scripts land byte-identical to the reviewed originals (as the existing experiment scripts in that directory already do — they carry `print()` calls for the same reason). `docs/experiments/README.md` indexes only the remediation-plan EXP1..EXP-R11 series and does not list the later live-diagnostic artifacts, so it needs no edit.

## Scope
- `docs/experiments/diag-runaway-transcript.md` (new, from `556708771e`)
- `docs/experiments/diag_runaway_transcript.py` (new, from `556708771e`)
- `docs/experiments/diag_runaway_matrix.py` (new, from `556708771e`)

No source, test, or configuration file changes. Nothing else from `556708771e` is included.

## Testing
No new testable behaviour: this change adds documentation and opt-in, local-only diagnostic drivers that are never imported by the package or executed by CI. The relevant check is that the added files do not perturb the existing gates, which the acceptance criteria below verify directly.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] All three cited paths exist on the change's tree — verified by
      `test -f docs/experiments/diag-runaway-transcript.md -a -f docs/experiments/diag_runaway_transcript.py -a -f docs/experiments/diag_runaway_matrix.py`
      exiting 0.
- [x] [operator-attested] The added files are byte-identical to their `556708771e`
      originals. Git history is not reachable from the verifier's read-only tools, so the
      blob hashes are recorded in a ticket comment. Locally verified by
      `git diff --quiet 556708771e HEAD -- docs/experiments/diag-runaway-transcript.md docs/experiments/diag_runaway_transcript.py docs/experiments/diag_runaway_matrix.py`
      exiting 0.
- [x] The change adds ONLY those three files — verified by
      `test "$(git diff --name-only origin/main HEAD | grep -vc '^docs/experiments/diag')" -eq 0`.
- [x] Both scripts resolve their imports against main — verified by
      `python -c "import ast,sys; [ast.parse(open(p).read()) for p in ('docs/experiments/diag_runaway_transcript.py','docs/experiments/diag_runaway_matrix.py')]"`
      exiting 0 and by `grep -q '_VERIFY_MIN_STEPS' src/rebar/llm/completion.py`.
- [x] `make lint` and `make typecheck` still pass on the change's tree.
- [x] The ticket's own findings comments and this description cite only paths that exist on
      main once the change merges — verified by re-reading the ticket after the merge.
baseline.summary: Instrument + diagnose completion-verifier runaway: measured root cause

## Reproduction Steps

Discovered while validating epic ce0e (xdist parallelization). The live-Jira reconciler E2E `test_delete_permission_probe` flakes on Jira's search-index eventual consistency when the *whole* live group runs (it self-skips in CI, so this only bites a local live run with creds).

- `pytest tests/integration/test_reconcile_live_e2e.py` (all 12, SERIAL, no xdist)
  → `test_delete_permission_probe` FAILS: `AssertionError: created issue REB-NNNN
  never became index-visible` (observed REB-1105 and REB-1107 on two runs).
- `pytest "…::test_delete_permission_probe"` in ISOLATION (serial) → PASSES.

So the failure is load/timing dependent (many live tests hammering the shared test project's index in one run outrun the test's index-visibility poll timeout), NOT caused by xdist — it reproduces with `-n0`. Independent of epic ce0e's change.

## Expected vs Actual

- Expected: the index-visibility wait polls long enough (or backs off) to absorb
  Jira's eventual-consistency lag even when the full live group has just created
  many issues.
- Actual: the fixed poll budget in the visibility helper (`test_reconcile_live_e2e.py:347`)
  times out under group load and the test fails.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] The index-visibility wait in `tests/integration/test_reconcile_live_e2e.py`
  is made robust to group-load lag so the full live group passes reliably.
  DONE via Gerrit 1914 (merged as 09abac969c): a `_fresh_search(client, jql)` helper evicts the
  per-JQL cache entry before delegating, so every poll iteration actually re-queries Jira. Root
  cause was `AcliClient.search_issues` memoizing per-JQL and caching NEGATIVE results forever,
  reducing the 120s poll to a single-shot check. This AC's original parenthetical ("longer/adaptive
  backoff") was misleading: no timeout, budget, or sleep interval was changed, and tuning them
  could not have fixed it.

- [x] A deterministic offline oracle guards the re-query mechanism: a test drives the helper
  against a real `AcliClient` stubbed only at the subprocess seam, and fails if the poll stops
  re-querying. Code-verifiable in `tests/integration/test_reconcile_live_e2e.py` at 09abac969c.

- [x] [operator-attested] Against the live test project, the previously-failing scenario no longer
  reports `never became index-visible`.
  provenance: environment=live Jira Cloud test project (REB) reached via acli; principal=the configured JIRA_USER API-token credential used by the reconciler; privilege_posture=production-equivalent; instrument=live-call — index visibility is a property of the remote Jira search index and cannot be observed from the repository at any commit, so no static or offline check can establish this outcome.
  Evidence: a live run BEFORE the fix reproduced the reported failure exactly (`AssertionError:
  created issue REB-3241 never became index-visible ... in 125.72s` — the full budget burned, as
  the mechanism predicts); AFTER the fix the same live scenario completes in roughly 5-8s.
  LIMITATION recorded honestly: the post-fix live confirmation was ONE run, not the repeated series
  the original wording asked for. Judged sufficient because this same AC was previously certified
  by three clean serial runs later PROVEN to be coincidence — under the cached-negative defect
  those runs passed only when the index happened to converge before the first query. Run-count was
  never the evidence that mattered; the mechanism is, and it is now pinned by the offline oracle
  above.

- [x] No change to CI behavior (these tests still self-skip without live creds).
  DONE: test-only change, no production code touched, `@_requires_live` guard unchanged.
baseline.summary: Live reconciler E2E test_delete_permission_probe flakes on Jira index-visibility under live-group load

baseline.description:
## Problem
The complexity ratchet penalises the improvement it exists to encourage, and it does so in the worst possible way: the local gate passes and CI fails.

`make lint` runs `python scripts/check_complexity_baseline.py --check`. That script states its own contract at `scripts/check_complexity_baseline.py:64`:

> ``stale>0`` alone is an allowed improvement (exit 0)

A `stale` entry is defined at `:61` as "key in baseline with no current diagnostic OR `current_score < ceiling`" — i.e. **the function got simpler**. So `--check` exits 0, and `make lint` is green.

CI disagrees. `tests/unit/test_complexity_baseline.py:123` asserts:

```
assert proc.stdout.strip() == f"active={live} new=0 increased=0 stale=0"
```

`stale=0` exactly. So the moment a change REDUCES the complexity of a function carrying a baseline ceiling, `make lint` passes locally and CI returns `Verified -1`.

## Evidence this is not theoretical
Gerrit change 1928 (`effective-cleansable-gull`, merged) hit exactly this. Its first patchset extracted a cluster out of `_validate_routing_entry`, which sat at its frozen ceiling of 17. Local `make lint` passed. CI failed `test_complexity_baseline.py` on three ubuntu shards. A real failure, correctly not rechecked.

## Why this is worth fixing rather than documenting
The contributor is left without a sanctioned move:

- Reducing complexity in a baselined function fails CI.
- The drain command that would resolve it, `--update-stale`, is maintenance-only. AGENTS.md is
  explicit that `--lock`/`--update-stale` are "maintenance-only, not a contributor's escape hatch".
- So the remaining options are to make the change complexity-NEUTRAL, or not improve the function.

That is what 1928 actually did: it replaced the extraction with an UNCONDITIONAL helper call, which adds zero cyclomatic complexity, leaving the enclosing function's score unchanged. That was a fine outcome for that change — the diff shrank from 305/47 to 267/5 — but it was reached by steering AROUND the ratchet rather than with it. A gate whose existence is justified by reducing complexity should not make reducing complexity the hard path.

The local/CI split compounds it. AGENTS.md already teaches that ambient-tool failures are environment errors rather than repository evidence; here the inverse happens — the local gate says the tree is clean when CI will reject it. That erodes trust in `make lint` as a pre-push check, which is the entire reason it exists.

## NOT a deliberate ratchet-up — checked against the gate's own commit
This project does tighten CI checks over time as normal practice, so the first question is whether the `stale=0` assertion is an intentional tightening. It is not.

Both the script's tolerance and the CI assertion landed in the SAME commit — `8eadb4fbc5` (2026-08-05, "Add shrink-only C901 complexity baseline gate", ticket c9f7-d6df-bce0-4b77). Nothing was ratcheted; they were authored together. And that commit states the intended contract explicitly:

> "The gate fails only on new or increased complexity; **reductions and removed functions are
> reported as stale and allowed.**"

> "Wire --check into make lint so pre-commit and **both CI lanes inherit the wrapper verdict.**"

So the design intent was (a) reductions ARE allowed, and (b) `make lint` and CI return the SAME verdict. The observed behaviour violates both.

The mechanism of the collision: `tests/unit/test_complexity_baseline.py:123` is not the gate. It is a separate BASELINE-TIDINESS test asserting the committed baseline is currently in sync with the tree (`stale=0`). That is a reasonable thing to want on its own. But because a contributor's reduction creates a stale entry, the tidiness test fires on THEIR change — converting "reductions are allowed" into "reductions fail CI" as a side effect nobody chose.

This reframes the remedy. The question is not "should CI be as strict as it is" but "how does a contributor land a legitimate reduction without editing a locked file". The tidiness invariant can be preserved while unblocking that; the two goals are not in conflict once separated.

## Investigation before choosing a remedy
Establish first whether the `stale=0` assertion is enforcing something real. The plausible intent is "the COMMITTED baseline must be exactly in sync with the tree, with no drift" — which is a coherent goal, distinct from the script's general-purpose tolerance. If so, the defect is not the assertion but the MISSING contributor path between the two.

Candidate remedies, to be decided on evidence rather than assumed:
- Make `make lint` match CI (fail on `stale>0`), so the local gate stops giving false assurance.
  Honest, but leaves the contributor with no sanctioned way to land an improvement.
- Give contributors a sanctioned drain for the narrow case where stale entries are caused BY THEIR
  OWN change and every other counter is zero — a strictly-shrinking baseline edit is not the
  escape-hatch risk the maintenance-only rule guards against.
- Have the CI test tolerate `stale>0` when `new=0 increased=0`, and enforce sync separately in a
  maintenance job rather than on the contributor's change.

Whichever is chosen, the local and CI verdicts must agree.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] `make lint` and CI's `test_complexity_baseline.py` return the SAME verdict for a tree in which
      a baselined function's complexity has been REDUCED and no counter other than `stale` is
      non-zero. Proven by a test exercising that exact state, not by inspection.
- [x] A contributor who legitimately reduces the complexity of a baselined function has a documented,
      sanctioned path to land it that does NOT require an administrator override and does NOT
      require making the change artificially complexity-neutral. The path is named in `AGENTS.md`.
- [x] The shrink-only guarantee is preserved: a change that ADDS a baselined symbol or INCREASES a
      score still fails, and no remedy weakens that. Proven by a test.
- [x] `.github/complexity-baseline.json` remains locked against arbitrary contributor edits; any new
      drain path is narrow, and refuses when `new>0` or `increased>0`.
- [x] `AGENTS.md`'s complexity-ratchet paragraph is updated to describe the actual contributor
      workflow, including what to do when a change makes a baselined function simpler.

## Provenance
Filed 2026-08-19 after Gerrit 1928 failed CI on this exact path having passed `make lint`. Both the script's tolerance (`check_complexity_baseline.py:61,64`) and the CI assertion (`tests/unit/test_complexity_baseline.py:123`) were read directly and are quoted above.
baseline.summary: Complexity ratchet: make lint passes on stale>0 but CI requires stale=0, so reducing complexity fails CI

## Problem
On origin/main, a project-supplied CODE-REVIEW criterion's `applies_to` is **stored, never validated, and never read**. The criterion runs on every review regardless of what changed.

Dispatch path, verified end to end on origin/main @ 721cb7d6ac:
1. `src/rebar/llm/workflow/gate_dispatch.py:427-447` — `_activated_code_review_project_criteria(repo_root)`
   filters on exactly two predicates, `criterion_id.startswith("project.")` and `exec != "DET"`.
   It takes no changed-files argument and never reads `applies_to`.
2. `gate_dispatch.py:499` — the result is passed as `project_criteria=` to `CodeReviewBatchRunner`.
   No diff or file context reaches it.
3. `src/rebar/llm/code_review/batch_runner.py:86-87` — appended to `active_criteria` when
   `step_id == ROUND_A`. The only gate is WHICH ROUND, not WHAT CHANGED.
4. The bypass shape: project criteria are appended AFTER `req.criteria` — the set the gate YAML's
   `when:` expressions already resolved — so they structurally sidestep the workflow's membership
   gating.

**The silent-failure variant is the real harm.** `criteria/overlay.py:336` stores the overlay entry verbatim, so `applies_to` survives into `effective_routing()` and is retrievable. But `_validate_routing_entry` (overlay.py:190-291) never checks it — no shape check, no unknown-key rejection — and no code path reads it for a `project.` id. A project can write `"applies_to": ["**/.github/workflows/**"]`, get no error, see it in `effective_routing`, and have it do NOTHING. ADR 0074 makes this worse by documenting `applies_to` as a `criteria_routing.json` knob WITHOUT scoping it to built-in overlay ids, actively inviting the trap.

Confirmed absent (adversarially checked, all negative): `glob_triggered_overlays` (`code_review/registry.py:256-265`) does glob-match `applies_to` but iterates the closed `OVERLAY_IDS` built-in enum, which a `project.` id can never join; `applies_to_globs` (`registry.py:236-240`) reads the PACKAGED `routing_index()`, so an overlay's glob field is invisible to it; `gates/code-review.yaml` `round_a` has 14 hardcoded overlay slots and no project slot, hence no `when:`; `overlay_union` computes only over `OVERLAY_IDS`; `prompts.select_reviewers` glob-matches the reviewer catalog, not criteria routing, and is never called from the gate.

**Asymmetry with plan-review corroborates it.** Plan-review DOES gate project criteria — `plan_review/orchestrator.py:302-306` calls `registry.project_trigger_fires(...)` and `continue`s on False, evaluator at `plan_review/det_gate_rules.py:165-208` (`text_all`, `file_impact_globs`, `file_impact_reason_re`), plus `applies_at` scrutiny at `plan_review/registry.py:450-460`. Both keys ARE validated at load (`criteria/overlay.py:249-291`). This repo's own overlay exercises both. Code-review has no counterpart to either.

## Scope — MINIMAL. Deliberately excludes the config-pointer layer.
Gate project code-review criteria on `applies_to` against the review's changed files:
- `code_review/registry.py` — a helper returning a project criterion's globs from
  `effective_routing(repo_root)` (NOT the packaged index), and a matcher returning True when the
  glob list is EMPTY. Reuse the existing `_glob_match` -> `_engine_support.commit_impact.glob_match`
  that the built-in path already uses.
- `workflow/gate_dispatch.py` — `_activated_code_review_project_criteria` takes
  `changed_files: Sequence[str] = ()` and drops a glob-gated criterion matching none; the call site
  threads `prep.dc.changed_files`, the SAME list the `triggers` step glob-matches, so both trigger
  paths agree.
- `criteria/overlay.py` — add the MISSING shape validation for `applies_to` itself (see AC4).

**Explicitly OUT of scope**, and this is a deliberate reversal of the abandoned change 1919: no `applies_to_config_key` indirection, no new `[code_review] ci_config_globs` config key, no `_config_schema.py` / `_config_sections.py` / `config.py` / `config_surface.json` changes, and no new validator in the SHARED cross-gate criteria layer for a key only code-review reads. Independent review found that layer to be roughly half of 1919's diff and to fix no part of the defect: the portability argument it claimed is already satisfied, because `applies_to` in `.rebar/criteria_routing.json` is declarative JSON owned and edited by the project itself. The config pointer was a second override layer over an already-project-owned field.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] A project code-review criterion with a non-empty `applies_to` is DISPATCHED when a changed
      file matches a glob, and NOT dispatched when none matches — proven by a test driving the real
      dispatch path, RED before the fix.
- [x] A project code-review criterion with an EMPTY or absent `applies_to` remains ALWAYS-ON.
      `project.review-phase-boundaries` — this repo's only activated project code-review criterion,
      which carries `"applies_to": []` — must be provably unaffected.
- [x] Globs resolve through `effective_routing(repo_root)`, never the packaged `routing_index()`,
      and match against the same changed-files list the `triggers` step uses.
- [x] `applies_to` gains SHAPE VALIDATION at overlay load, so a malformed value (a bare string, a
      non-list, a non-string element) fails LOUDLY instead of narrowing to `[]` and silently
      reverting to always-on. This is the ordering 1919 got backwards — it shape-checked its NEW
      config key while leaving the pre-existing silently-ignored key unvalidated.
- [x] No new config key, and no change to `src/rebar/config.py`, `_config_schema.py`,
      `_config_sections.py`, or `tests/golden/config_surface.json`.
- [x] ADR 0074 records two things: that `applies_to` is honoured for project code-review criteria,
      and the SEMANTIC COLLISION on the key — for a BUILT-IN overlay an empty `applies_to` means
      "escalation-only, never glob-fires" (`registry.py:262`), while for a PROJECT criterion it means
      "ungated, always runs". The project meaning is forced (project ids are not in `OVERLAY_IDS`, so
      the base reviewer can never escalate to them, and "empty = never run" would make them dead) —
      but one key with opposite meanings must be documented, not left to be rediscovered.
- [x] `make lint` and `make typecheck` pass; complexity ratchet shows no new or increased entries.

## Provenance
Split from `unaroused-undead-ibisbill` (CLOSED as rejected) and Gerrit change 1919 (ABANDONED) per operator decision 2026-08-19. The criterion that change was built to support is rejected for this project; this defect stands entirely on its own merit and is filed independently. Conditionally approved by the operator subject to independent confirmation, which is recorded above and was performed against origin/main rather than the abandoned change's worktree.
baseline.summary: Project code-review criteria ignore applies_to: stored, unvalidated, never read

`bridge_fsck` reads `prev_snapshot.json` off disk as its offline Jira oracle and uses the **field values**, so narrowing prev to a key-set (A4-2) would silently degrade its drift classification. Fence it first. session_log **1cb6-d553-6565-49b4** (measured facts; do not re-derive).

## Why first
`bridge_fsck.py:306-308` loads the file as `jira_snapshot` and passes `fields=jira_snapshot[key]` into `ObservedJira.PRESENT` at `:344` and `:380`. With `{}` entries, membership still works but every field-based classification degrades. This is an **out-of-band consumer of the file itself**, not of `ctx.prev_snapshot`, so no test that exercises `reconcile_once` would catch it. It reads the **working tree**, so it is unaffected by clone filters.

## Approach
Make the field-dependence explicit: classify on membership where that is sufficient, and where a field value is genuinely required, report the classification as **indeterminate** rather than inferring from an empty dict. Do not silently treat absent fields as absent values.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Against a **key-set** prev fixture (`{jira_key: {}}`), `bridge_fsck` drift classification is
      identical to its classification against the equivalent full-payload fixture for every case that
      does not require a field value, and reports **indeterminate** (never a false drift) for cases
      that do. Tier: **unit** with paired fixtures.
- [ ] Against a full-payload prev, behaviour is byte-identical to today (no regression for the
      pre-A4-2 world). Tier: **unit** golden comparison.
- [ ] `rebar bridge-fsck` exit code and JSON shape are unchanged for both fixtures. Tier: **CLI
      subprocess**.

## Files
`src/rebar/_engine_support/bridge_fsck.py`, tests

Scope: S. No dependencies (independent of A1/A2/A3).

## Context / Problem

Follow-up to the S2 LLM-review advisory on 438a-e1d9-29d3-4081 (patchset 4). During a single outbound reconcile pass, `compute_outbound_mutations` (`src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/outbound_differ.py`) resolves per-project effective config **once per ticket**. The `_effective_*_for` helpers (`_effective_status_map_for`, `_effective_type_map_for`, `_effective_priority_map_for`, `_effective_create_defaults_for`, `_effective_link_map_for`, `_effective_excluded_sync_types_for`) each call `config.effective_*`, which calls `mapping_config.load_mapping_config(root)` → `read_reserved_section("mapping", root)` → `_discover_project_config(root)` — a filesystem stat-walk plus the three-layer overlay resolution — on every call. Over N tickets spanning M distinct projects (M < N) that walk runs ~N times per axis instead of once per distinct project. This is **perf-only**: the result is identical for a given `(project_key, root)` within a pass, so correctness is unaffected.

## Approach

Add a **pass-scoped** memo: a plain `dict` created locally in `compute_outbound_mutations` and threaded (like the existing `mapping`/`repo_root` kwargs) into the per-ticket consumers (`_compute_outbound_select_absent_gets`, `_compute_outbound_create_mutation`, `_compute_outbound_update_mutation`) and the `_effective_*_for` helpers. A single tiny module-level helper `_memoize_effective(cache, axis, project_key, compute)` performs the `(axis, project_key)`-keyed lookup-or-compute; each `_effective_*_for` helper routes its expensive per-project resolution through it via a `compute` closure. For the five helpers that delegate to a single `config.effective_*` call (`_effective_status_map_for`, `_effective_type_map_for`, `_effective_priority_map_for`, `_effective_create_defaults_for`, `_effective_excluded_sync_types_for`) the closure is that call. `_effective_link_map_for` does **not** call a single `config.effective_*`: it inlines `mapping_config.load_mapping_config` + `resolve_for_project` + `validate` + `dict(resolved.link_map)`; there the closure wraps that whole inlined block, so the same filesystem discovery + resolution is memoized per project. Keying on **both** axis and `project_key` keeps every project's map distinct (no cross-project leak). The cache defaults to `None` (memoization disabled) so every existing direct caller and test of the helpers is byte-for-byte unchanged. Because the dict is a local in `compute_outbound_mutations`, it is created fresh each pass — no process-global state, so `[mapping]` re-reads across passes/tests are never stale. To hold complexity flat (McCabe ratchet: no `new>0`/`increased>0`), the memo logic lives in the new small helper rather than as added branches in existing functions; each `_effective_*_for` body gains no new branch.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/outbound_differ.py` — add `_memoize_effective`; add an
  optional `cache` kwarg to the six `_effective_*_for` helpers; create the pass-scoped dict in
  `compute_outbound_mutations` and thread it to the loop's `_effective_excluded_sync_types_for`
  call, to `_compute_outbound_select_absent_gets`, and to the two mutation builders.
- `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/outbound_mutation_builders.py` — add an `effective_cache`
  kwarg to `_compute_outbound_create_mutation` / `_compute_outbound_update_mutation` and pass it
  to their `_effective_*_for` calls.
- `tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/diffing/test_outbound_effective_map_cache_d378.py` — new
  held-out test (below).

No public API, output, or on-disk format changes. Module-size cap (800 LOC) respected: outbound_differ.py is ~728 LOC; the change adds well under the margin. This is a pure in-process CPU/IO-avoidance change with **no** dependency on any specific CI provider or external service (portability: the memoization is a local dict, exercised entirely in-process by the unit test, working identically under any or no CI).

## Testing

New held-out test drives the real `compute_outbound_mutations` entry point:

- **Perf oracle (call-count proxy, not wall-clock):** spy on `config.effective_status_map`
  (delegating to the original) to count invocations. Run the differ over N unbound tickets
  spanning M distinct projects (M < N). Assert the spy is called exactly **M** times (once per
  distinct project per pass), not N. Give it teeth: the pre-memoization behavior is N calls
  (confirmed RED first; reverting the cache re-reddens it).
- **Correctness invariant (output unchanged, per-project):** with distinct per-project
  `[mapping.projects.<KEY>.status_map]` overlays in a discovered `rebar.toml`, assert each
  ticket's emitted mutation reflects **its own** project's overlay and the full set of create
  mutations (count + resolved `_bridge_target_project` stamp) is exactly as expected — proving
  the cache returns the right map per project (a cache keyed without `project_key` would fail
  this) and that memoization does not change observable output.

Assertions target observable behavior only (call count of a public seam + emitted mutations); no wall-clock timing assert.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Within one `compute_outbound_mutations` pass, per-project config discovery
      (`config.effective_status_map`) runs once per distinct project, not once per ticket —
      verified by the new test's call-count spy asserting exactly M calls for N tickets across
      M projects (M < N).
- [x] Emitted mutations are unchanged vs. pre-memoization: each ticket's mutation reflects its
      own project's `[mapping]` overlay and the create-mutation set (count + resolved project
      stamp) matches expected — verified by the new test's correctness assertions.
- [x] The cache is pass-scoped (a local dict in `compute_outbound_mutations`), not a
      process-global — verified by inspection and by the test running multiple passes/fixtures
      without cross-pass config leakage.
- [x] `make lint` (ruff + format-check + module-size gate + complexity ratchet +
      wall-clock-assert gate), `make typecheck`, and the reconciler test suite
      (`python -m pytest tests/unit/rebar_reconciler -q`) all pass; no function's McCabe
      complexity increases and outbound_differ.py stays under the 800 LOC cap.
baseline.summary: Cache effective status map per project per reconcile pass
